Mr. Chairman, I express my appreciation very gladly of much that has been said by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) and of the spirit that animated all he said. He evidently has been anxious to do one thing only, and that is to get to the rights of the question. I am, of course, no authority of my own knowledge on the value of vessels for fighting or for training purposes, and in so far as that is an issue here I would like to see the committee favoured with the report of the best officers of the department, of the best experts in the service of the country, as to what the values of these vessels are that have constituted the nucleus of the naval service of this Dominion; and by that I would be very largely guided. I do not, in all respects, think the hon, member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is an informed critic on that question. Were he a public officer, possibly, with some training, one might give some weight to what he says; but he is a party man, he is a follower of the government; and I do not think, speaking from that position, in view of his lack of acquaintance with naval matters in the military sense, that his judgment is really very dependable.
Is the right hon, gentleman any less a partisan on the other side than I am on this?
Certainly; but I am not affecting to give personal opinions as to the value of these vessels. That is the difference between me and the hon. member.
The hon. gentleman did,the other night.
No, not at all.
Oh, yes.

Not at all. I stated when they were bought; I stated the character of them. I do not know how they are fitted for these things, save to the extent I have been advised. I think it would be fair to the committee if the committee were favoured with th'e opinion of the officers- I do not know who they would be. I have heard Commander Hose mentioned by the minister; Admiral Kingsmill is now out of the service; there may be others. Let us have their opinions. My opinion would be -judged only by what I have been advised; judged only by the information that came to me when they were purchased-that these vessels were admirably adapted for the purpose. But of personal knowledge or expert opinion I have none; I am just in the

position of one who, as the hon. member for Lunenburg says, knows very little about salt water and salt water matters. It is my recollection-and I give it only as my recollection-that this vessel is not one of those of the type which is being scrapped by the Imperial Navy. It may be that the words quoted by the Prime Minister referred to covered this vessel, but I do not think so; it is more likely, I think, they referred to a vessel of the type of one that had been under negotiation, for which subsequently the Aurora was substituted. The Aurora was understood at the time, I know,-and was so represented to us-to be modern in every way, fitted in every way for coast, harbour and river defence, and for training purposes. Let this point be remembered as well: If we are to do any training we ought to have ships fitted to do the training upon. And if the Niobe was a ship of the right class why did the government sell it?
The Tory government did it, not this Government.
Certainly, (because we did not think she was of the right class.
You did not know that.

My hon. friend's style of reasoning may have the effect of exposing his reasoning powers to the committee even if it does not have other effect. We determined the character of our naval service on the advice of the officers of the department, and we decided1 that the Niobe was not useful at all in view of present naval conditions. Consequently we determined to sell her, and did so. They took her back and sold her again. Yet my hon. friend says the Niobe is just the ship for training purposes.
I do not say that.
Well, far better than the Aurora, and still they sold her for $41,000.
I would like to know why? You ought to be able to tell me, it Was your government that did it?

I say she was not a vessel of the requisite type. I have gone far enough to expose the hon. member's strange reasoning; it is certainly not worth pursuing further.
Now I come to the other question, as to the value of the ships for the purposes for which they are intended. Acting on the best advice we could get the late government felt they were. If the present Gov-

Supply-Naval Service
eminent has different advice let it present that advice to the committee; let it present the advice of men who are -at least in the best position to judge of the character of these vessels. In that connection, I only suggest this: We have to decide whether we are to have a naval service or not; we have to decide what our fair portion of the burden of naval defence -is and undertake that portion in a naval service; we ought to -get the -best results we can obtain for our expenditure. We are now at the point of deciding-this is what I emphasized when I spoke first, but really it seems to me it is the whole question we -have to discuss- are we not in the place where it is our duty to establish a modest but a real unit of naval service? Hon. members say we are in difficult financial circumstances. They say we have a great debt, more debt than we had before the war. Very well, that it correct; we have more debt than we had before the war. But are other nations not in the same condition? Is Britain not even more emphatically in that position than we? Is the British debt per capita not two to three times what ours is per capita, and their resources, their natural resources, per capita very much less? Are we not in a position fairly eamparable with Australia? Yes, fairly comparable with Australia, for her debt would run, I think, about three or four per capita to ours- two or three anyway-and New Zealand the same. But we find all these countries maintaining naval services on a scale far transcending ours-yes, -by hundreds of per cent. Then the question comes: Are they doing more than is essential? Is there extravagance in naval construction? Are the -Mother Country and Sister Dominions going anywhere a't all beyond the margin of safety itself? Has any hon. member discussed that point in this committee? I have not heard the point debated by any hon. member opposite. Now, does any hon. member think these countries are -doing too much? What are they -doing? They are striving to maintain a one-power standard as the aggregate naval strength of the British Empire. Now, do we say that is too much? Will even the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), will any hon. member, stand up in this House and say that in his judgment that is too high a standard for the British Empire to set for itself? I do not think any one will.
Such being the case have we a right to say, "Oh, we will do nothing; let the other fellow do it." We have a duty to perform. How would the Prime Minister feel,
sitting before the Prime Ministers of the other Dominions and the Prime Minister of Great Britain, telling about what the debt of Canada i's? When the debts of the other Dominions were shown him to be far greater than ours, and much harder for them to bear, would he not consider the argument closed on that score? If he has any further argument at his disposal to advance in answer I would like to hear it; I personally do not know what it could be. Very well, is it the part of honour, is it the part of manhood, is it just to the sense of honour of the Canadian people, is it fair and right and just to the manhood of our country, to stand up and say "Oh, we will unload ourselves for a while. We will build wharves, we will expend1 money on facilities here and there at home, and we will let you, Australia, you, New Zealand, and you, Great Britain, take care of naval defence"?
It may be all right to economize, undoubtedly it is; but as the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) says:	We must
take care where we apply economy. I would suggest this maxim: That it does not do an individual or a nation great credit to apply economy at the expense of somebody else. Let us economize first at our own expense; let the Government go into any department and make a saving as we of the late government did; let the Government go into any one department and apply the knife there as we did in three departments-and we took the political penalty for our action-and in any one of eight departments they can save more than the additional amount that is necessary for the continuance of the nucleus of the navy that we have.
Of course, if we were an independent people we might stand bravely before the world and say: "We throw down our arms; we have more common sense in these enlightened days than to build instruments of destruction." That would be courage; -most people would call it insane courage, but at least it would be courage. But such is not what we are doing at all. No; we are in effect saying this: "We don't throw down the burden of defence, we just lay it on somebody else; we just expect Tommy Atkins and the Weary Titan to. carry it. We expect our Australian brother and our New Zealand brother to carry it. While we are spending 28 cents".-as we were last year-"to your $2.80 in Australia, we will reduce our 28 cents to 17 cents, and all that even though now we have reached the Stage where we realize the
Supply-Naval Service

aggregate responsibility of the Empire." I cannot understand the course of reasoning which arrives at that conclusion.
An hon. member read some reference to reductions having been effected by New Zealand; I do not know whether he included Australia or not. Is it any wonder when they look over here and see us contributing only a fraction in the matter of handling this naval burden-only a mere fraction of their burden-and they see no reason for it; is it any wonder that they feel like taking that course? They may feel that in this way they will bring the matter to a head. Perhaps it will be brought to an issue. I cannot but think, from what experience of life I have had, that by allowing the Dominion of Canada to pursue this course the Government is ultimately going to drift our nation into a shoal where it will pay a disastrous penalty for playing such a part as this. I never knew a similar course to be pursued by an individual, where that individual did not ultimately reap the bitter reward. The fire in the end came upon his own head. He finally had to pay in shame and in suffering more than he would have paid if he had pursued an honest and an upright course. In what form our penalty will come I do not know, but I cannot conceive that we can successfully play the part recommended by this Government, virtually dissolving the naval service, and relying more and more upon others to do what we know those others must do, and of which we get the advantage, the same as they-we cannot so act and not at some day take our punishment.
1 But if the Government cannot come to that conclusion, then do not make a farce of the whole service. Do not pretend to be training men for the defence of this country in naval service by putting them an hour or so a day, for two or three weeks, in an armoury, or sending them out on a fishing scow or a trawler on the Pacific for two or three weeks to get sick. Do not let it go abroad that we believe such conduct is a naval service. I could not but admire the euphony of the hon. member from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) when he expressed the fear that this would turn out to be no good, and a negligible factor at the end of the year. It will turn out to be a joke; in fact it is an obvious joke to-day. No other nation ever attempted such a thing. If this is all we can do, it is better to do nothing. Let it all go, and let us stand before the world in our true position. This policy simply adds the offense 
of waste to the offensive poltroonery and national mendicancy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member means what he says, why does he not bring'in a motion to that effect?
Because it is not my policy.
I would judge from the tenure of my right hon. friend's argument, that it is based on the assumption that Canada should do her share in Empire defence.
Yes, precisely.
Do I gather from the remarks of the leader of the Opposition that Canada is bound and obligated to the policy of the one power standard?

Canada's obligations are purely bounded by a sense of duty. I believe in the one power standard as a standard for the Empire. I do not believe the Empire dare in the vital interest of all of us go below it. I do not believe many in Canada take any other view, nor did I ever hear anybody in this House subscribe to any other belief, and I am prepared to take the responsibility of endorsing the one power standard, and if the hon. member feels that it is the will of the country that the British Empire go below the one power standard, in my judgment he does not know the will of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked about the suitability of the Aurora for training. I am not going to shield myself behind my officers or anything of that kind. This matter has been discussed and the concensus of opinion is that the Aurora is not by any means the best type of ship for training. In the first place, she is so speedy and narrow that she is loaded down with machinery, and space and draught are sacrificed for speed. The Aurora is 410 feet long and 39 feet wide, a very narrow boat. Her draught is only 13J feet and she would go over the sills of one of the St. Lawrence canals. I think any person, even though not a naval officer, would say that a boat of that size, with a speed of 28 to 30 knots an hour, would not be an ideal boat for training, although training could be done on her. The Niobe, in her class, was a superior boat for training, but I am of opinion that when she was sold recently she was in such a condition that it would have taken almost as much to refit her for training work as it would

Supply-Naval Service
to buy a first or second class new boat of the same size. Now we are all striving to ascertain what is best in this situation, and it is my firm belief that what the Government proposes is superior to what the Government found to be in existence, for the benefit of Canada, and for the performance of her share in the defence of the British Empire when the programme reaches its culmination. The Government is beginning at the bottom, and not at the top. We are starting to train men to be ready for the service, instead of getting the service and then starting to look for the men. It is said that no country in the world would take this attitude. In other words, that they would not have a naval reserve force. The United States has 30,000 of these men now.
Trained in this way?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Thirty thousand trained in the naval service.
They are defined in our act. This then does not provide to really train a naval reserve in the sense that the United States does so?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend asked me to give him the view of the technical officers in the United States. I am going to give it to him. I will show him our authority with regard to this scheme:
A great deal of criticism has been levelled at the policy of developing a naval reserve system. The main arguments have been that with two or three weeks training in a year you cannot make a sailor.
Such an argument confuses the function of the permanent naval officers and men with those of the volunteers.
To produce the highly skilled officers and'men who must necessarily form a large proportion of the complement of modern men-of-war ranging from the battleship to the submarine undoubtedly requires years of training.
Permanent work and study of the problems of defence against the types of vessels and weapons by which the shipping making and leaving our ports and coasts may be attacked, is also essential for a certain number of officers and men in order that the complicated organ-iation of coast and port naval defences may be put into operation in quick time when necessary.
But there are large numbers of officers and men required to carry out defence work afloat which calls for but a small amount of technical training combined with principles of discipline, knowledge of technical terms and orders, which may be acquired by men who are anxious to learn in a very short time.
The essential defence work of minesweeping, patrols, examination service etc. was very largely carried out by all countries in the last war by these "amateur sailors" organized by a nucleus of permanent men, and the story of their work and its value will be undying.
If money spent in such methods of defence were useless one can hardly conceive of Great Britain including in her naval estimates provision for the maintenance of a naval volunteer reserve of 484 officers and 5,000 men

men who are not sailors by profession-in addition to a naval reserve of merchant seamen of 2,029 officers and 9,000 men. The latest information from the United States is that they have a naval volunteer reserve of some 2,000 officers and 30,000 men.
That is just what I am describing as the naval volunteers, and I want hon. members to bear in mind that this is only part of the naval reserve scheme. These are volunteer naval reserves. There are men who need not necessarily be sailors to attend to the work I have outlined here, and surely in modern warfare the laying of mines and mine-sweeping, and all the other similar duties, form the most modern style of defence against any effective attack. In this scheme, the development of which will come later, there is the naval reserve, and this will be composed of seamen who can be given technical training, discipline, gunnery and all that kind of thing, and do not have to acquire the process of seamanship, because the men will be selected when the time comes from seamen themselves. It looks then as if, instead of running away from our duty, the Government have taken the risk of some adverse criticism in arriving at a substantial basis from which a navy of any size can emanate in years to come.
I do not know that I can say any more except in reply to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). I was somewhat worried in regard to the boys in the naval college; but I do not think much stress need be laid on the few months' work that these boys have done at Halifax because they have been started on a career; they have done a few months' work of initial service that will stand them in good stead wherever they go. As I have pointed out already, all those who have graduated through the naval college at Esquimalt are, if they so desire it, in the Royal Navy now, paid, not by the Royal navy, but by Canada, and this Government does not propose to change that system. Therefore, every boy who has graduated up to the present time will be paid during his training overseas. The fact that the situation has been changed in Canada does not decrease that boy's chance of a career in the Royal navy; but at the present moment, no matter what navy we might have had in Canada, no difference

Supply-Naval Service
would have been made in the standing or in the opportunity of the boys who had graduated through the naval college. If any of the officers who have graduated through the naval training college wish to retire, they can retire on a gratuity scheme under the Naval Service Act; but we believe that the young men in the Canadian navy can be absorbed and used in this new scheme.
During the first year, of course, nothing much can be accomplished, and the hon. member for Halifax will probably be right, because we shall have approximately half the year gone under the old expenditure, so that there will be probably three or four hundred thousand dollars left for the reorganization and all that sort of thing.
But I am convinced, from what I have read, from the discussions which I have had with members of the naval staff, that Canada can save quite a large amount of money and yet begin a system that will not lessen our ability to protect ourselves and serve the Empire, but that will, in a few years, prove the foundation for a service that will intensify our ability for service and protection. I say quite plainly that if the cost were the same under the scheme that has existed and under the one now proposed by the Government, I would suggest to Parliament to accept the new scheme, because I believe it gives a broader and wider opportunity for doing the thing that Canada in years to come will probably have to do, and for launching on a permanent naval policy. There is to be an Imperial Conference where all these things will be discussed. I must not forestall any attitude that any member of the Government might take; but these things will be all discussed in a friendly manner, and if I were Prime Minister of Canada with the scheme outlined by the Government, I would not be ashamed to sit in with and face any of the prime ministers of the Empire and say: "This is our policy which, when developed, will give us a medium for performing our whole duty to ourselves and to the British Empire."

The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) made the statement that there were eight departments of the government service where economies could be practised that would amount to more than the present Government proposes to spend and, I think, he said more than the late government spent, on the navy. At all events, he said that the economy would amount to a very large sum of money. I would ask the right hon. gentleman to name

those departments and to tell the committee and the country how those economies can be practised, how those savings can be made. In my judgment, as a member of this House and a citizen of this country, any man who has information of that character and who does not give it to Parliament and the country, is not fulfilling his whole duty. Another question which I have to ask is this. What, in the opinion of the leader of the Opposition, is our share of the one-power standard? I do not know whether he would feel like answering that question or not, but that is information which I should like to have.

I am sure it is the
duty of the leader of the Opposition to inform members on the Government side on matters of policy, and just as far as he can to answer their hunger for information, long unsatisfied in looking around them. In the first place, the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) will, I hope, be more accurate in listening to what I say now than he was in listening to what I said before. What I said before was this, that there were departments in which more could be saved than the Government was saving to-day, more than would be necessary to keep up the necleus of the navy that was kept up. The hon. member wants to know what the departments are and how to effect this saving. Just the way we effected savings in connection with the departments which we took up. For example, in the Printing Bureau alone, not a large department, by any means, nearly $600,000 a year was saved, and that is more than the Government is trying to save this year over the expenditure of last year in the matter of naval defence. In the Post Office Department we effected a still greater saving, and in the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue, still more, by their amalgamation, not by merely nominal amalgamation, keeping all the staff. That is how the saving was effected. An organization was put into these departments to make recommendations that would enable us, through the Civil Service Commission, to effect the saving.
Was that done by reducing the staff?
By reducing the staffs, almost altogether.
When was that done?

That was done during the last two or three years when my hon. friend was back in Prince Edward Island.

Supply-Naval Service
When was the staff increased to enable the late government to make this reduction?
Mostly during the fifteen years preceding 1911. That is when the increases came in that were unnecessary. Certain necessary increases were made during the war.

Thirteen thousand
were replaced by 26,000.

The reorganization
undoubtedly effected very great savings in those departments, and similar savings can be effected in other departments of the Government. A saving can be effected in the Department of Trade and Commerce presided over by my hon. friend (Mr. Robb), in the Department of Public Works, and in the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Building another merchant marine.

But I despair of this
ever being done the way the minister has started out. A considerable saving can be effected even yet in the Department of Railways and Canals, in all the large departments of the Government. That is where the Government has an opportunity of applying its reorganization efforts. We got through with three of them and we effected great reductions, indeed.

The question has been
asked whether or not the responsibility resting upon this country to take part in Empire defence is recognized. Personally, I thought that point was well and clearly established; that this House was unanimous upon the question whether or not we would contribute to Empire defence. But if it is not I think it should be brought out in this debate so that we might know where the members of this House stand on this question, because I do not think we can come to an intelligent conclusion on the subject unless we know where the members of the House stand. The resolution which was adopted by this House in 1909 and which was referred to before in the debate, will be found in volume 2, of Hansard of that year at page 3564. This resolution represents my view as regards the obligation of this country to take part in Imperial defence, and particularly the last two paragraphs of the resolution, which state:
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full symipalthy with the- view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will he found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty cooperation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and honour of the empire.
I understood the Prime Minister himself (Mr. Mackenzie King) to refer to that resolution and to intimate that he endorses the sentiment expressed therein; and if there is any section of this House which does not stand behind that resolution wc* should have an emphatic declaration from each and every hon. member. We should know where we stand on the subject. That resolution says that the House stood for a speedy recognition of the policy mentioned therein. That was in 1909, and very little has been done yet.
Now, several members have asked the question whether or not we have had the opinions of experts as to the policy of the Government this year. I have before me an opinion which is certainly concise and terse, expressed by Vice Admiral Sir Edmund Pears, K.B.E., C.B., R.N., a retired officer of the royal navy. He says:
To reduce the present very small naval force means the killing of the Canadian navy.
That is his opinion with reference to this year's estimates, and it is my own view of the subject. My feeling has been that the reduction which has been proposed recognizes the principle of doing away with the navy; it recognizes the principle of shirking the responsibility of taking any part in empire or national defence. So far as I have been able to observe, the great argument that has been urged against the maintenance of a navy and in favour of the present proposed reduction in the estimates, has been that the present taxation is all that we can stand. Well, I agree, and I think that every one else agrees, that our taxation is practically all that we can stand. But, as has been ably pointed out before, are we not in the same position as all other countries in this respect? Can it be said that to-day the people of Great Britain are suffering less from taxation than we are? Or can it be contended that our duty is any less than that of the Mother Country or any other partner in this Empire of nations? If we recognize the principle that we are a part
Supply-Naval Service

of the Empire-and the fact is so often brought to the front, that we are an integral part of it-then we must recognize our duty as a partner; and if there is a responsibility for the maintenance of a navy for Empire defence we must assume our share of that responsibility, whatever it may be. I am not expressing any opinion as to what our share should be. I do say, however, that, whatever it may be, we should play the part of men and declare without hesitation that we are prepared to do our duty to the fullest extent.
Now, are we suffering in any material sense from the contribution we have been making towards our national defence? Let us compare the positions of Australia and Canada. The comparison has already been made, but I want to place the positions of Australia and Canada before this committee in a slightly different light from that which has been shown heretofore. Australia in 1921-22 had a total expenditure of approximately $275,000,000; our expenditure for the same year was approximately $650,000,000, about two and a half times Australia's. And yet Australia was able to spend, out of that $275,000,000, the sum of $30,000,000 for national defence, while we, on the other hand, were able to find, out of our $650,000,000, a total of only some $15,000,000. The fact is that taxation has nothing to do with this question; our contribution to naval defence is only an infinitesimal part of the total expenditure of the country. There is no country in the world where the expenditure on national defence is such an infinitesimal proportion of the total expenditures as Canada's naval expenditures were last year. If we recognize our duty as a partner in the Empire we must recognize the principle that was laid down by Mr. Lloyd George recently, with reference to the weight he carries in the conferences of nations. He said:
My word in conference is as strong and efficacious as is the muscle represented by the British navy.
If it is a fact that we are a partner in the Empire, can we honestly say that we are doing the right thing in scrapping our navy or even in taking a breathing spell? It seems a rather strange thing that the Liberal party should find it possible, in view of their past attitude towards the naval situation, to repudiate, as this proposed reduction does, their declaration as stated in the resolution to which I have referred. I do not approach this subject in a partisan spirit, and I only refer to

that attitude because I believe this fleet unit which we have now represents exactly the declared policy of the government many years ago, and again affirmed by the Prime Minister last week. If that is the policy of the Government, surely It cannot be considered a waste of money to add another $500,000 so that the navy can be continued in force until we know what is the best course for Canada to adopt.
Some hon. member said: Well, you have offered no concrete proposal as to what we should do. It seems to me a very simple thing to determine upon the course that we should pursue. If we are still a part of this great Empire,-and no one wiu assert the contrary-then it seems to me that a conference of the partners should be able to solve in a comparatively short time the exact policy that it is desirable for this country to adopt. I for one am absolutely prepared to see this country take part in a conference of the components of the Empire; and, further, I am prepared *-and I think the people also are prepared 

to stand behind the policy that such a conference shall lay down. Unless we are prepared to do that, our action must amount to a repudiation of our position as a component part of the Empire.

I have listened to the remarks of my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark) with a great deal of interest, and as one who had the opportunity of sitting in this House in the days when the resolution to which he referred was first discussed, and when his party so valiantly fought against the assertion of the principle contained in that resolution, the changed conditions prompt me to say a word or two in this debate.
The Prime Minister in the early part of this debate declared most emphatically where the Liberal party stand. We stand to-day where we stood in 1909 and 1910- for recognition of the fact that Canada will share in the naval defence of the Empire along the lines of developing our own defence on the sea in conjunction with the British navy. That is where we have stood all through these years; but in 1911 my hon. friend's former leader and associates " sold out " the whole question of the participation of Canada in the naval defence of the Empire to the men in Quebec who declared that they would never take any part in naval defence-men headed by Henri Bourassa, who put his Conservative friends in power in 1911 as the result of that union.

Supply-Naval Service
Let us see what happened after that date when the responsibilities of office were assumed by the Conservative party. At once they absolutely disregarded the resolution to which they gave unanimous assent in 1909. They proposed a contribution of $30,000,000 to the British exchequer instead of carrying out the policy of building up a Canadian navy. Is there a man in this country to-day who in view of the events of the war would undertake to say that Canada would have done wisely in making that present of $30,000,000 to Great Britain? I venture to say that no hon. gentleman who understands the position of matters would support that policy to-day.
We hear of Australia participating in naval defence. Well, what happened in her case? She scorned the idea of a contribution, and whatever share she took in naval defence was based on the principle that she should work out her own problem in her own way. Australia is essentially interested in this question, because she is an island-continent, every foot of her shores is washed by the Pacific ocean, and she is in close proximity to the nations of the East who at all times might menace her security. And New Zealand is situated in exactly the same way. That is the position of those two great dominions.
But when the responsibility of dealing with the situation came upon the Borden government in 1914, what did they do? They proceeded to tie the Niobe up at the wharf, and to scrap whatever existed in the way of naval facilities for defence as created by the Liberal government in 1911. In looking back upon the debate in this House in 1916 I find that at that time there was only one vessel in any position to defend our shores, and that was the small gunboat Canada. We in the Maritime provinces who are not dependent upon time provinces who are not dependent for our knowledge in the matter upon windy orations, know that in the days when German submarines were off our Atlantic coast we had to depend upon the cruisers and torpedo destroyers of the American navy to defend us.
America was not in the war from the beginning.

My hon. friend who comes from an inland pointupthe St. John river probably does not know what happened to the people who live along the shores of Nova Scotia, but I repeat now the assertion, that we were dependent upon
the United States cruisers and torpedo boats for the defence of our coast from attack by German submarines.
You are making a mistake; the United States did not enter the war until 1917.	'	.

I made the statement then, and perhaps I may inform my hon. friend that the then leader of his party undertook to send it to the First Lord of the Admiralty, and that correspondence took place, which perhaps it might be interesting to give to the House in full, as to why certain criticisms were made and certain discussions took place at that time. My hon. friend will allow me to remind him that along the shores of Nova Scotia numerous fishing boats were sunk by German submarines in 1917. Off the port of Halifax, outside of the mine sweepers which are so much despised today, the only active force upon which we depended was the cruisers and torpedo destroyers of the United States navy. That illustrates in a striking way how the leaders of my hon. friend's party discharged their responsibilities in regard to the naval defence of the country. Millions of dollars were thrown away in the construction of vessels of no value whatever in the way of defence and which were sent up and down our coast for no purpose.
That is the history of the policies of the two great parties in so far as our participation in naval defence is concerned. Last year my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) attended the Imperial Conference in London which solemnly decided that action by the dominions and the Mother Country in regard to naval defence should be postponed until another conference was held following the then proposed Disarmament Conference in Washington. The latter conference took place and resulted in an agreement for naval disarmament by all the great naval powers. Therefore the Prime Minister, realizing, as we of the Liberal party do, that with our enormous railway deficits and burdensome taxation, and with the many serious problems facing us, this is not the proper time to decide our naval policy, declared that for the time being we hold by our original policy on this question until after the next Imperial Conference, and that in the meantime we should not spend $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 on a naval service which would be neither an effective defence for Canada nor a contribution of any value to Empire defence.
Supply-Naval Service

I understood my hon. friend to say that the United States previous to 1917 supplied torpedo boats for the protection of our shores. He knows, of course that the United States did not come into the war until April, 1917. I wanted to know if he meant that her vessels protected our shores prior to that time.

After the United States came into the war the situation was this: by arrangement with Great Britain, American torpedo boats and des-stroyers patrolled the coasts of Nova Scotia and of the Maritime provinces generally. They were the vessels which protected our coasts and our fishing vessels and acted very largely as convoys of the steamers which crossed the ocean.
Will my hon. friend inform the committee whether the sailors who manned those destroyers were trained in drill halls, as is proposed here?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member for South Wellington says that men cannot be trained on torpedo boat destroyers.

My hon. friend's friends did not attempt to train any of these fishermen who live down by the sea under their Volunteer Reserve Act, which was on the statute book at that time. In fact, when Hon. Rupert Guinness came from England, supposed to be looking for men to serve in the British navy, my hon. friends sent him into the agricultural counties to find men instead of into Lunenburg and other counties along the Atlantic coast where any number of men could be found who had been trained on the sea. That was the wonderful effort which was made by my hon. friend's friends to create a naval service in this country; so that if my hon. friend wants to know whether or not these men were trained in drill halls, he will have to consult some of the hon. gentlemen who were in Parliament at that time, and whom he supported; probably they will inform him.
In view of the conclusions arrived at by the Imperial Conference; in view of the arrangements in regard to disarmament made at Washington last year, why should we spend millions at this time when there is no necessity for doing so? There is full recognition of the principles, so far as we on this side are concerned, set forth in the resolution which we placed upon the record of Parliament in 1909, principles which were embalmed in the Naval Service Act and in respect to which hon. members now I" Mr. Macdonald.]
of the official Opposition sold us out for the support of the Nationalists. That is where we stand; and as matters develop and the necessity arises, this policy will be carried on. In the meantime, why should we spend any money unnecessarily?

Will the hon. member tell the committee what progress his party had made in October, 1911, when they went out of office? While New Zealand and Australia were building their navy, how much had the Liberal party, of which the hon. member was a supporter, accomplished?

My hon. friend, if he was in the House the other day, heard the statement made in regard to that. He will recall that after the act was passed in 1910, the Government of the day proceeded to call for tenders from all parts of the world for the construction of a certain number of vessels. But when the hon. gentlemen's friends came into office they refused to go on with these tenders; they cancelled the whole business.
Mi'. SUTHERLAND: Did not the hon. gentleman's party leave these tenders pigeon-holed during the whole summer?
WThy did you not let the contracts?

speechtext: Order.

My hon. friend is aware that we arranged for and obtained the Niobe and the Rainbow. In dealing with questions involving millions of dollars it was wise for the government, knowing that they were going to the country, to await the result of the election. No one would have raised a more terrific row than the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) if the government of that day had undertaken to let these contracts in the face of an approaching election.

They did not let them.

Britain also; but what I wanted to find out is this: If we are to have this volunter naval reserve force, is it contemplated by the policy of the Government to have any kind of regular navy at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It depends on what my hon. friend would call a regular navy.

A permanent force, a
small one?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The present arrangement will provide for a destroyer and small vessels on the Pacific, and a like number of vessels of the same type on the Atlantic for training purposes.
Will there be a permanent force on these vessels or will they be taken care of by this volunteer force?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We would require to have on each of these vessels a permanent force. I think the permanent force required to begin with will probably amount to about 300 men, speaking from memory.
I would like to revert to the question of the sale of the Niobe. Why was the New Brunswick Rolling Mills allowed to back out of the contract for the purchase of the Niobe?
I do not want to say that the firm was insolvent. As a matter of fact, if I remember the circumstances rightly, the bank had practically all the assets of that company as security for advances made.

I would like to quote from the discussion which took place on this matter on May 27 last year, when the estimates of the then Minister of Marine were being considered. In reply to a question from Mr. Fripp, of Ottawa, Mr. Bal-lantyne said:
We did make careful inquiries with regard to the standing of the New Brunswick Rolling Mills, and the information was that the financial standing was good.
Then, in another place, Mr. Ballantyne said:
I do not see any reason at all for letting this firm out. They knew whajt they were doing when they tendered for the Niohe and the submarines. We have $20,000 of their money, and we have the Niobe. The firm is financially good and it is the intention of the government to see that they pay for the Niobe and the submarines according to the contract price, $135,000.
If that firm were good financially they should not have been allowed to back out of this contract; if they were not. I would
feel like censuring the former Minister of Marine for awarding a contract to them at all. The former Minister of Marine further stated that he had received an offer last year from an Ottawa firm of $100,000 in cash, for the Niobe alone without the submarines. At least an offer of $88,000 was made but it was not accepted, and the tender was then increased to $100,500. Another firm offered $135,000 for the Niobe and the submarines, but could only pay $20,000 down and were willing to pay $10,000 a month, if I remember aright. Now, if this firm's financial standing was good they should have been compelled to stand by their agreement. If their financial position was not good, their tender should never have been accepted. How long is is since the Niobe and the submarines were bought in the first place.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Niobe was bought in 1910 and the submarines in 1914. The Rolling Mills paid only $25,000; the three ships were purchased by them for $135,000. We got back only the Niobe. I may say that the government entered suit through the Minister of Justice and the company made application for release of the judgment. The Finance Department sent down a man to investigate conditions and he made a report to the Minister of Justice. On the advice of the Justice Department we got all we could, $5,000, and they paid the costs and we got the Niobe back.
The minister says he got $5,000. Was the $20,000 that the New Brunswick Rolling Mills put up as a deposit returned? Did the Government hold that and get $5,000 more?

As I said this afternoon we got $66,000; the sum of $41,000 for the Niobe, and $20,000 from the New Brunswick Rolling Mills first. That made $61,000 and there was also the $5,000 referred to, making $66,000 received altogether.
Did the Government ever issue an execution on the judgment taken out by the previous administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think not. We were advised not to do it because there was nothing to base an execution on.

The usual way to find out is by return of the sheriff's writ. What ground had the Government for compromising the judgment obtained for the full amount? Why did the Government not issue a writ of execution and endeavour to collect the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The situation was that the Government was trying to get all the money it could, and having received the report that it could get nothing on execution, as the bank had all the assets of the New Brunswick Rolling Mills, after full investigation the Government accepted $5,000. Then the Rolling Mills paid the costs and the Government took back the steamer.
The bank might have all the assets assigned to it by way of security, but that would not say that the company was bankrupt by any means. Why did not the Government get out a writ of execution?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not posted on the legal niceties of the matter. Those proceedings would have added more costs without obtaining any results for the Government. An officer was sent down to report to the Government as to what it would likely get if it issued an execution. The report was that the Government would get nothing, if I remember rightly.

Would it not have been a lot cheaper to have had the sheriff make a seizure than to send an officer from Ottawa? A private individual acting in this way certainly would not be acting in his own capacity. The Government did not exhaust its remedies to collect that money.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Would the position not have been this, that if we had gone on with that method of procedure we would not have got the $5,000?
Maybe you would have got a lot more.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not so far as the Justice Department ascertained, and it strikes me we would not have got the Niobe back.

Did they get delivery of the Niobe? The late minister told us they did not deliver the Niobe at all^that they would not give delivery till the purchasers made payment. Can the minister tell me on what date judgment was secured?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: June last, I think.
No, much later.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Perhaps it was. The deputy informs me it was last summer, he thought last June.

I know the late Minister of Marine on the 7th May last told us it was in the hands of the Justice Department, and he expected action to be

taken at once. After the judgment was secured last May or June, why was it allowed to run all summer? The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) criticised the present minister for not issuing a writ. It was in their hands until last December. I think there has been some easy work somewhere. I do not know where to lay the blame, and I am not particular where it lies.
I think the hon. gentleman is very particular.
Indeed, I am not.

Yes, he is very anxious to have it lie to his right, and not across the floor. When his line of thought hurts any one opposite he changes his tune right off. I have never been able to understand the geography of the hon. member. I cannot see why he does not sit with these gentlemen opposite. He would feel much more at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We would like to have him.

The writ was issued some time in the summer, I cannot recall the date, nor can I recall the date when judgment was rendered. I think judgment was taken out pretty late in the fall. At all events these parties were endeavouring all the time to get some settlement, and did their best to get a settlement, but we did not make a settlement. We resisted. However, when the new Government came in they had no trouble in getting a settlement. They did not even issue execution although the judgment was in their favour. An officer of the Finance Department went down there, came back and said the company had made an assignment of its assets, and I suppose the present Government, feeling they would score on the late government more by sacrificing the Niobe, pursued their own course. The sale of the Niobe by auction was about the best method to get the least money they could get. If they had advertised for tenders, as the late government did, and if, in their opinion the offers were not high enough and they had tried again, they would have secured higher bids for this vessel. We would have sold it for a smaller sum if we had taken the first offers by tender, but we went back and got larger offers. The reason we accepted this offer was because it was the largest, and we thought that, with $20,000 down, we were safe. If we had sold to a lower tenderer, even though it was all cash, we would

Supply-Naval Service
have been criticised and told that we should have had $135,000 out of it. It was in the exercise of the government's best judgment to get the largest amount possible and we took that course. To say that the government could not get the Niobe back-well, perhaps, the minister did not know, but the Justice Department would know, that, even though the Niobe were delivered, which I understand it was not, the subject matter of the sale can always be taken in execution. I am not satisfied by any means. I would like to have the report that this financial officer read to the House so that we could see how far he went into the assets of that company. We would like to know just what his report was, to support the statement that the Government were not in the position to realize the sum they desired.

The leader of the
Opposition is an artist. He is trying to lay the blame on this Government for a bad transaction of the late government. That government sold that ship for an amount which seemed rather large, $135,000, and, I think, they only got $20,000 out of the transaction, and accepted promissory notes for the balance. The judgment was delivered later, on the promissory notes. Did the minister collect the notes? He allowed the company to become insolvent, and when this Government had to deal with the matter, and to close it up, it sent experts to ascertain what the conditions were, and they reported that the best way out of it was to take back the Niobe, keep the $20,000 the late government had received, to get another $5,000, and to try to make'the best of the Niobe afterwards. This Government considered the matter very very seriously and: thought that was the best way out of it. That company was far from being a friend of the present government. We thought it was the best way to get out of a bad situation created by the late government.
How would it be for the hon. member to answer my question after he has told us what we all knew?
Nobody asked me a question.
I asked the minister a question and the hon. member undertook to do the answering, but he did not answer.
Not at all. I undertook to place the blame where it belonged.

It looks to me as though neither side was in a position to criticise the other. I think the late administration made a fair deal in a mighty bad proposition, but the present government made a mighty poor deal with a good concern. I would like to know why the loss of $8,000 or $9,000 was necessary. The present government has sold the ship for a very much reduced sum, which means a loss of $8,000 or $9,000 over the first contract price.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The first contract was made at a time when scrap was very much more valuable than at the present time. I think I am safe in saying that the scrap value of the ship would not be over 50 per cent, at the time we were compelled to dispose of it, of the value at the time of the first contract. The value is getting less all the time.

Were
tenders asked for?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Oh, surely. I was
going to correct the impression I left on the mind of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) when he suggested that I should advertise for tenders. We did advertise and sold to the highest bidder.
The hon. member in his first statement said it was sold by auction.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I meant to say by
tender. It was advertised and sold by tender.
How many tenders were received and what were the amounts?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There were three tenders received as follows:
John Simon	 $ 7,000
J. Lipsitz & Co., Chelsea, Mass... 16,600
H. H. Hinteris & Sons,
Philadelphia, Pa.. ..	40,175
We sold for the latter amount, which, under the circumstance, and considering the value of the ship as scrap, I consider a good price.

Notwithstanding the sting which the right hon. leader of the Opposition manages to get into every little fling, I want to give the late Minister of Marine credit for not having accepted the first tenders that were sent in last year. He got one for $20,000, another for $80,000, and another for $88,000. He did not accept any. He called for tenders again. He got one tender for $80,000 and another for

Supply-Naval Service

$88,000. He did not accept them. I think the minister was well advised in not accepting the first tenders. It looked like a cheap price for a vessel that cost over a million. He called for tenders and the party who had tendered for $88,000 put in a tender for $100,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That was for the three boats, I think.

But the point I am making is that these people kept tendering higher and higher when these tenders were not accepted. A. Garson & Co., St. John, offered $110,000 and the New Brunswick Rolling Mills offered $135,000, which they did not get. If our marine vessels are going to run down in value at this rate,^ it does not look encouraging for this Parliament to vote money to provide ships for anything more than is absolutely necessary at the present time. I want^ to commend the minister for not putting into commission all the ships which he had. I think the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) spoke this afternoon in regard to how fast vessels deteriorate in value when they are not in use.
That was the whole trouble with the Niobe.
I do not know whether those vessels were in use all the time, but it looks like very fast deterioration in value for a vessel to come down from $1,000,000 to $41,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On one occasion they were bought as ships to he used in commission. In this case they were sold merely for the value that could be got out of them . as scrap. They are not being used in commission at all.
Was the Niobe a new vessel in 1910?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. She was an old vessel in 1910. She was purchased by the then government for a training ship.
It strikes me that the reason why the Niobe was tied up was that she met with an accident on the shores of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand she was repaired after that accident, and was in commission afterwards.

I understand that the settlement was made on the report of an officer of either the Justice Department or the Finance Department. Surely, it would be

proper for us to have that report before this estimate is passed. Is there any reason why we should not have it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a matter altogether with the Justice Department. That was a question that was handed to the Justice Department before this Government came into office, and on the advice of that department after it had all the information, we made the settlement.

That would not be a reason for withholding this information from the committee. An officer was sent down to see whether or not this judgment could be realized. The ordinary course would have been to have awaited the issue of an execution by the sheriff, and that may have been done; but I understand the settlement was made on the advice of an officer of the Justice Department. We ought to have a report from that officer, whether he was from the Justice Department or this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not see what advantage is to be gained by bringing down that report, because the matter has been settled and we have the money. I have given every detail; in fact my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) has (given more details than I have. Acting in the capacity of minister in charge, I advised the Justice Department that we were satisfied, and I thought that was the best settlement that could be made. I submit that it was a good settlement, considering the price of scrap at that time. Had the settlement been delayed for five or six weeks or two months, we would not have secured as good a price, as scrap was going down rapidly in value. The hon. member will remember that nations the world over are busy scrapping ships, and the price will soon be at rock bottom.
The settlement was made on information which the minister received from somebody, and surely it is reasonable for us to have the report before dealing with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The ship has been sold. Of course, if my hon. friend takes the ground that he would not care to decide as regards our naval policy until he finds out what that report says, he has a perfect right to take that attitude; but the Niobe was sold, and the money is in the hands of the Receiver General. The Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) is 'here, and I will ask him to send over to his department if he has that report handy, but it seems to me it has a very remote connection with the question before the committee.

I got the information from the minister himself, and if it has no connection, I do not know why it was given. I am not seeking to criticize; I am only endeavouring to find out the reason for the minister doing what he did.

It seems to me generally
agreed that this matter of naval expenditure in Canada is one of the most important subjects to which we give attention; and since there seems to be a disposition in some quarters to believe that those who sit in this corner of the House are necessarily opposed to all naval and military expenditures, I should like to state briefly my views on this subject in general. First, I would wish most emphatically to dissociate myself from any policy that might follow from sentiments expiessed by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). While we all look forward to the coming of the time when men's swords will be beaten into ploughshares, yet at the present time we must come down to solid facts, and just as long as we need policemen on our streets, I am afraid human nature will be such that we shall require some military and naval defence. As soon, of course, as we are able to get rid of policemen on our streets, we shall probably get rid of all military and naval expenditure. This question has concerned the people of Canada for a number of years, and I have no hesitation in saying that the views that I have held in the past have been to the effect that Canada shoulc assume her fair share of the responsibility that ought to rest upon her as one of the nations of the world.
The time was when we considered this from the standpoint of our duty to the Empire. We may not consider it from that standpoint to-day; but I should like to consider it from the standpoint of what part Canada, as one of the community of civilized nations, should bear in assuming the burdens of the world. The position in which we stand to-day is that our real status is not, perhaps, very clearly defined, and until such time comes I think we might very well adopt what might be termed a "marking-time" policy. The present is not a time certainly to enter upon any agressive military or naval policy. The present condition of affairs in regard to naval expenditures generally is such that no person knows what an up-to-date battleship is. No person, in view of the advances that have been made in aircraft and in other directions, knows just what service the most modern battleship can render or how long it will remain modern. Therefore, it seems to me that, in view of the present financial position of the country and other conditions, we might very well adopt what might be properly spoken of, although the Government has not named it such, as a "markingtime" policy.
There are, in the proposition of the Government certain things that have made some appeal to me. I do not propose to express any opinion on the technicalities of naval affairs; like many other hon. gentlemen, I know absolutely nothing about them. I accept the general proposition, however, that we have had navies in the past, and probably for some time we shall have navies; but just what navy we shall require, or what Canada's share of this world's responsibility is, we are not in a position at the present time to determine. Whatever the future may lay upon us, for my part, I would prefer that we, as a self-respecting people, should be willing to bear our fair share of what we might speak of, if we like, as the white man's burden.
One thing is the suggestion of the minister made some appeal to me, although I am not in a position to criticize the merits or demerits of one policy or another, and that was the establishment of a volunteer reserve. That is a policy that was advocated for many years by that good old newspaper, the Montreal Witness, a paper that, I think, perhaps, has done more to mould my thinking along public and economic lines than anything else in this Dominion. The suggestion was made again and again that we might pursue a naval policy that would secure the establishment of a naval reserve along the coasts of the Maritime provinces. Now, some criticisms are made in this regard that have no point at all. It is argued, for instance, that a few weeks' training given to men from the country must necessarily be entirely inadequate. Well, I agree that it would undoubtedly be inadequate if given to men from the prairies or from the constituency of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), which also happens to be the county in which I myself was born. But the matter has been very well placed before the committee by the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) ; and while I cannot agree with all that that hon. gentlemen says in the House, yet I think he did em-
Supply-Naval Service

phasize a good point, that there were thousands of men in his own constituency-
At least ten thousand.

who were already initiated in the elements of sea-faring life. I readily understand that while a short term of training would be absolutely wasted upon men from the interior of the country who do not know the first thing about the elements of sea life, men who have been accustomed all their lives to the sea and are already welll instructed in the rudiments of a seaman's education, would quickly respond to a few weeks' training in the technicalities. So that while I would not undertake to pronounce an opinion as to the merits of one policy or another, or as regards the technicalities of the subject, and while I would not offer any view on the question as to whether a certain amount of good could be achieved by the expenditure of a certain amount of money, at the same time it does seem to me that this particular feature of the policy enunciated by the minister (Mr. Graham) might very well commend itself to us. And in view of all the considerations, among the most important of which is our present financial situation, in view of the fact that we are already oppressively burdened and that the men who passed through the late war have a tremendous claim upon us which we can hardly meet, this is an opportune time to pursue what I have referred to as a marking time policy, provided we are heading in the right direction; and for the present, having regard to the unsettled condition of naval matters in general, I think we might well adopt some such policy as has been recommended to us by the Government. For my part I have no hesitation in supporting the policy that has been submitted to Parliament.

While I cannot express surprise at the conclusion of the hon. member, I must make some comment on the reasoning by which he arrives at it. He states that this is an opportune time to adopt a marking time policy. He has well described the policy he purposes supporting. The reasons he gives are these: First of all, our status within the empire is not clearly defined as yet; consequently mark time in the matter of assistance in naval defence. Secondly, we do not know how long it will be before a modern battleship is obsolete; that is to say, how long it will be of actual service; consequently mark time in naval defence. Thirdly, we have a heavy bur-

den, and therefore so long as we are marking time in the right direction he is satisfied to do very little. Now, let us examine the last first. Surely it occurred to the hon. member that we are walking in exactly the opposite direction to the one he assumes we are pursuing. We are not walking forward at all; we are going backwards. If there was anything to be complained of in what we have been doing, it has been that we have not been doing our share; our contribution has been much below our share. There were special reasons for that, none like those my hon. friend advances, but reasons of a very practical character. We did not know whether or not there would be armaments to any extent at all necessary. Now we are informed on that point, and we are going in precisely the opposite direction to what the hon. member says we ought to go. Consequently he will vote for such a policy. But he states that we are hard pressed for money, and because we are we must not undertake now to bear our fair share of the white man's burden. Well, are not the rest of the white men pretty hard pressed for money, and have they not their burdens to bear? Every thousand dollars we throw off we simply throw on to someone else.
No.

Is not that so? Any hon. member who denies that statement becomes sponsor for the theory that the British Empire, in undertaking to maintain an equality with every other power, has assumed more than she ought to. Unless he is prepared to back that up there is no logic in his position whatsoever. So much for the last reason. What is the first? It is this: We do not know our exact status. I have not the least doubt as to my hon. friend's sincerity in advancing that position, but let me tell him this. I think our status is just as clear as it ever was or is ever likely to be. The status of a nation within the empire, yea, the status of a nation in the world, is a matter of evolution, a matter of growth; and the more you attempt to fix it within the terms of a definition, the more harm you do the status. Our status to-day is on a solid footing; it has been established by our history, by our record, by our achievements. Men establish their status in the world in that way, and so do nations. There is no dispute about our status; no contention of ours as regards the rights of Canada is met with a negative by the British government or the British people. There

Supply-Naval Service
is no controversy whatever as regards the relations between us and the empire as a whole, and consequently we cannot advance any argument in that direction, and that excuse for marking time is gone. Indeed, it never existed.
Now, the hon. member's second reason is this: We do not know how long a battleship is going to remain modern. I admit that, and I ask the hon. member if he expects that we ever shall. Does he think that twenty years from now the most advanced type of battleship will be any more certain of remaining in the first class than any other ship? If Britain accepted the theory of my hon. friend and acted upon it, then she would cease to have any muscle at all on the sea,- and Britain's representatives in the conferences of the world might just as well be the representatives of Uraguay or of some island in the Pacific. The words of the Prime Minister of Great Britain are as true as human lips ever uttered. His voice in world's conferences and among the powers of the world counts for as much as the muscle behind it as represented in the British navy. We may deplore that fact, we may weep over it, we may lament it; but it is true, and those words would be supported, endorsed, affirmed by every prime minister, I venture to say, of any power in the world to-day. So I repeat that if Britain followed the theory suggested by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) there would be no arm of defence at all. And are we or are we not interested in the arm of defence of the Empire? If we are not, very well; let us stand out on our own feet. That is the logical manly thing to do for those who hold these premises. I do not hold them; I say we are interested; we are interested because of the traditions of this country, because of the sentiments and the feelings of the people of this country; we are interested as well because of the tremendous economic advantage it is to this country to join the rest of the empire in matters of defence, thereby lowering the burden on each. That is the plan we are following. But that plan will fail, and collapse sooner or later-probably sooner [DOT]-if other parts of the empire pursue the course which we, under the leadership of this. Government, now propose to take.
Before I conclude I wish to deal with one other point which the minister (Mr. Graham) mentioned shortly before six o'clock. I was asking that he read to the House some expert authority, preferably
in his own department, if he has it, but an expert authority within the empire, to the effect that he is actually going to get practical results by training men the way he proposes. He read some memorandum, but he did not give us the author of it. That memorandum did not go to the extent that the hon. minister seems to think. True, it did speak in favour of a volunteer naval reserve. That is all right; we have always stood for a volunteer naval reserve. I think it is section 19 of our Naval Service Act that provides for such a reserve. But I assert that no country has ever attempted to produce a volunteer naval reserve or any other kind of reserve by this process. It is the process of education and development that I complain of. I understand that something of the kind, not like the hon. minister says, but bearing a faint resemblance to it, was attempted by Newfoundland. I venture to say, however, that the United States do not produce their naval reserve by training men a few hours a day for two or three weeks in trawlers, or by putting them on trawlers to patrol pelagic waters; you cannot produce a naval reserve in that way. I am quite prepared to admit that boys, such as those described by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) will learn more readily and probably more perfectly the ways of the sea and the technique of naval training than will inland boys, but to say that they are getting anything whatever of the technique that comes from the five or seven years special concentrated training that men must have to be of any value at all on a naval ship under war conditions is, I venture to suggest, to contradict the plain dictates of commonsense. It could not be done, no matter how assiduously the minister might address himself to the task. Experience shows that it cannot be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I never said it could be done.

Then when he is
through, what has he got in the event of trouble? He has good material, we will assume that the men must have the technical training to be of any value at all on active service. These men will have merely the atmosphere of naval life, but they will not have the requisite technical training. How are you going to give them that training? After all, that is what naval service is for. You could do that to a very useful extent under the modest
