expenditure that was made before. That is to say, to the extent that you get the boys in, to that extent you make them really valuable in the event of trouble as trained naval men; but the course proposed by the minister does not get him anywhere, the only result is to get rid of the money, and I do not think it is good policy to be prepared to spend money so long as we are quite certain that in our expenditure we do not contribute anything effective to naval defence at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My right hon. friend does not mean, of course, to misconstrue what I said, but I confess that I do not see how he could misunderstand it. It was pointed out in the memorandum I read that Great Britain had thousands of what have been referred to in the course of this debate as "amateur sailors," men engaged on trawlers doing work which I described, such as mine-sweeping and mine-laying, work which is absolutely necessary. During the war these men made a name for themselves that will never be forgotten. They did not need the intensive training as sailors that the ordinary naval seaman needs; they are engaged in coast and harbour protection. The officer who gave me that memorandum described what their duties were, and he pointed out that such argument as that used by my right hon. friend now was beclouding the issue, mixing up the work of what might foe called a naval reserve force consisting of trained seamen with the work of these other men.

Will the minister permit me two questions? Will he say that Great Britain trained those men to be useful in that way by the process he advocates here, that is, by two or three weeks' training annually, partly on land and partly afloat? And will he say that those men, except in co-operation with the rest of the navy, would be of any value at all under war conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They would be absolutely of value unless my technical officers are all wrong. So far as my information goes, thousands of these so-called "amateur sailors" performed the duties to which I alluded, and they were seamen only by partial training.
Not like this training.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But my hon. friend does not know.
Will the minister say it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
asked me this afternoon to give him the opinion of a technical man on that point-[DOT]
And the minister did not get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: -and I gave it to him. It was the opinion of the head of our Canadian Naval Service, Captain Hose.
Will the minister himself say that Britain's method of training was what the minister now proposes for these very men, or comparable to it in any way? The memorandum did not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The memorandum was given by the head of the Canadian Naval Service, who received his training in the British navy. He did not get his suggestions from imagination; he must have got them from his experience and knowledge He pointed out in his memorandum that the use of these men must be recognized as Great Britain used thousands of them during the war, and I think she still has five thousand of them in service at the present time. I will read the memorandum again so the House will be seized with what he says concerning the whole scheme.

I feel it a duty at this time to enunciate my views as I think the question of naval defence is perhaps one of the most difficult to decide as well as one of the most important that has yet come before this Parliament.
During our childhood as a nation we have been guarded by the Great Mother and have felt safe in that guardianship. We are looking now to attaining, and indeed we have attained, to all intents and purposes, the status of nationhood. But even now we must not entertain the idea that the problems of empire are any the less for us in view of the condition of world affairs to-day. We have to take our place now as one of the grown up members of a great family of nations, and it d-.es not matter who owns the ships, or who from now on commands the naval forces, we are part of that great empire and its defence will still be conducted over the Seven Seas. Although it is our first duty to guard our own shores, and that is the share of empire defence that is assigned to us, even that is necessarily an empire duty. We shall still shelter in the guardianship and strength of the great Empire to which we belong, and I hope we shall go on belonging to it. The defence of the Empire will still have to be maintained, and it is for us now to

Supply-Naval Service
decide whether we want the status of nationhood by accepting our share of that defence on the Seven Seas.
We shelter under and share in the strength of the Empire to which we belong, and we must do our part to maintain that strength. It is a national duty, it is a duty we owe to the Empire, it is a duty we owe to civilization. It is true that Britain has agreed to considerable disarmament in response to the proposals from Washington. She has lowered, too, her two-power standard, thereby relieving herself of the boasted position of mistress of the seas. Even at that the burden is great, and she fairly claims our aid. Indeed, iSir, I am afraid that a great portion of our people, living as they do, so far from the sea, have but a small consciousness of the interests of empire to-day, and are quite willing to join in the cry of "No navy.'' If it ever comes to pass that the strength of the Em-pie is weakened in proportion to the strength of other nations, we shall be unprepared, not only in time of emergency, but even in the days of peace; and we shall he made to feel the effects of that condition in one hundred and one ways of which we can now form no conception. Particularly is this true in view of the fact that we have become a world-trading nation. If there has been one outstanding feature of the British Empire for the last hundred years, it is that her subjects have been safe in any part of the world; she has been willing to spend millions of dollars to rescue even the most insignfiicant of her subjects from any danger in which they happened to find themselves.
In a recent issue of the London Times I saw the report of a statement made by Lord Lee of Fareham, now First Lord of the Admiralty, I believe-who, by the way, is very heartily in sympathy with the Washington arrangement-in which he expressed rather forcibly the disappointment of the Mother Country in the fact that while demanding full equality of nationhood, the sister nations of the Empire have left the burden to be borne by the Mother Country at a time when she most needs help. I take it that this is an appeal, this is a challenge to Canada at this time; and what is our answer to it? There is no doubt that everyone in this House is in accord with the Washington policy of reducing armaments, but the fact remains that the Empire of which we are a part, and of which we shall remain a part, needs defence. Do we, as a nation, consider that defence a part
of our duty? We see that Australia is maintaining her navy. I believe if we were in Australia's place, and not alongside the United States of America- whom Miss Canada has come to look upon as a great big, protecting brother-we would realize our inconsistency, and take part in the defence of the Empire on a scale consistent with the size and dignity of Canada as a nation.
I believe the amount to which it is proposed to cut down this estimate is so small as to render the whole thing a waste. We should, at least, maintain a nucleus around which effective training on a larger scale may be carried on whenever we see fit. We must go on, I think, along safe lines of policy, even though something has been accomplished by the various conferences Which have been held throughout the world. We do not want to make Canada a military nation, but she has an obligation to fulfil. I believe that we might well cut some mil-lins off other estimates rather than be too scant on this one.

This question is of such vital importance, not only to this country but to the world in general, that I would not like the item to pass without expressing my views in regard to it, particularly in view of some of the arguments advanced by supporters of the policy of the Government before the committee rose at six o'clock.
National defence is a problem with which every country has been confronted throughout all the ages, and it is one which will engage the attention of people as long as the world lasts-as long, at any rate, as human nature is what it is. Much as1 I would like to see the world reach that stage where all disputes should be settled by more conciliatory methods than have been adopted in the
9 p.m. past, I hardly think we can hope for very much in that direction at present. In spite of the terrible ordeal through which the world has just passed, we find that to-day conditions are probably more unsettled than they were prior to the outbreak of that terrible conflict which began in August, 1914. That being the case, can we afford to take chances on any policy which might not provide for our proper defence in case of another emergency arising? It is true that years might pass, and quite a number of them, without any occasion arising under which we would have to employ those methods of defence which nations considered it wise to adopt.

I cannot recall that during the last general election the policy of the present Government with respect to naval matters was dealt with before the electors. I cannot recall a single instance, in the province of Ontario, at least, nor have I. seen any reported, in which the Prime Minister enunciated the policy now being advocated by the Government. I would ask hon. members whether it is fair, whether it is right, that we should change the policy that we have been endeavouring to carry on, without informing the people of what we intended to do? Hon. gentlemen opposite claim to be a very democratic party, particularly during the last few years, and have been asserting that the autocratic party was the one which was in power when they were in opposition. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) before the committee rose at six o'clock, was proclaiming in a very loud voice that the policy of the Liberal Party prior to 1914 was the policy which would now continue. All the different branches of national defence are now to be merged under one head-the militia, naval service, and air force.
I was much impressed by the question which was asked by one of my hon. friends to my left this afternoon with regard to the students who were taking courses in the naval colleges, and what was to become of them when you close the naval colleges? These young men are being trained to be of service in the defence of our country should necessity arise. One hon. gentleman made a comparison of the cost of an education in ordinary civil life and the cost of educating these naval students, and asked why the country should be put to the expense of training these young met! in methods of skill in naval defence. But the comparison is not a fair one. These young lads intend to devote their lives to the service of their country; the other young men referred to are being trained for an entirely different purpose. It is quite true that in the event of trouble large numbers of civilians might volunteer for naval service. But has it not been proven conclusively that the efficiency of the Canadian forces during the late war was owing to the fact that we had trained men to take command, that we had quite a large number of officers who were thoroughly competent, by reason of the training which they had received, to lead and to train other men for service.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) spoke in rather a doubtful tone this
[Mr. Sutherland.!
afteroon as to whether the policy which the Government is now advocating was the correct one or not. I am not surprised that he should do so, if he remembers the speech which he delivered in the House just prior to the outbreak of war in 1914. I wondered whether the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) had forgotten the speeches which were delivered during the debate at that time. As late as June, 1914, taunts and sneers were being thrown across the floor of the House at the Prime Minister of that day because of the emergency which he had foreseen. These hon. gentlemen declared the emergency had passed away, that the sky was clear, that everything was lovely, and no occasion existed for making the preparations to which the Prime Minister of that day alluded. Yet the need for those preparations was well established by the information placed before Parliament at that time and the confidential information to which the then leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) was given access.
What did the Prime Minister of that day do? Did he retaliate when those jeers were indulged in; did he debate the matter with the opposition of that day, some of whom now confront me in this Chamber? No, he realized that the question was all too serious, that party politics should not be allowed to obtrude in a matter of that kind, and I am going to point out what he did in spite of the disparaging attitude of the opposition. His promptness in acting accounts for the fact that Canada was able to quickly mobilize her men and send a contingent across the seas in a credibly short time.
The then Prime Minister made absolutely no reference to the speeches which were made by the leader of the opposition and his chief lieutenants on that occasion. But he organized a committee empowered to report to him from time to time, a committee composed of the following: The Under Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Governor General's Military Secretary, the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service, the Deputy Minister of Justice, the Commissioner of Customs, the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Deputy Postmaster General, the Deputy Minister of Railways; with the Director of Military operations; Major Gordon Hall, the Director of Gunnery, and Lieutenant R. M. Stevens. The work commenced in January, the necessary arrangements were practic-

Supply-Naval Service
ally completed during July. Every department of the government was instructed to follow one line of action in detail, and the whole was subsequently co-ordinated and incorporated into one scheme, indicating the course to be followed by the government as a whole upon the outbreak of war. The committee's work resulted in the preparation of a war book which was completed only a few weeks before the appalling struggle began. Such was the view of the government at this time, and the methods adopted were such as I have described- methods adopted in spite of the attitude and protests of the hon. gentlemen opposite and my hon. friends from Halifax and Pictou were among the opposition at the time. Now the officials that I have enumerated are responsible heads of branches of the public service of to-day, and they will confirm the statement which I have made as to the methods pursued at that time.
In spite of the attitude of the opposition at that time hon. gentlemen sitting opposite to-day get up and confidently again assert that there is no danger. According to them we can afford to take a naval holiday. The hon. member for Pictou stated the other day; it is time we were having a naval holiday. Well, in view of the report which appears in the press of to-night containing the statement of the Premier of New Zealand I am afraid we are inclined to take a little more of a holiday than our self-respect warrants us in doing. Why, the impossibility of anything happening in 1914 was referred to by numerous speakers' at that time. For example I have before me the speech of the hon. member for Halifax and I will quote a few paragraphs from it. Speaking on January 20, the hon. gentleman said:
There was presented to parliament last session a measure providing for an expenditure of $35,000,000 for the construction of three battleships and the presentation of them to the British Admiralty. This policy was urged upon the ground that Britain's supremacy was imperilled and that a great conflict was imminent between two great European Powers. Tokens and signs we were told were not wanting. There were pealings of thunder and flashes of lightning, premonitions of this terrible naval conflict between two great Naval Powers, and upon this ground we were urged, cajoled and threatened to support this measure of the gov-erhment, we were told it was purely an emergency policy; that the government had in mind the adoption of a permanent policy which they would shortly present to parliament. Several months have at least elapsed since then. The evidence of the emergency conditions and of the European Armageddon has vanished: Time has vindicated the position which the hon. gentlemen on this side of the House took upon that occasion.
The hon. member for Halifax to-day was a little bit doubtful of the wisdom of the policy which is now advocated by the Minister of Militia and the Government. The Prime Minister the other night in dealing with this question referred to the co-ordination of the three departments concerned and the object which was had in view, and discussed the arguments which had been advanced that it might be the part of wisdom to wait until another Imperial Conference was held before deciding upon any policy with regard to this question. In dealing with the matter he said:
"We are seeking to consolidate the great departments of defence and to bring into one department, under one minister, the naval, the military and the air forces. What is the object? Avowedly, it is for the purpose of economy; avowedly, for the purpose of retrenchment. If we are ever to have retrenchment in military and naval expenditures this is the one moment in which it is possible to bring about something of that character. The government regards that as its first duty, its first obligation. It is sensible of all its larger duties and obligations, but it feels that it will best serve the interests of the British Empire as a whole when it helps to enlist, in the matter of defence, whether on land or sea, the sympathies of all our citizens throughout the Dominion, rather than antagonize their just sentiments by experiments of different kinds which will only tend to increase taxation antd render no effective service in the long run.
He emphasized the value of sympathy.
The Prime Minister was also very emphatic in condemning the dreadnaughts which it was the policy of the government in 1914 to assist in building in order to prepare for the events which later developed. He said:
The large dreadnaughts were of little or no service and supposing that resolution had carried, what would be the situation as regards those ships to-day? They would have been in British waters throughout the whole period of the war without being of any real service at all, and to-day they would have been among the number of capital ships consigned to the scrap heap.
Let me ask hon. gentlemen opposite where the war was won? Was it not in the North sea by the Royal navy? Was it not the Royal navy which was stationed day and night in the North sea, that policed from that point the waters of the world? Did Colonel Roosevelt not publicly proclaim at Oyster bay, when the United States entered the war that the only reason why war had not been brought to the shores of the United States was that
Supply-Naval Service

the British navy had been on the alert to prevent it. He paid a tribute to the British navy for what they had done during the war, and, in the face of that, in the face of history which is there for every one to read, was a government ever more justified by events in the methods which they pursued than the government of that day? Would they have been justified in building navy yards at that time to build men-of-war to sent over, years later, after the war had begun? What use would they have been?
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) referred to what Australia and New Zealand had accomplished. Yes. They entered upon the task of carrying out the arrangement which had been reached at the Imperial Conference, but did Canada do so? The government called for tenders, it is true, in July of 1910. The tenders were opened in the department on the 1st May, 1911. The government did not go out of office until October of that year. Those tenders remained in the office of the Minister of Militia or Naval Service. Not a keel was laid, not a contract was given during the years the hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. That was the manner in which they endeavoured to carry out their part of the Imperial compacts upon that occasion, and those are evidently the methods by which they are prepared to meet any other emergency which may arise, but we cannot afford to take chances on anything of that kind happening. Our self-respect as a people and the fact that the youth of this country expect a better example from those who are older and who are administering public affairs, are things we cannot afford to lose sight of.
But is there a policy at the present time? What is the policy of this Government anyway? They are introducing items in the estimates and cutting them down. Anything in the nature of effecive national defence meets with disapproval at the hands of the Government. Why is this the case? The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in a very loud voice, proclaimed the attiude of the hon. members on this side of the House during the election of 1911, where they were appealing to the people.	,

In 1911. He said:
But I can remember how he and his friends in the province of Ontario went up and down the back concession. declaring that Laurier's
TMr. Sutherland.]
creation was a tin pot navy. They told the .people that he was a French-Canadian and would do nothing for the Empire; and while they were making these representations in one province, other of the right hon. gentleman's friends were going up and down the province of Quebec saving that Sir Wilfrid Eaurier and his party were too imperialistic, and were trying to force Canadians, by conscrption, upon warships in order that they might be brought into European and Japanese broils.
This is the charge that the Prime Minister of Canada throws at those of us who were in opposition to him in 1911. As far as the people in the constituencies near where I reside are concerned, I say that nc reference was made to such a matter af all. We had been told on previous occasions, by hon. members on our left, that Reciprocity was the issue in that election, and that we did not do our duty by the country when we rejected Reciprocity. The hon. Prime Minister finds it convenient to-day to sneer at the Opposition and states that they were condemning the government of that day because of their tin pot navy, and making base appeals to the passions and prejudices of the people of Ontario. For my part, I resent any such imputations being thrown at me.
The Prime Minister came into my constituency during this last election and brought with him the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb), who, I believe, came there to deliver a certain message, in regard to the fairness of the people of Quebec, and how they absolutely refused to discuss any question of that kind. He . asked the people there to remind their member, the next time he referred to any such matter, of the absolute fairness of the people of the province of Quebec, and how they avoided any appeals of that kind. I wondered at fthe time what (particular message they came there to deliver, but looking over the report of their meeting I came to the conclusion that this was the message. There is not a man, woman or child in the constituency of South Oxford who has ever heard me make such an appeal in that constituency or elsewhere. The rebuke which the people of South Oxford gave the right hon. Prime Minister and one of his lieutenants was evident on the night of the election. We have however had some by-elections in Quebec recently. There was one election down in Yamaska, when the House was in session a year ago.
And we won.

I will quote from a Canadian Press despatch in the Ottawa

Supply-Naval Service
Journal of May 18, 1921, some of the arguments which were being advanced on that occasion, to show that the naval question has been a real live issue in some constituencies, even if it did not reach western Ontario. Mr. Boucher was the Liberal candidate in that constituency.
He is a member now.

Yes, this despatch is as follows:
Mr. Boucher said there was no knowing when war would break out again, and he clung to the argument for the "solid block" in Quebec, urging that if it was necessary in 1917, it was no less necessary now.
The Farmer candidate, J. Lambert, did not appear for this meeting. Yesterday at St. Bonaventure Mr. Mondou challenged his opponents to declare themselves in tariff matters. Mr. Boucher, on the other hand, claimed that with civil war in Ireland, India on a volcano, Japan and the United States at daggers drawn, France mobilized and the British navy ready for action, war might come at any time and the Liberal party want no change in relations between Canada and England and further do not want any commitments engaging Canada to the expenditure of a cent for military or naval purposes. Mr. Boucher said there had been Liberal traitors who had left Laurier, such for Instance as Hon. W. S. Fielding, and like L. J. Gauthier, recently.
These are the arguments which have been advanced. Mr. Boucher who is a member of the House at the present time, was elected in Yamaska constituency and re-elected in the last election. I quote now from the Ottawa Evening Journal a few words in reference to a by-election in Hull in September of 1919-
Deafening applause greeted Mr. Lucien Cannon when he went to the platform to speak. Like the other speakers, Mr. Cannon practically confined his remarks to praises of Dr. J. E. Fontaine and strong condemnation of the present Government. The member for Dorchester declared that Dr. Fontaine was known for his great devotion to his constituents and his party.
Must Fight For Rights
"I have gone into the House to vindicate the rights of the French-tCanadians," stated Mr. Cannon. "I do not regret in any way the battles that I have fought and I consider that they are an incentive to greater effort. I am not here to preach revolution, but I do say that we, having come here first, are the masters in this country. We have the right to vindicate the rights our forefathers won, but if you want victory with respect then you must fight with courage and with all your heart. I regret to see that in Ontario there does not exist that bond of fellowship between the Irish and French races that is so desirable."
Further on:
He spoke at great length of the manner in which Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King had supported Sir Wilfrid Laurier during the dark times, and he was sure that all French-Cana-dians would give the new Liberal Chieftain the support they tendered to Laurier.
And they did.
They did.

They surely did. I have a quotation from the Toronto Globe during the campaign in 1911, and I might as well give the views of the present Prime Minister on that occasion. The Toronto Globe reports the Prime Minister as follows :
Hon. Mr. King read extracts from Hon. Mr. Borden's speeches in the House of Commons in which the Conservative leader referred to the danger of war with Germany, and urged the Government to go to Britain's aid with a dread-naught or a cash contribution.
"Are the people of this country going to place at the head of affairs a man who will be precipitated into such a position as this, who will take from the treasury of this country and who would have taken enough money to build two dreadnaughts and send that money to England so that they could spend it as they pleased? And against what country? He was ready to send money to build warships to fight Germany."
Actually to fight Germany. These are things that are on record and that indicate what the policy of the party which is in power to-day is. There is a solid block from the province of Quebec; they are in the saddle and they are riding hard. There :s no question of that. I know the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham), in his heart, disapproves the policy which he is advocating; he cannot do anything else. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) does not approve this policy. I question whether any but a very small percentage of the people of this country favour any such policy. You are going to destroy absolutely everything that we have that has a tendency to create efficiency in training men for national defence. You are going to spend money, it is true, but for what? For national defence? No, nothing of the kind. You are going to spend a great deal of money to keep friends of the Government employed here, there and elsewhere. That was.made quite evident by a letter that was read in this IJouse the other night from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), with regard to the dismissal of the harbourmaster at Quebec. Was ever anything more apparent than that it was the policy of the Government to remove from office those who could not be made partizan servants of the Government? There was no charge against the harbourmaster at Quebec; on the contrary,
Supply-Naval Service

he had demonstrated that he was an efficient public servant and soldier and he had created reforms there that were a credit to him. For the first time and under his administration there was a substantial surplus in connection with the management of the Quebec harbour.
There is another item in connection with national defence, because the militia, the navy and the air service are all being merged. The air service is, as some one has pointed out, being absolutely destroyed, and the Government are attempting to hire out what will be left of the force to the different provinces as fire rangers. Five million dollars worth of aeroplanes were given to the Government by the British authorities in order to maintain and keep up a small air service; but instead of doing that, the Government, if they can, are now going to hire these young men'out as fire rangers to the different provinces, if the provinces wil take them over, and in the event of the provinces not doing so, we do not know what they are going to do. Is not this a magnificent system of self defence that the Government are adopting? In one province they state that they will not countenance the spending of a dollar for militia purposes or for naval defence and they come before this House and ask us to reduce this estimate so the balance will be of no effect; will not be efficient or of national service in the event of trouble arising. The Prime Minister laughs, and he thinks that it is a light matter. Well, it may be a light matter to him, but it was not a light matter to many people in this country when the nation was in danger and they had to make sacrifices on behalf of the nation.
Everybody made sacrifices.

Yes, everybody
made sacrifices. I know some people think they made tremendous sacrifices, they think, because they could not turn out so much stuff at high prices as they would have done, if they had only been able to get more help, that they made great sacrifices in that respect. I am speaking however of the real, actual sacrifice of those who took their part in the battle line; and to the credit of our system of national defence be it said, those who had training in military service or in the navy were not slow to respond when the call of duty came. It will be a dark day for this country, if the occasion arises for the rest of the Empire to look upon the people of Canada 
as spongers; we cannot consider ourselves anything else if we adopt such a policy as is enunciated by the present Government. If in years gone by we have refused to do anything in the way of national defence, during the war crisis the people of Canada responded nobly, made great sacrifices and fought as bravely and gallantly as it was possible for men to do. But you cannot afford to stop there; you cannot afford to permit those, who refused to recognize Canada's duty to participate in the war and to do what she did on that occasion, to control the affairs of this country under present conditions. I stand here to-night to register my protest against any such policy as that. You may say that conditions in Canada do not justify the Government in making this expenditure. The first call upon the people of any country is that of national defence; the duty of the citizen to the state is the first duty of the citizen. In the time.of Chatham, it was a maxim that the navy was the standing army of Britain. Are you going to force the old land to take care of these vigorous young colonies which have grown up to nationhood? Are they still willing to allow the old land to bear the whole burden of defence? Look at the burden which Britain is contending with to-day in the East, yes, and fighting heroically at conferences of Nations to prolong the peace of the world. Until the very last minute the British exerted every ounce of energy which they possessed in an endeavour to prevent the outbreak of war which took place in 1914. It was through no desire on their part that the world was plunged into that war; but it was in spite of every effort which human ingenuity could gring to bear that that war occurred, and that, I am satisfied, will be the policy of Britain in the future. As has been pointed out by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Britain's power and influence in this world will depend upon the energy and force that she is able to throw into a conflict in the event of its taking place. I am absolutely opposed to a reduction in this item of expenditure, even under present conditions. I think our self respect demands of us that we shall do our duty in the future, even if we did not do it in the years immediately preceding the war.

It was not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to take any part in this debate, but seeing that my name has been mentioned by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, with reference to the election which took place, a year ago, in

the county of Yamaska, I deem it my duty to give this House some explanation on the subject.
First, let me state that the newspaper extract from which the hon. member has just quoted, contains in parts the words which I used in May of last year, at the meeting held in St. Bonaventure. However, I take exception to that part of the article in which the newspaper accuses me of having said that the hon. Mr. Fielding, at present Minister of Finance, had been a traitor to Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I strongly protest against such language being attributed to me, and I wish to state emphatically that never were such words uttered by me against the hon. Mr. Fielding, in whom we all have-on this side of the House at least-the greatest confidence and for whom we also have the highest esteem. There is another point to which I want to draw the attention of the speaker who has just preceded me in this debate. It is still in reference to this election which took place in the county of Yamaska, and if I remember well, it is a question which was put, in this House, to the hon. Minister of Marine of that day (Mr. Ballantyne), by the present Minister of Marine (Mr. Lapointe), to ascertain if the Conservative party had a candidate in the field, and the hon. Mr. Ballantyne answered that the Government's candidate was my opponent, Mr. Mondou. Now, what was the principal argument which I brought forth in this contest against Mr. Mondou? I made use of the newspaper, "La Presse," which had published an interview given by Mr. Mondou, and in which he declared that the Conservative party by choosing Mr. Meighen to replace Sir Robert Borden, had given itself a tyrant instead of a leader, because in his opinion, Mr. Meighen was an autocratic tyrant, owing to the way he had treated Quebec during the war. However, this did not prevent the right hon. Mr. Meighen acknowledging Mr. Mondou's candidacy in the county of Yamaska.
It is not, Mr. Chairman, by crying down imperialism or censuring the naval policy that I won my election. I won it through the weakness of the candidate who was put up against me, because of his lack of sincerity in supporting Mr. Meighen's policy, the same individual that he had accused, some time previous, of being an autocratic tyrant.

A little while ago we had the pleasure of listening to an hon. gentleman who first saw daylight in our little island far across the sea, and I thought
perhaps I might take a few minutes to express my views along a different line. We have heard a good deal to-night about patriotism, and it seems to be generally assumed that those who advocate further armaments and greater expansion in naval affairs are more patriotic than those who urge the opposite course. I have been astonished to listen to some of the arguments advanced to-night. Now, I do not want to take a critical attitude or to suggest that things might be done somewhat better or debated from a different standpoint, but I do protest against having to sit in this House and listen hour after hour to the recapitulation of ancient history with which we were all perfectly familiar before we came here. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) was rather severe in his criticism of the member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). I think that if he had paid attention to what that hon. gentleman said he would have realized that the member for Lisgar was not so much concerned with Canada's status as a nation as he was in regard to the question as to what position Canada was going to take in the Empire in reference to naval and military matters. We know there is going to be a conference of the premiers of the various parts of the Empire, who will assemble to discuss this question; and perhaps some mutual arrangement will be arrived at whereby each part of the Empire will know what it is expected to do. That is what the hon. member was referring to when he spoke about our status.
We have heard much about conditions as they exist to-day. I heard one hon. member to my right make the statement that after every war the view was always put forward that never again would war occur in the world. But conditions have never existed before in the same degree as they exist at the present time. Never was war so horrible, nor its ugliness and sinfulness so patent as it is to-day; and those who have studied the question cannot but realize that every nation and individual will look upon the possibility of future wars with feelings of horror and terror. War in the future will not be war in the ordinary sense. Going back over the ages, we see the time when warfare consisted in hand to hand conflict; then armour and machine guns were introduced; and after every war, it is true, men have felt almost convinced that warfare would be improbable in the future. But what is the situation to-day? War has passed from individual bravery on the battlefield and is carried on by the
Supply-Naval Service

chemist in his laboratory. To-day it is the scientists and mechanics who really wage war, and not the men on the battlefield; and I venture to make the statement that the nations of the civilized world will ponder a very long time before going to war under present scientific conditions. At the close of the last war it was said that an American chemist had invented a poisonous gas that would devastate whole countrysides. What would battleships avail in such a case? I can assure hon. members that the nations will think twice before going to war, and we in this country should carefully weigh matters before spending money to-day on a scheme the benefit of which we cannot foresee.
I want to say a word in regard to the naval reserves. I am not a seafaring man myself, but I was born in a seafaring country and I know a little about the conditions as they exist around the coasts of those wonderful little islands over the sea. I have lived a long time in Canada and am a good Canadian, but, if I may be allowed to say so, I hope the day may never come when I can look across the ocean and not be sensible of a warm spot in my heart for my native land. So that it will be understoood, I -trust, that it is not because of any lack of fervent regard for that land that I am not ready to vote for the expenditure of vast sums of money at the present time for the purpose of building up naval armaments. With regard to the naval reserve, let me say that the fishermen in the villages around the coast of England, from Grimsby to Hull, manned the boats and ships that swept the seas around Britain for mines. And this work was done by these men *without any long training, because I know that friends of mine in the Old Country were engaged in that work a short time after the mines were laid by the Germans around the British coasts. I am perfectly certain that the naval reserve scheme is a good one, and that the naval reserve can be created from the ranks of the fishermen. I shall not follow the arguments of the leader of the Opposition. If we had been discussing the policy of spending twenty or thirty million dollars on a naval programme, I could understand the length of time that has been devoted to this debate. But we have taken up a day and a half discussing what an hon. member said could be entirely covered by $500,000. Surely there is not such a tremendous difference between the two policies that it takes so much of the time of this House to discuss

such a small matter. Had it been $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 that hon. gentlemen on my right were advocating should be expended, then I could have understood the. stand they are taking.
A good many slurs-perhaps that is too strong a term-statements are sometimes made that we do not take a wide enough view, that we are not patriotic. I repudiate that statement. I believe every hon. member is patriotic. Perhaps we view things from different standpoints, but I think we ought to treat one another as patriotic gentlemen, no matter -what part of the country we come from.

If I rise to say one or two words anent the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) I hope he will not feel that I resent anything -he has stated; indeed, I have confidence that he was addressing himself sincerely to the question. I would be the last -man in the world to question his patriotism. I do not know whose patriotism has been questioned in this debate. Such taunts are usually flung merely for the sake of the reply. The patriotism of -hon. members never is called in question at all. Now, while I am sure the hon. member's heart beats just as true for the Old Land as mine, and that he has just as keen a sense of national obligation as I have, I am afraid that some pre-conceived ideas have warped his judgment at this moment. While I am afraid of that, I express confidentially the hope that the time will come when he will decide that the hour -for action, rather than aspiration, is at hand, and that he will be just as ready to do something practical as myself. He says I misconstrued the words of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown).
Misunderstood.

Well, misunderstood. I do not think so; and that is really my only reason for rising. The hon. member for Lisgar expressed the view that the question of our status within the Empire is In doubt. He may have had in mind merely as to our share in defence; however, he did not use those words. I do not think myself that he had reference merely to our share in defence. But suppose he had? The hon. member for Brandon says: "Let us wait until at some Imperial Conference the share of each is agreed on-the share of Canada, the share of Australia, the share of New Zealand, the share of South Africa, the share of Great Britain." I believe the hon. member for Brandon sincerely looks

Supply-Naval Service
forward to that consummation. Well, let me tell him that if he does he will sit in this House and he will be a resident of this country a good many years before he will ever see it come to pass.
Let me ask hon. members opposite, let me ask those supporting this policy, if they are ready to wait and have the share of this country fixed at any Imperial Conference held this year or any other year. Will any of them say, "yea"? Not one who supports the Government in backing away from our naval obligations will do that

not one. Years before we adopted the principle that we must ourselves determine what our share is, that we cannot be dictated to at a conference. Very well, that must go comcommitantly with the honest and practical effort to do our share from year to year. I am pointing out to the hon. member that he will look in vain for an agreement at the Imperial Conference that this country will feel to be binding, or that any hon. gentleman opposite will feel to be binding upon our country.
Will the right hon. gentleman permit me one question?
Yes, or two.
While the right hon. gentleman had the honour to represent our country in London last summer, did he make any engagement to the Empire on naval defence?

The right hon. gentleman has answered that question at least six times in the course of this debate. The only acknowledgment is that contained in the one resolution, which is as clear as sunlight, and which lays upon the Parliament of Canada the obligation of determining what this country should do in the matter of naval defence. It is wholly a question for Parliament to decide. I quite aprove of that principle. I believe anything else is impossible. But while I approve of that principle, I say it essentially follows that we must here and now determine what we will do, and not be forever preaching that some day in the future there is going to be another Imperial Conference. We have been putting this decision off on the plea of conferences for many years-we put it off twenty years ago on that plea, we put it off thirteen years ago on that plea, and we have kept out of our just obligations all that time. When the war was on we were prevented from carrying out our obligations. Under the late government we were quite prepared to do
so. And much that has occurred in this debate would indicate that there is a Whole lot to be said, even in ordinary times, in favour of some system based on contribution.
If I felt hon. members were right in saying:	You cannot do anything effective
in the way of naval defence by spending $1,000,000 more, $2,500,000 more, $6,000,000 more, or even $7,000,000 more,- I would think they could not make a stronger argument in favour of contribution. In fact, that argument is unanswerable, but, for myself, I do not think it is correct. I believe we were doing something of some value before. But now that we know what the whole collection of nations known as the British Empire must do, we know, too, that the measure of help we were giving before was not our fair share; we must do more than that. But let me point out to the hon. member for Brandon that the error is this:	Instead of going
forward we are going behind, humiliatingly behind, indefensibly behind, we are moving in exactly the wrong direction; and that is why that movement is resisted in this vote. If the Government were making a serious effort to really place Canada in a respectable position before her sister nations, then there would be little cause for opposition in this House; but instead of that the Government is yielding to the demands of those who do not want to do anything practical and effective in the matter of naval defence.

I wish to ask my right
hon. friend one question to elucidate, if possible, a point upon which there has been a good deal of discussion. Is it a fact that at the last Imperial Conference, or at any previous conference, the question of defence was made a joint affair for the Empire or was it not? Is that the position we are in to-day, that we are under an obligation to contribute? True, we fix the measure of the contribution-
And the method.
and the method. But is it a fact that we are under an obligation to make a contribution to Empire defence? And to what extent are we under that obligation?

We are not under any contractual obligation at all-no obligation based upon a resolution. The whole obligation to defend ourselves is just the same as the obligation of every nation on earth,

Supply-Naval Service
and when we are part of the Empire we share in the common obligation. It is an obligation that is incident to our existence, and from which we cannot escape save byloading it on someone else.
But my right hon. friend is skating around the point.
Hear, hear.
No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Perhaps I am uncommonly dense this evening, and unable to see the point, but I think a very great deal, Mr. Chairman rests right upon that question. In 1917 it was definitely understood that a constitutional conference would be called after the war to define Canada's status within the Empire. That was the agreement reached in 1917 at the Imperial Conference held that year. Now, as I understand it from my reading of all the literature dealing with the question, our position as far as the defence of the Empire was concerned would not be determined until that constitutional conference was held and we knew what our status within the Empire was. I may be wrong in that, but if that is correct, then I submit that the whole ground upon which my hon. friends to the right are arguing this question is absolutely and entirely wrong. If we take the ground that Canada as a matter of right, in her own defence-as has been argued here-should create the nucleus of a navy, should engage in naval training on the assumption that that navy is absolutely her own and that she may send it tc war when she cares to send it and keep it at home when she cares to keep it, then there is a fair ground for argument. But as I understand the discussion that has taken place here to-day-and indeed, before to-day-one of the strongest reasons urged by my hon. friends to my right why this vote should not be reduced is that we are not making our fair share of contribution to Empire defence. Consequently, I think . it is a fair question to ask, when was that obligation reached? When was the understanding arrived at that we should make aa contribution to Empire defence? We have not had that elucidated, and I submit that if my hon. friends to my right are to be on sound premises in the argument they are making, they should explain that point.
Now, we come back to the general question. It was not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to take part in this debate, because

in my judgment this vote should have been passed two days ago. However, the matter is being discussed, and now that I am on my feet there are one or two observations that I should like to make upon it. I support the reduction made by the Minister of Militia. My regret is that the minister, if I may say so, did not stick to the first programme he laid down, because I think the second programme involves a further expenditure of money which at the present time this country is not in a position to face. My hon. friends argue that we must have a navy, and they have argued also that our militia establishment must be kept up. Against whom must we have a navy? That is a fair question; against whom is Canada to arm?
Oh, oh.
Some of my hon. friends say, "Oh, oh." Well, what is the result of the Washington conference? Who has Canada to fear? Are we going to build a navy against the United States?
What has the United States got a navy for?

That is their affair.
What I am asking my hon. friends is this: are we to arm against the United States? Are we to arm against Japan? Canada is a party to the treaty which resulted from the Washington conference, a treaty which will be presented to this House for ratification.
Against whom are they arming?
They are disarming.
Not half as fast as we are.

That is all very well; but my right hon. friend knows that a treaty was signed as a result of the Washington conference-we are signatories to it- whereby all the great nations who could possibly be the source of any danger to Canada have by mutual understanding agreed to adopt a peaceful method) of settling their disputes. That is one reason "why-putting it on the very ground upon which my hon. friends debate the question -we can reduce this expenditure this year. The second reason has been mentioned several times to-day.

After the United States has proportionately disarmed, and after Japan has proportionately disarmed, who is England proportionately arming against?

India.

My imagination is not vivid enough to enable me to see the relation of my hon. friend's question to my argument.
I come now to another point. Reference was made to-day, and has been made several times during the course of the discussion, to the financial position of this country. I wish to direct that point to the attention of my hon. friends who are advocating this expenditure. What do we see in the United States to-day?
10 p.m. What do we see in Great Britain? In both those countries we see reductions in expenditure and reductions in taxation. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is coming down to-morrow to deliver to this House the annual budget. I may be mistaken- I hope I am-but I venture the prediction that the Minister of Finance, if he discharges his duty to Canada, will not take the way of reducing the taxation, but must find additional taxation; there is no way out of it if this country is to meet its obligations. In the face of that situation, therefore, are my hon. friends on good ground in arguing that we must spend a million dollars more on the navy this year?
My right hon. friend the other evening, and some of the other gentlemen to my right, dwelt at great length on the extent to which Canada- had sponged on Great Britain in the matter of defence. They cited what Australia was doing, what New Zealand was doing, what Britain was doing. Why, they said, Britain is spending $10 per head on her navy; Australia is spending $6; New Zealand is spending $2.50, and we are only spending 17 cents per head on our navy. Well, how are my hon. friends going to do away with sponging? By having the Canadian people spend another 11 cents per head on the navy.
We did not say that.

Well, then I do not know what my hon. friend is arguing upon. I presume he contends that this vote should remain as it was last year. I may be mistaken; if I am, I am doing him an injustice. But he has not made his position clear in the House, and if he made his position clear I think I am correct in saying that it would mean another 11 cents per head to be paid by the Canadian people. The thing is absurd. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) made the other day what was, to my mind, the most sensible
suggestion that has been heard in this debate, namely, that if we are going into the naval business we should go into it in earnest and quit playing with it. I think this country could well take a naval holiday for five years. My hon. friends who are opposing this reduction in the estimates say: "Oh, Canada must make her fair contribution to defence." Has Canada done nothing for the defence of the Empire-placing it even on that basis? What did we do in the war? We sent 500,000 men overseas. Canada did her part in the war toward the defence of empire. But she did more than that, if her contribution rests upon something more than men and ships. We discovered during the late war that food, for instance, was just as vital a thing in the waging of war as were munitions and ships. And what has Canada done in that respect? It is not a fair comparison to put Canada on an even keel with Great Britain in the matter of these expenditures. We have spent hundreds of millions of dollars in the building of railways and in the opening up of new country, and every time we built a mile of railway; every time we opened up new parts of this country and brought additional areas under cultivation; every time we contributed to the material wealth of this country, we were adding to the strength of the Empire. Canada has made her contribution, and a very notable one, in that respect. And I would point out for the information of my hon. friends tc my right that the doctrine I am preaching in this respect is not a new doctrine; it was preached by one of the most eminent men of the Conservative party in this country, the late Sir Charles Tupper. In the last decade of the last century, the question was mooted that Canada should make her contribution to the British navy, and Sir Charles Tupper took the ground that Canada should not be expected to do that. He argued that when Canada built her railways across the Dominion, linking up New Zealand and Australia with Great Britain, she was contributing to Empire defence. Alluding to things I have just mentioned, he says:
These actual facts illustrate, in my opinion, the best mode of contributing- to the strength and defence of the Empire. In my judgment, instead of adding to its defence, the strength of a colony would be impaired by taking away the means which it requires for its development and for increasing its defensive power if it were asked for a contribution to the army and navy.
He was alluding there to a contribution, and the same thing would apply to

the expenditure of a similar amount of money in the building of ships.
Any such contribution would be utterly insignificant in its value compared with what is now being accomplished.	[DOT]
Those are not my words, those are the words of Sir Charles Tupper. I submit that is the line along which Canada can make her best contribution to Empire defence.
Will the hon. member permit me a question?
Certainly.
Does the hon. member think that in the building of the Canadian Pacific railway, Canada has contributed her part to the naval defence of the Empire?

I am not going to give my hon. friend my opinion. I have given him the opinion of Sir Charles Tupper which was that Canada had done so. If my hon. friend wishes to repudiate that great statesman of the past, that is his affair.
The party has changed since.

-This question, I think, must be considered in the light of what Canada can do at the present time. I have stated time and again-I have said it so often that I am afraid hon. members in this House and people in the country will get tired of hearing the assertion-[DOT] but I repeat it here, that the most pressing thing before this country to-day is to get its finances in order. The Finance Minister comes down to-morrow possibly with a programme of increased taxation. I do not know, I hope not; but if he does not, I do not know how he is going to make his budget balance this year. But say he comes down with that proposition, what is the problem before this country, and before this House? It is to keep our taxation down. If you run your taxation up in this country in view of the scattered area of the Dominion it becomes a question how long will you hold your people. To my mind that is the most serious question pressing upon us financially, and for that reason I gladly support the reduction suggested by the minister in these naval estimates. Moreover I will tell the committee I would have been prepared to go a great deal further than he has gone.

I would like to ask the hon. member if he would wait 
until the enemy was at his gate before preparing to do anything to defend himself?

In all my life I have
never heard such a system of quibbling as that advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite, and some other hon. members, in order to make excuses to get away from assuming our share of responsibility for naval defence. The statement has been made that this is one of the most important subjects which has been taken up this session. I agree with that statement; I say it is just as necessary to maintain the navy at proper strength as it is to support the Canadian National Railways, and we all know how absolutely necessary that is. Because if you have no navy then you have no support for your merchant marine; and if your merchant marine suffers then your National Railways will be prejudicially affected. I am not so familiar with naval affairs as I probably am with matters concerning the militia and therefore I do not propose to go into the discussion of details. But I heartily endorse everything that has been said in favour of the maintenance of the navy, and I do hope the Government will see to it that at least a sum equivalent to the expenditure of last year will be provided to keep our navy in as efficient a condition as possible.
The maintenance of the navy should not be regarded as a .political matter. It is absolutely a matter of business and every hon. member here should give his support to the maintenance of an efficient navy. Let there be no suspicion entertained in the outside world that we as Canadians, are not prepared to do our share towards the upkeep of the British navy. We should be British enough-because we are all Brit-tishers in Canada-to wish to continue to sing "Rule Britannia, Britannia Rule the Waves." This country owes a great deal to Britain and we ought to show, in some tangible way, that we appreciate what the Mother Country has done for us. A number of hon. members opposite have been talking about events of the past. Well, a great many of us here do not want to hear so much about the past; what we are interested in is the future. I hope the Minister of Militia will see to it that a substantial contribution is made towards the maintenance of the navy.
Shall the resolution carry?

My opinion is the opinion expressed by the leader of the Liberal party in this House -that this question should be dealt with from a purely Canadian viewpoint and from no other viewpoint at all.

Has the minister definitely decided on the abandonment of the Lindsay arsenal as a government arsenal in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I may say that the department has been approached in the matter but the parties who made the advances were told that if they came prepared to talk in a definite way we would discuss the matter with them. My own view is that there is no definite need for the Lindsay arsenal-that the arsenal in the province of Quebec can provide all the ammunition we need in Canada for our annual training. If that be the case why should we have two arsenals to do the work of one?

May I ask .the minister if he has seriously considered this matter. I understand that the Lindsay arsenal is an up-to-date factory, the most up-to-date and modern factory on this continent. If there is any question of disposing of an arsenal why not dispose of the one at Quebec instead of that at Lindsay?

The hon. minister (Mr. Graham) has not answered my question. I have wondered at times why the Lindsay arsenal, a new building, modernly equipped and more centrally situated than 1331
the Quebec arsenal, should be closed down, instead of the Quebec arsenal. The minister states that the arsenal in Lindsay only manufactures small munitions, but I cannot see what other ammunition we need. Why do we need larger ammunition?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In military training we use other ammunition, outside of the small arm ammunition, and, although we possibly have a supply on hand now, if we have our annual training, it will not last very long. The munitions are turned over every seven years.
It would only mean moving machinery from Quebec to Lindsay.

Did I understand the minister to say the other evening that he negotiated with some four firms in connection with disposing of the Lindsay arsenal, but at the present time he has nothing definite view?

speechtext: Parties waited on the Government and discussed the question of the disposition of the Lindsay arsenal. Some discussion had taken place between a deputation from Lindsay and myself and afterwards between the Minister of Railways and myself. I thought some use might be made of the building by the Canadian National Railways, but I have been rather discouraged along that line during the last week or two by the Minister of Railways. Another party approached the department, but had nothing definite in view. I suggested that if they had anything definite to discuss to come back.
Could the minister tell us what the Lindsay arsenal cost?

I did not hear all the answer. The reason why the arsenal at Quebec was kept on and the one at Lindsay closed was not quite clear to me. Another point struck me very forcibly was this: All hon. gentlemen know the geography of this country fairly well, and in case of aggression from outside, I think, they will agree that it is quite possible the arsenal at Quebec could be blown to pieces much more quickly than the one at Lindsay.^ Although I am not a militarist, never having fired a gun, perhaps, in my life, it seems to me it would be more practicable to retain the arsenal at Lindsay, which is situated far enough inland to enable us to

maintain our position against attack much longer than we could in the case oi the arsenal at Quebec. With regard to making small arms at Lindsay, I think it is quite possible to make larger arms there if necessary. In my humble opinion, it would be well if both these institutions could be kept running. In case of aggression, we would be in a much better position with this arsenal at Lindsay than with simply one at Quebec. Has this matter been taken into consideration? I would like to get the views of the minister with regard to the possibility of something happening the arsenal at Quebec, in case of aggression, and as to the position we would be in if the arsenal at Lindsay were closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But we must maintain a reserve.

I think this reserve is one of the things that we should eventually aim at. The reserve was fixed by a suggestion made by the present Lord French, then Sir John French, in the year 1910, when he came through Canada at the invitation of the Liberal government then in power and made an examination of ail the military establishments in the country. In his report he stated that 40,000,000 rounds, the quantity which was then the reserve of our rifle ammunition, should be doubled. I have never seen where the figure 90,000,000 was used.

Was that a private
report?

No. I have it here. It is in the Library; it is circulated, and everybody knows about it. Our reserve may have been climbing up to that figure, but we have never reached it. We have maintained a reserve at just about the figure at which it stands to-day, namely
40,000,000 or 45,000,000. The annual training and the Rifle Association will use probably eight or ten million rounds. I think that is the case when the whole volunteer establishment is trained. The effort, however, has been to get up to the proper reserve limit. I will ask the committee to note that this appropriation is entirely for small arm ammunition; nothing is asked for in this appropriation in the nature of artillery ammunition, and this kind of ammunition can all be made at Lindsay. I have had occasion to go through both the arsenals, and they are both very good institutions. The one at Lindsay is, of course, the more modern, and I think the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) is quite correct when he says that at this date it is the most up-to-date ammunition factory in America. In round figures, it cost $1,750,000,000, and it is only three or four years old. I do not believe it can ever be sold for anything approaching the figure which it cost. There is room in that arsenal to manufacture, not only our rifle ammunition, but our heavy ammunition, and I know that during the last two years the proposal was made to remove the heavy machinery from Quebec and to bring it to Lindsay. The reason for the suggested change was that Lindsay strategically was the proper place for an arsenal, whereas Quebec did not offer the same advantages on account of the exposed situation. There is no doubt that one cruiser in the river could, with a single shot, put the Quebec arsenal out of business.
The same thing might be done at Lindsay by an aeroplane.

But that can be said
of every arsenal in the country. One is in an exposed situation; the other is remote from our frontier, well inland, and I think any military man in the department -and the minister can make inquiries for himself-will agree with me when I say that, from a military point of view, Lindsay is the best situation for an arsenal.
We know that we have on hand in the way of rifle ammunition, because we have just been told that, and we know approximately how long it will last. We have also a general idea of what we have in the way of heavy ammunition for our artillery. If we did not know that; the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) tried to inform the country last fall as to what we had, and he said: "this country is becoming literally a storehouse of high explosive shells and the like." We know what the quantity is; it is 500 rounds per gun. It has been so stated on oath before the Public Accounts Committee. That was our reserve before Lord French came to this country to make his report, and we have that reserve of 500 rounds per gun. The question for the committee to decide is whether the suggestion of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) is not a good one, whether we cannot afford to take a holiday at both arsenals,-if the one, why not at both? The most modern arsenal is at Lindsay; the best situated is at Lindsay; all they propose to manufacture is .303, the small arm ammunition, which could be made at either of them. It is for the committee to decide where that ammunition ought to be made.

How much land is
there in connection with the arsenal at Lindsay? How many acres?

speechtext:
I have the cost of the

I have been told on
some authority that the gentleman who owned the land received $10,000 for it. Where did the balance go?

How many employees
are there at Lindsay?

When did the
Government decide upon its policy of disposing of Lindsay arsenal? Negotiations have been on foot, and apparently it ts the intention of the Government to dispose of it. I do not believe this matter was discussed during the campaign last December, and it must have been very recently when the Government discussed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service

I could not exactly
give the date, but the Minister of Militia and Defence recommended to his colleagues that, as the Lindsay arsenal was .not necessary, a large amount of money could

be saved annually. That suggestion was accepted by his colleagues, and consequently the recommendation is made to the House.

Cartridges, small arm
bore, .303, mark VII, approximately 16,000,000 rounds; cartridges, filled, B.L. 12-pounders, 15,000 rounds; shrapnel and blank, 97,000 rounds. Did I understand the
hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Thurston) to state that when the Lindsay arsenal was built, the land was bought by the government for $39,000, and that the owner of the land received only $10,000. Where did the other $29,000 go?

Mr. Rogers was Minister of Public Works at the time.

I would suggest that if the hon. member for Victoria (O.),

(Mr. Thurston), has any charges to make in respect of that purchase he make them in the usual way. I will ask for no special formality; let him demand an investigation by the Government without delay.
The member for Victoria (O.) is under no necessity to lay any formal charge.
I do not think he will.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Public Works Department carries on that part of the business for the other departments; I have not the information available. I should think that the land was bought in 1916 or 1917.
Perhaps the hon. member for Victoria (O.) has the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does the hon. member know the date?

I do not know the date, but I am told by Lindsay people that this man owned a hundred acres and that he received $10,000 for the land, and I was wondering why the cost should be represented as' $39,000.
Do you know the year?
I should like the minister to give the information before the vote carries. I object to leaving the matter in the shape of an innuendo.

We have heard a great deal for the past two days about cutting down expenses, and we have listened to that sort of thing until we are almost tired. Now if there is one item that has come before this committee, since the House met, that can stand cutting down it is this item of $425,000. The militia is cut down, the mounted police estimates are cut down, and the navy is practically abandoned. That being the case, why do we want ammunition? I move in amendment that this item be reduced by $110,000 for the Quebec arsenal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) moves that vote No. 96 be reduced by the sum of $10,000.

No, Mr. Chairman,

I stand corrected, but I thought that we had passed that item and were on No. 97.

The location of an arsenal is an important matter to the whole country. There are two arsenals in Canada, one of which is about to be closed, and this perhaps might be approved by many. But the Government have intimated that they have entered into negotiations for the disposal of one of these arsenals without consulting Parliament or bringing the matter before the people. Now, the location at Lindsay was selected because of its distance from the international boundary and the facilities at hand for its proper defence, while the other one at Quebec is in a more exposed position. During the war the arsenal at Quebec was exposed to danger. This was recognized by no less a personage than the leader of the Opposition of that day, who, in the city of Quebec on December 8, 1916, delivered an address from which I shall quote a paragraph to show the danger in which Sir Wilfrid Laurier supposed that arsenal to be, from its exposed position.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member that we are on item 96 "Dominion Arsenal, Lindsay-$25,000."

The location of an arsenal, Mr. Chairman, is a matter of great importance to the country, and the abandonment of the arsenal at Lindsay has a direct bearing upon the remaining arsenal at Quebec. I contend therefore that I am in order in discussing the relation of the one to the other.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Provided the quotations are relevant to the item under consideration, and conform to the rules, they may be read.

If I contravene the rules I bow to your decision, Mr. Chairman. But my contention is that the policy of the Government in regard to the location of the arsenal at Lindsay is a matter that has a distinct relevancy to the other arsenal at Quebec. Of course, if I am not in order I do not wish to proceed in that direction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If item 96 is passed it will be quite in order for the hon. member to discuss it in connection with the following vote, as he is doing.

I take it that if this particular item is disposed of I shall be out of order in later adverting to it. I hold, Sir, that we should not dispose of the Lindsay arsenal as the Government proposes to do. I was stating some reasons why this should not be done, and I think I am well within the rules of the House in doing so. I was going to quote from the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, spoken on December 8th, 1916, in the city of Quebec, when he pointed out the danger to which the arsenal there was exposed at that time.
Sir Wilfrid then read extracts from a plan prepared toy the German General Staff and published before the war, showing that it was their intention to add two more provinces to those taken from France. He could prove that the German idea was the imposition of Deutsch turn, or German domination, on the world, and he added that the war had shown how near they had come to succeeding.
Will my hon. friend allow me a question?
Let me finish the quotation.
What document is the hon. member quoting from?

If you will permit me to read the extract I shall be glad to answer any questions afterwards. The report goes on:
If it was 'possible for merchant submarines to enter United States ports it was possible for armed submarines to enter Halifax, St. John and Quebec ports.
What document are you quoting from?
From the Toronto Globe of December 8, 1916.
Reporting a speech which was supposed to have been made at what place in Canada?

At Quebec. Now, Sir, we have had an intimation from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) as to what the policy of the Government is in regard to the harbour at Quebec. I also desire to draw the attention of the House to another matter. I hold in my hand the Canada Gazette of April 6, 1918, in which I find an Order in Council passed by the government on the 4th April of that year. It is in these words:
Whereas on the 28th day of March last the opposition of a large number of the population of the city of Quebec to the enforcement of the Military Service Act 1917 and the regulations thereunder broke out in open violence and serious riots ensued on that day-
