speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must call the hon. -member's attention to the fact that this Order in Council, so far as it has been read, is not relevant to the item under discussion, the Dominion arsenal at Lindsay, and therefore he is out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I do not desire to be out of order, but I have read only a part of the recital. I think if you will permit me to read the remainder of the order I shall be able to demonstrate that I am well within my rights, and that this Order in Council proves conclusively that Quebec city is not a suitable place for a Dominion arsenal.
And whereas-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has already been advised that the Order in Council he is attempting to read is not relevant to the item before the committee. Therefore under Rule 13 (5) he is clearly out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to appeal to the House from your ruling, although I think if you had permitted me to read the Order in Council you would not have taken exception to it. I was endeavouring to point out that the location of the arsenal at Lindsay was much more suitable than at Quebec, and my reason for doing so was the danger with which we might be confronted in the event of a national crisis. I pointed out that the arsenal at Quebec is situated on an international waterway which in all probability will be the main international artery of this continent in a very few years. During 1918, while we were tested and tried to the limit of our national capacity, we found that Quebec was the one point in the whole Dominion where martial law had to be enforced in order to suppress rioting and an outbreak of its citizens-at a time, I repeat, when we were being called- upon to exert our utmost energies in the successful prosecution of the war, and yet I am prevented from reading this Order in Council to substantiate my statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have already declared the hon. member to be out of order in regard to the reading of that document.

Would it not be well if hon. gentlemen opposite were kept in order and some decorum observed in this House? That is infinitely more important than the mere wisdom of reading a particular order-in-council.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the right hon. gentleman is quite right, and that an effort

should be made on the part of hon. members of this committee to give a courteous hearing to every hon. member discussing these items. I would ask hon. members to follow that practice.

The location of our dominion arsenals is of too great importance to be passed over lightly, what has happened indicates what the policy of the Government is with regard to our national affairs. We have extracted from the Government at different stages information as to their policy in regard to national defence, and while a great proportion of the party opposite sit back and say nothing, yet the ministers who are responsible for the administration of their departments express in a half-hearted way what has been taking place behind the scenes. I ask this committee whether they consider it to be in the interests of good government that the Administration should negotiate for the disposal of one of the most important features of our system of defence without consulting Parliament or the people. When a policy of that kind is entered upon the people are entitled to know something more about it than has been furnished so far. And when by insinuation and innuendo it is made to appear that the people of Ontario are absolutely opposed to the best interests of this country, I think the Government have to put up some better arguments than they have advanced so far. The insinuations thrown out by the Prime Minister were such that every self-respecting citizen of Ontario will, I am sure, resent when the proper time comes they will call him to account. I refer to the campaign which he claims was carried on in Ontario in regard to national defence. Now, Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the evident desire that certain things should be kept from the public, so far as I am concerned I may say that I am going to protest as vigorously as I can on behalf of my constituents against the disposal of the Lindsay arsenal and^he maintaining of the arsenal in the city of Quebec. In doing so I do not wish to be understood as advocating the manufacture of large quantities of munitions at the present time; but we should have at our disposal the facilities for turning them out in the event of their being required, and, above all, we should have an arsenal located at a point where there will be absolutely no danger of any interference with those who would be there carrying out there duties in the event of a crisis arising.

Item agreed to.

As intimated the other day by the hon. Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham), I beg to move that this item be reduced by the sum of $50,000.
I beg to move an amendment that the item be reduced by the sum of $110,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It strikes me as peculiar that when we shut up one arsenal some hon. gentlemen object, saying that we should keep it open to manufacture munitions; yet they now show signs of being in favour of cutting $110,000 off the vote for the other one.
It was ruled, the minister will remember, that we could not discuss the proper location of the Quebec arsenal while the other vote was under consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Does the Chair contend that that had no relevancy at all to the question as to the proper location of the arsenal?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is no point of order in this, that I can see. I have made my statement as to the inconsistency of assuring the House that the Government should not think of shutting up the Lindsay arsenal, because of its being required to manufacture small arms ammunition, and of thereupon arguing that the Government should take $110,000 off the vote for the*)ther arsenal. I could understand the attitude if hon. gentlemen were in favour of not cutting either down. Now, the Government proposes, as moved by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that this item be reduced by $50,000. This, together with the reduction in the case of the other arsenal, is, I think, a big jump in the reduction of expenditure so far as these two items are concerned.
How much was spent last year at the Quebec arsenal?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For ten months, $311,000.

Will the minister inform the committee who is propounding the policy of the Government, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or himself? There is a motion to adopt this item, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, another member of the Government, proposes to reduce it by $50,000. I am wondering whether or not we have any government at all. This is surely becoming a spectacle such as has never before been witnessed in any civilized country. It is a peculiar procedure for one minister to move the adoption of an item and then for another minister, in order to forestall our friends to the left, to jump up and introduce a motion to cut the item down by a large amount. Surely this is an innovation in responsible government. I would like to know from either one minister or the other, which is the policy of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend I know, is thirsting for information. I would ask him this: if the vote related to works in the county of South Oxford, would he move a reduction, as the Minister of Marine did? I rather think he would say, on the contrary, that he wanted more. However, owing to the ruling of the Chair that the minister in charge of the estimates cannot properly move a reduction, as has been the custom in the committee for many years, it becomes necessary for someone else to move that reduction.
Why does the minister submit the estimate, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend will permit me to answer his question. As a matter of fact, if someone other than a member of the Government, had moved the reduction which I told the House some days ago we intend to move, the hon. member would immediately have raised the point that although the Government were responsible, they were getting a private member to move the reduction. So we make it absolutely governmental; a member of the Government living in the city of Quebec has asked the reduction.

The minister says that $311,000 was spent during ten months of last year at the Quebec arsenal. The proposal now is to spend $425,000 for this year; that is the economy the Government practices, it is not economy as I view it. We have a tremendous amount of large am munition; we certainly do not want any more of that. From what the minister has

told us to night, we have 45,000,000 rounds of small arms ammunition, enough to last, under ordinary circumstances, for four years; yet the minister proposes to reduce this item by $50,000 as an evidence of practical economy. It is economy, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

If that is economy as you have been preaching it for some time, it is not economy as I view it. You do away with the need for this ammunition by partly doing away with the annual camps; yet you now propose to make more ammunition.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not so much. My hon. friend is mistaken; he forgets that some ammunition was manufactured at Lindsay last year.
I understand that perfectly well.

speechtext: I think my hon. friend is right but I have the 18-pound in my explanation and it is an error that it does not appear in the estimates, surely.

The patriotic spirit in the hon. member for Lincoln has always been known in this House, but this year he is evidently changing his attitude. I do not understand how my hon. friend can think of putting questions to the minister of such a nature as to cause our military secrets to be divulged. The hon. gentleman has always been a very strong supporter of the British Empire, has likewise always been in favour of our taking part in the defence of the Empire. Is it fair therefore that my hon. friend should to-night ask the minister such questions that tomorrow every foreign power will k*ow exactly the amount of ammunition we have in this Dominion. I think the hon. gentleman is treading on most dangerous ground and I appeal to you, Mr. Chairman, to protect our military secrets from disclosure.

I rise to say that I think that when the conditions of this country have got to the pass where my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) taunts my hon. friend from Lincoln with lack of patriotism, we really should reconsider this vote. In view of the cuts that

Supply-Militia
have been made in the various estimates- in the militia estimates, in the navy estimates, in the estimates for various other branches of defence-it is only reasonable that the hon. gentleman who has moved a reduction-and he informs me that it is quite in proportion with the other cuts that have been made-should be supported. I find that as a result of the different motions which have been made in the House we have a nation without defence; we have a navy without sailors; we have a militia without annual training; we have estimates without consistency; and now hon. gentlemen opposite are proposing ammunition without an army. In view of these circumstances I am going to have very much pleasure in supporting the hon. gentleman who has moved the amendment to the amendment.

I am thankful to the hon. member for Dorchester for referring to me in the very kindly way in which he did. Let me say to him that we have very much missed his voice in the discussion of these estimates. But his voice was not lacking last year; he was one of those hon. members who were very persistent in moving for reductions. As I say we have missed him very much this session, we would like to hear something more from him; and yet to-night we find him defending an estimate which cannot rightly be defended. Let me say one word in respect to the accusation of giving away military secrets, I only asked for what is published in the estimates. That information is set forth there in black and white; it is there for anybody to see from one end of the Dominion to the other; and anywhere else for that matter. While I am on that question I may say that I have had placed in my hands a copy of last year's estimates and I find, although the minister would not give me the information, there is a matter of some six or seven thousand rounds of artillery ammunition referred to. I do not know what the price was but I think a reasonable figure to put it at would be about $25 a shell, which would represent a sum in the neighbourhood of $175,000 or $200,000. If I said the minister was misleading the committee, you, Mr. Chairman, would probably call me to order, but I certainly would like to have an explanation from him.

I am very grateful to the hon. member for his statement that he has missed my voice this session. If I have not taken as active a part in the debates
this session as I did in former years, the reason, I may inform the hon, member, was that I was studying the Roumanian question.
If it were in order, Mr. Chairman, I might ask my hon. friend what he learned from studying the Roumanian question so hard.
Axes sometimes cut.
If the Chairman wished to be fair to the committee he would tell my hon. friend that he has no business to talk about such a matter at such a time.

Surely the minister in the case of a large item like this, is going to tell the committee that he is acting on the advice of his technical experts. I may say that the freight charges for the carriage of small arms and ammunition in Canada is very great and that is one reason why an arsenal should be more centrally located. It certainly should not be established near the border of the country; that lesson has been driven home to us by examples during the great war. Surely from the standpoint of national defence a Dominion arsenal should be located where it is not easily open to attack. Suppose a hostile fleet ever sailed up the St. Lawrence what would become of the arsenal at Quebec? Is the minister going to depend on a few fishing boats and trawlers to protect the place, or does he expect it to be defended by the British fleet?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The suggestion for a reduction of $50,000 has not been made without full consultation with the officers responsible in the department. As I pointed out a few moments ago danger to any building in the future, as shown in the recent great war, will likely come from the air rather than from approaches by sea or land. There is no part of Canada, as far as I know, that could not be attacked by bombs from an aeroplane.

The minister was
asked, what portion of this sum of $428,300 had relation to small arms last year and what proportion to heavy arms or bombs? I should like an answer to that question, notwithstanding the pleasantries of the hon. member from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), and upon that answer I shall make a further inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The amount expended last year was divided between small arm

Supply-Militia
ammunition and artillery. I think there were about 6,000 rounds of artillery ammunition-

Give it in dollars and cents. That is the only way, in my ignorance, I can interpret it. How much of this $428,300 was for small arms, and how much for heavy ammunition? I am told there was $311,000. How much for small arms and how much for 18-pounders? It seems that the answer is not readily forthcoming, and I would almost think that the member for Dorchester, in that happy manner of his, has to draw aside an intelligent answer to that question. What do we find? This Government has proposed, and has succeeded in its proposition, to strike $700,000 from militia service estimates, and $1,000,000 has gone from the naval service estimates. That means that $218,300 have gone from the appropriation which was made last year to the Lindsay arsenal, and the proposition now is that, notwithstanding that $1,700,000 have been stricken out of the amount this country is going to have for its defence and, that $218,300 have gone from the Lindsay appropriation, we shall -strike only $110,000 from the amount that is voted for the Quebec arsenal. Under all the circumstances, from the amounts that have already been stricken out, this amount of $110,000 should be increased. Upon any reasonable solution of this proposition there is no question the amount should be larger, and if hon. members opposite want to justify the larger vote than the vote, minus the $110,000, they ought to explain it to the members of this House. In view of these large amounts that have been proposed, not by the Opposition not by the Progressive members, but by the members of the Government themselves, to be stricken from the naval and militia estimates, I have great pleasure in supporting this $110,000 rebate which the Progressive member asks, but which I think is altogether too small a sum, and I would support a proposition to strike off any other sum which could be saved to this country on this deal.

I do not propose to approach the consideration of this question from any political point of -view. I -have sat several hours in this House through what I would 'like to characterize, if it would not be too harsh, as a succession- of farces. - It seems to me the -navy has sailed back again into the Militia Department, and really when hon. members ask

for information, from the minister, I do not know whether they are asking it from the Captain or "Little Buttercup." The nearest thing we get is that it is shady-it is shady, for we cannot -obtain any exact information. I do not propose to vote for the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. mem/ber for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) unless I am forced to do so for want of information. It -does not square with my idea of the manner in which military or naval subjects should be treated in this House. I	am
prepared to give here an absolutely non-piartisan vote in support of any estimate that the Government will bring before this House with a sense of responsibility and- with a courage that faces the House and the country and -says the amount is required for the defence of Canada. Anything else would be exceedingly small politics indeed. I invite the hon. -minister to give us frankly the advice that 'he surely must have had from his experts and show us what this vote is for. Evidently what appears on page 29 of the Estimates is either a mistake or a sham. Let him give us What ought to replace that, and show us what they intend to do with it. I will assume that what was done at Lindsay last year is to be done at Quebec this year. That is a question of territory, and a question of politics, but if -ammunition is required for the Canadian militia it must -be made somewhere. The Government has to -settle that question. The -hon. member thinks the only danger is from the air. I think there is too much danger from the air in this House. We want to bring the thing out of the air, and get it down to concrete form, so that we can understand it and vote intelligently upon it. Can we have a plain direct statement as to the ammunition, not that some political body has recommended, hut that the officers of the Militia Department have recommended, as being necessary. Tell us the reasons of it and the cost of it. For one, I am prepared to vote for that cost, but I want more information and I want it here. I would like, at the same time, although it is not so important, to- -have an explanation to this House of why, when the estimates, which are supposed to be thoroughly considered and prepared by the minister with the assistance of his staff, were brought before the House they were brought down with apparently $50,000 more demanded than the minister thinks necessary now. I make no cavil with regard to the fact that the Minister of Marine, or some other member of the Gov-

Supply-Militia
ernment moves an amendment, but why should it be necessary to amend the estimates? Will the Minister of Militia tell this House one single bit of technical advice he has received from his experts since these estimates were laid on the Table of the House weeks ago, that he can transmute into $50,000, and show as a justification for cutting off that amount? Is this a real bona-fide reduction because his technical officers advised him that the original estimates were prepared in error, or is it a bit of cheap political stage play before the members of this House and the people of Canada? Let us have the reason. After all that, even if he finds it is only because the political club has been shaken, or because he wants to gain favour with some members of the morganatic alliance, if he will say he cannot stand the reduction suggested by the hon. member for Cariboo, I will vote for what he proposes, because I do not propose to take the responsibility in the matter. If, some months later, an emergency should arise, I do not propose to be counted as one of the men who refused to do what the military authorities of this country said was necessary.

Two or three times since this session opened, we have heard something about alliances. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) spoke, in the early part of the session, of a proposed alliance of which the banns were forbidden. The hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Baxter) for the second time has used the term "morganatic alliance". When those expressions were used, I for one could not but recall a certain illicit alliance that was entered into at one time, an alliance of which hon. members to my right have been reminded two or three times by hon. gentlemen opposite, an alliance that was entered into, as such illicit relationships are often entered into without very much regard for the consequences,-consequences that at one time threatened to be serious to the people of Canada, and consequences which were serious. I should like just to remind our hon. friends who speak of morganatic alliances that they ought to remember some of those alliances of the past-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that while he introduced his remarks on the appropriation for the Dominion arsenal at Quebec, his remarks in the committee up to the present have not been relevant to this particular appropriation.
Go ahead.
I submit that my remarks may not be relevant; but neither were the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Baxter).

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Baxter) rather suggested that I was concealing information. The decision to reduce by $50,000 was not made by the Government. That made, of course some little difference in the details. I read out to my hon. friend a few moments ago all that the Government proposed to manufacture at Quebec with the $425,000. The change would be that we would drop some of the small arms and manufacture 5,000 rounds of 18-pound shells.
What is that in money? No one has told us that yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have informed one hon. gentleman that I have no calculation as to the cost and I cannot possibly give that to him to-night.

I want to know if I understand the minister aright, that at the time the estimates were brought down to the House, he did not know that shell ammunition would be required; that he has been informed since then that shell ammunition is required, and that he will have to cut down the small arm ammunition in order to make room for the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I want to give my hon. friend all the information. As I stated a few moments ago, an error was made in leaving out the 5,000 rounds of artillery ammunition.

In reference to the 5,000 rounds of 18-pound ammunition, we have no information as to the cost. I ventured the opinion a while ago that it would be worth probably somewhere between $20 and $25 a shell. Might I ask the minister, as his deputy is present, if that includes the explosive, the cartridge and the primer, the whole thing complete, loaded?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed by my deputy that that is the whole shell complete.
At $25 apiece, that would mean that the small arm ammunition would be cut to the extent of $125,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not finish my remarks. I did not state any price.

The minister has not done so yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am doing my best to do so. I am informed that the complete shell will cost from $18 to $21.

The committee is in just the position in which it was when this estimate was first brought up. The estimate is for virtually the same amount as that of last year. The only reason advanced so far by the minister for its reduction is that some 5,000 rounds of 18-pound shells extra are required. That might be a reason for increasing the estimate. No reason at all is given for the reduction; but, of course, we all know the reason; the reason is simply a demand made that it be done. But inasmuch as everything else is reduced that is of service, I for one do not know any reason why it should not be $110,000 less, or even $150,000 less, just as much as $50,000 less. We have no information on the subject at all. I need not comment on the inconsistencies of the Government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) went through the last campaign-and ever since, indeed, he has continued the process-storming against the quantity of ammunition that was in the country, promising all sorts of exposures, all sorts of scandals about it, complaining that ammunition that we owned was brought here at the mere cost of carrying it, and now he comes to Parliament and wants us to vote $375,000 to make some more.
No reason whatever has been given as to why the Lindsay arsenal is closed and this one continued. The minister says: "There is danger as regards both being destroyed in the event of hostilities." We all know that there is possibly equal danger from the air; but the one is in very grave danger from the chief source of peril, and the other in no danger from that source at all. In point of danger, as regards geographical location, the argument is wholly in favour of the Lindsay arsenal. The minister never attempted to make any reply to that, nor to shift from the shoulders of his Government the very obvious explanation that it is merely a political move, keeping the one and abandoning the other. Inasmuch as we have no explanation at all why $110,000 cannot go off just as much as $50,000; inasmuch as the minister has reduced the provision for the rest beyond what he admitted, once at least, was the margin of safety, and inasmuch as he had virtually abandoned the training or, at least, the greater part of the training, can he show us that there is not on hand sufficient to enable them this

year to get along with the quantity that would be allowed by the amendment of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) ? Indeed, so far as information is given to the committee, there would not require to be any made at all, except perhaps of one line. If I have understood all the information given, there is enough of the rest on hand to last from four to nine years. Why then go ahead except with the line as respects which there may be some shortage? In a word, unless we are to get information that puts the responsibility up to us, I know of no reason for voting money here at all. We have enough to produce just what the minister says we need.

I want to make my position clear on this item in just a word or two. I want first of all to congratulate the minister on his courage in making these reductions, not only this particular reduction, but reductions in other items that we have already considered. It is my judgment that these reductions will be received throughout this country with considerable satisfaction, if not with enthusiasm. It is my hope-and I trust I am justified in that hope-that these reductions will be interpreted as economies effected in the interest of soldiers' civil re-establishment. Even this afternoon and for several days I have been moved-and I possess a somewhat phlegmatic nature-by the kindling eloquence of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). His speeches in the interests of Canadian defence were eloquent. He says that the policy of a country-referring to its defence-is reflected in the moral character of the citizens of that country. I was deeply moved by his appeal. But I cannot understand his position at the moment.
Well, I do.

I cannot understand the attitude which hon. members to my right are taking. Even allowing that we have no militia at all, would not common sense tell us that ammunition itself is a factor in national defence in view of the thousands of trained men we have throughout the country? Now, these are the men that talk about national defence, and sing "Rule, Britannia." I do not take second place to any member in this House in my loyalty to the British Empire. I had the good fortune, or the misfortune, whichever you like, to come from a part of the country that has suffered more than any other part of the British Empire in the

Supply-Militia
determination to adhere to that Empire. But I say I cannot understand at all the position taken at the moment by the right ' hon. gentleman to my right, and I want to congratulate the minister (Mr. Graham) on his courage in giving way to the wishes of Paidiament in this regard and in making these reductions in the interests . of economy, thus relieving the people from the oppressive and ponderous burdens under which they are labouring.
Mr. Chairman-
Speech No. 34.
I am grateful to hon. gentlemen for the applause they have seen fit to accord me.
Will the hon. member allow me a question? Is this the first time he is speaking?
If it is your will, Mr. Chairman, and the will of the committee that we convert ourselves into an entertainment association we might import movies here with some degree of success.

We do not have to when
you are here.

The subject is treated as one purely of levity on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite. They seem prepared to spend money so long as it is spent just in the way they want, and when they get sufficient fun out of it in the House. I am not at all surprised at the position taken by the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Hoey). I make no comment on any alliances; I let the facts speak for themselves. The records of this House is a pretty good disclosure to the people of the country as to just the relationship between that hon. gentleman, at least, and some others near me, and hon. gentlemen opposite. He says that he does not understand me. As soon as it is shown to me that the further manufacture of ammunition to this extent is necessary, as soon as the minister states it on his responsibility and gives me the facts to prove that it is necessary to have this ammunition on hand for our purposes, I will support him, and support an increase in the vote.
He has already given that explanation.

The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Hoey) is easily satisfied. And if any hon. gentleman thinks the action courageous of a minister who brings an estimate to Parliament, declares it is the
minimum for the safety of the nation, and, because a roar is raised behind him, reduces it, then the relationship is pretty easily established between him and such a minister. The minister has stated that he cannot give any figures at all to show the cost of the extra ammunition he wants, nor will he tell us what it is proposed to make. We do not need to know accurately at all, but we should like him to give, even roughly, an estimate as to how long what is on hand will last, and what the cost will be of what it is proposed to make. As soon as we have that information and it is shown that we need that extra ammunition I am prepared to vote every dollar of the $50,000, every dollar of what in the first place he said would be required.

The Minister of Militia before leaving the Chamber said that he anticipated the greatest danger to the arsenal from the air. I would ask the Minister of Marine (Mr. Lapointe) who has moved to reduce the item, when the Government decided on this reduction? Was it after the estimates for the air force had been reduced by $617,000? This reduction was made in the expenditure on the Canadian Air Forces a short time ago in connection with the policy of the Government on national defence. The minister informed the House that he anticipated a greater danger from the air than from any other source. Possibly that is the reason why the arsenal has been removed from Lindsay to Quebec. Now it will be a long way from the headquarters of the remnant of the air service which was and might be situated at Camp Borden, and I think that Lindsay would have been a much more suitable place for the arsenal. Does the minister anticipate danger to the Quebec arsenal from our own air force or from some foreign force? Will he inform the committee as to when it was decided to reduce the item $50,000? He has told the committee that he made an announcement to the effect some days ago. Evidently I was not in the House at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That has been explained already.

In last year's estimates the total amount of small arms ammunition proposed to be made was seven and a half million rounds, or perhaps about eight million. According to the estimate, at page 29, this year it is proposed to make seventeen million rounds. This is what the minister calls practising economy. He
Supply-Militia

proposes to make nearly seventeen million rounds of ammunition as against seven or eight million rounds last year.
Does not the hon. member think that the reduction proposed is a fair one in view of the fact that a truce has just been signed for eight months at Genoa by thirty-four nations of the world?
There is no reduction. I have just pointed out that there is an increase of some nine million rounds of ammunition this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend does not understand the facts. The nine million which he has added to the seven million have been deducted from the list.
Well, you never said so before. At page 29 of the Estimates, there are two figures, seven millions and nine millions.

How many years'
supply have we on hand in the way of reserve? Can the minister tell us that, and on what authority? The only information I have heard has been that we have forty-five million rounds and that the utmost that has been used were ten million. There will be less used this year on account of the reductions in the other estimates. What is the minister's policy, and what does he base it on, as to the number of years' reserve that should be on hand?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If I remember correctly the figure given by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), it is eighty million rounds.
There is that reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service

No. I do not say that
any Canadian government has maintained that reserve, but it is the opinion of Lord French that a reserve of eighty million rounds should be maintained. I imagine that provides for ten million rounds in addition being used each year.

That is for a very
much larger force than the minister contemplates by his policy. What is the minister aiming at himself, and on what does he base his opinion as to what we ought to have by way of reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My officers think that
we ought to have eighty million rounds in reserve, but we have not anything like that number of rounds.

The hon. minister's

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one of
the amounts in this item is $500,000 for the battlefield memorials. I admit without any hesitation that I think it should be separate. A committee composed of members of both Houses was named to deal with this matter. I might by repetition detail the history of the appointment of that body, but as the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) is chairman of it, I would suggest that he give to the House a resume of what has been done.

Mr. Chairman, I
agree with the minister that this item should have been placed among the miscellaneous votes, but I do not criticise its inclusion in this vote.
For the information of some members of the House who were not then members,! may say that in 1920 a committee of the House [DOT] was appointed to consider the question of Canadian battlefields' war memorials. That committee sat for some time, took evidence, and made a report to the House, recommending that certain memorials be erected in France and Belgium. Eight sites were selected as follows: No. 1, St. Julien; No. 2, Passchendaele; No. 3, Observatory Ridge; No. 4 Vimy Ridge; No. 5, Drury Crossroads; No. 6, Bourlon wood; No. 7, Cour-celette; No. 8, Hospital Wood.
Subsequently a commission was appointed consisting of the Hon. . Mr. Lemieux, General Sir Richard Turner, Colonel Leonard, Senator Turriff and myself, a purely voluntary commission, to consider the erection of these war memorials. A competition was held for designs, open to architects and sculptors all over Canada, and very complete rules were printed and issued. Something like 160 competitors submitted designs. The assessors appointed to consider those designs were, Professor C. H. Reilly, representing the Royal Institute of British Architects; M. Paul P. Creats, representing the Societe Centraie des Architects (Paris); and Mr. Frank Darling, representing the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada. Those assessors selected seventeen designs

Supply-Militia
for the second stage, and from those two awards were made, one to Mr. Allward of Toronto, the other to Mr. Clemenshaw of Regina.
The memorial designed by Mr. Allward, of which a photograph has been on exhibition, and I think is now in the Speaker's room, was proposed by the commission to be erected at Vimy. It is on a large and magnificent scale and has received great commendation throughout not only the length and breadth of this country but of England and France.
Working in conjunction with the Imperial War Graves Commission, we discussed the perpetuation of the names of Canada's missing. As you are all aware, the Imperial War Graves Commission is a body incorporated by Royal charter of which the Prince of Wales is chairman, and with which all the overseas dominions are associated. They are charged with perpetuating their quota within the war cemeteries by a headstone of simple design placed over the grave of every officer, noncommissioned officer and man. It has been unanimously decided that we should consecrate the names of Canada's missing within this one large memorial which we propose erecting at Vimy. Those names at the present time, I regret to say, run to about nineteen thousand.
The other seven memorials, exactly similar in design but on a very much smaller scale, will be erected at the other seven points. Land has been acquired at the eight different points at very low cost, one of the areas having been presented to the Canadian Government. General Hughes has been over there as engineer in charge; he has laid out the plans for the grounds, arranged for the grading of roads, and so on. We are hoping at an early day to complete the contracts for the erection of these memorials. I may say that this vote was brought into the House by myself in 1920 and again in 1921; it is now again presented this session. It was strongly recommended by the committee of the House appointed in 1920, and it has been practically a revote ever since. As I have already stated, this work is being carried on voluntarily iby the gentlemen whose names have been given. We hope this vote will pass the House unanimously, in order that we may be enabled to make some headway with what we look upon as the least this country can do to perpetuate the deeds of heroism of those Canadians who fell in France and Flanders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I wish to say just one word in regard to this vote and to the work of the War Memorials Commission. The hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) has spoken of what has been done in the way of the proposed erection of monuments. I hope the commission will consider very seriously indeed-I know in fact it is considering it-the advisability of acquiring a very considerable tract of land along Vimy Ridge as a permanent memorial. Whilst sculpture may do a great deal to commemorate the sacrifices of our men, Vimy itself is one of the world's great altars, on which a perceptible portion of our manhood has been sacrificed in the cause of the world's freedom. As a national memorial nothing can equal the preservation of the ridge itself, if it can be acquired. I hope the commission will go just as far as it can in acquiring what to Canada will ever be consecrated and hallowed ground.

I am glad the Prime Minister referred to that; there is just one word that I omitted to say. We took expert evidence as to the location of these memorials from all the officers, from the corps commander down, and in the decisions we arrived at we have been backed up by their opinion as well as by that of Professor Reilly, who went over and viewed the sites. The unanimous opinion was that the large memorial ought to go to Vimy. Many of the army officers held that Vimy was by no means the most important battle that was fought by the Canadian corps; yet it is agreed that there is something distinctive regarding Vimy that comes very close to the hearts of Canadians. We have a small site there and we feel that sufficient of that ground should be acquired; we trust that Parliament will approve whatever recommendation we may finally make with that idea in view. The base of this memorial will occupy very nearly an acre of ground, and we hope we can acquire at a reasonable price certain portions of Vimy to perpetuate for all time the outstanding features of Canada's exploits on that ridge. That, I think, is what the Prime Minister referred to. I may say that all the members of the commission are unanimously of that opinion, and General Hughes has agreed to continue the negotiations with the French Government and some of the owners with a view to seeing just what land we can acquire for that purpose.

I quite agree with the suggestion that additional land be procured

Supply-Militia

on Vimy Ridge. I was familiar with the work of this commission, because it is under the Department of Militia and Defence, as is also the War Graves Commission. I had an opportunity of personally inspecting all the eight sites which have been referred to by the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn). At the time I examined the sites, the work on them was progressing. A good deal of work has been done on some of them in the way of levelling, cultivation, and the construction of permanent roadways, which have made them very accessible and also very beautiful. But what struck one on looking at the eight sites was that Vimy Ridge was too far removed from the main road and that many people might pass by without their attention being specially called to the fact that this site had been chosen as the location of the memorial. Originally the memorial was to have been erected on Hill 62, near the Ypres salient, but on further consideration, those more concerned than I was with the matter-the officers who had charge of it-decided that Vimy would be a more suitable point. It so happens that there is a large tract of the ridge running right out to the main highway which can be secured, I believe, on very reasonable terms from the government of France, who still own it. I quite agree with my hon. friend from East Hamilton and with the Prime Minister that the Vimy site should be secured right to the main road. It cannot cost very much, and the result will be to add materially to the value of the property as a monumental site.

As this is a nonpolitical matter, Mr. Chairman, I may, perhaps, be allowed to say a 12 m. word. I had the honour to be appointed a member of this commission by the late government, and have attended all its sittings. The work has been most harmonious, and I must thank the late government for the appointment of my friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) as chairman of that commission. I have asked the new Government, since there has been a change, to maintain him as chairman of that commission. Very little has been said in the Canadian press about the monuments which have finally been selected, but in looking over the British and the French press- and, I may say, the American press, because our secretary has collated all these reports and comments published in the newspapers-we find with pride that the

monuments designed by Canadian artists equal, if they do not surpass, the memorials to be erected on that great battlefield by other nations. It has been stated-and I repeat, word for word, I think, what I have read in one of those most artistic reviews from France-that as regards grandeur, simplicity and reverence combined, there is nothing to equal the masterpiece that Allward, a Canadian, has produced. I re-echo the views expressed a moment ago by the Prime Minister. To Canadians, Vimy Ridge is hallowed ground, and it will be acquired by the commission if that can be done. I have nothing more to say; I repeat that I would not have taken part in this debate had the subject not been a non-political one. I am proud to serve on that commission and under my good friend the member for East Hamilton.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as this_
commission comes under the Department of Militia and Defence, I want to assure the committee that up to date everything connected with the commission has been most harmonious. The commission has had but one object in view, that of carrying out the wishes of Parliament in order that honour may be done to our dead and a lesson be thus taught to the living. I have visited some of the battlefields overseas, and take this opportunity or assuring any hon. gentlemen who are personally interested in the cemeteries over there that they are being taken care of in minutest detail.
When the work of the War Graves Commission is completed Canadians who go overseas will find places not only of beauty but places of reverent instruction, places helpful in forecasting the possibilities of the future viewed in the light of what has happened in the past. When I went overseas two years ago I was waited on by some gentlemen there who wished to get the views of the Canadian people on the suggestions that had been made, that the remains of the boys who had fallen should be brought back to Canada. It is a delicate question to discuss, but after having consultation with the War Graves Commission, and after visiting the cemeteries, I have no hesitation in giving it as my view that the boys ought to be left to rest where their day's work was finished. I believe that is best in the interest of the world as a whole because, in the years to come, these monuments erected to the memory of the Canadian boys will stand as a part of the history, in a sense, of the world's revolution, and if these bodies were to be removed we would lose one of

Supply-Militia
the great lessons of the war. These cemeteries will form in the years to come a monument to Canada's ideals, to Canada's courage, and to Canada's devotion to what the people of this land deemed to he the right. I hope in a year or two, if I live, to visit these graves again, and I feel assured, from the sites that have been located for the erection of these battlefield memorials, that every Canadian who visits that land will feel a greater thrill of pride when he surveys these memorials.

I am sorry the leader of the Progressives party is unavoidably absent at this moment, but having talked this matter over with him I know that had he been here his voice would have been raised in commendation of the work of the commission in reference to these war memorials. I believe too that he would have supported the idea of the Prime Minister that the commission should acquire a larger acreage in connection with the memorial at Vimy, and that this wonderful piece of work should not suffer for lack of space. It has been my privilege to view a photograph of these memorials and I am sure that all Canadians will feel great pride that we are to have such a memorial to commemorate the work of our men on Vimy Ridge as well as the smaller memorials at other points in the battle area.

I wanted to make one observation which I am sure the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) would have uttered had it not perhaps inadvertently escaped him, and it is this: I think the public should know that these monuments are being placed on spots which, to Canadian soldiers at least, are all historic ground. It is unnecessary to say that the monument at Vimy Ridge is essentially one of that character; but perhaps it may not be known that numbers of the others too, commemorate probably some of the greatest engagements in which the Canadian soldiers took part. I need only mention that the contemplated memorial at the crossroads near the little town of Dury commemorates the successful attack on the Hindenburg line, in which the Canadian corps formed the spearhead on that particular day in September. Might I also mention that the memorial proposed at Bourlon Wood commemorates the Cambrai attack in the latter part of September, 1918. So too it will be recalled that the proposed memorial at Courcellette commemorates the attacks on the Somme; and
similarly with the remainder. There is just one thing which occurs to me, as a tragic incident in connection with the war, and which probably will bring home to people who perhaps, at this distance, are not sufficiently impressed with the tremendous and awful horrors of war, and that is that to-day there are 19,000 Canadians, out of a total of 60,000 dead, who are missing. I think that is a tragic circumstance, and one that perhaps will not lose its significance upon those who seem to think that the horrors of war are overstated.

There was some arrangement with my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) that it should be discussed, but I know that my leader was under the impression that the rest of the vote would not go through to-night.

speechtext: Very well, we will hold it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: With the exception of this item; we are through with this particular resolution.

That is perfectly satisfactory.

That is, the debate'

On section 1-maximum compensation reduced.

As this Bill went through its second reading so quickly, I had not an opportunity of making a few remarks at that stage, but they probably can be made just as well now. As most hon. members are doubtless aware, since 1906 an act has been in force providing for certain compensation for animals on account of their being slaughtered to prevent the spread of contagious disease. That act has been changed from time to time with regard to the amount of compensation in proportion to the increase in value of animals on the market, whether pure bred or animals for commercial purposes. Now it is thought advisable to reduce the compensation to correspond with the reduction in value of animals on the market. That is the purport of this bill. There may be a difference of opinion as to the amount of this reduction on the various classes of animals; but I do not think there will be any difference of opinion in the committee as to the principle of reducing the compensation in proportion to the reduced value of animals on the market today. As a matter of fact, many animals are not worth one-half what they were two years ago; and as this bill is for the purpose, not of purchasing animals, but rather of indemnifying owners who have had animals examined and slaughtered, it is obviously inadvisable to leave these indemnifications at the high rate at which they are at present. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY HON. W. S. FIELDING, MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speechtext:
Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance, member for Shelburne and Queens), moved:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, eleven years have passed since I last had the pleasure of delivering the Budget Speech in this House of Commons. During these years, and particularly since the year 1914, a great change has come over the financial position of the Dominion. I am sometimes afraid that the full character and the consequence of that change are but inadequately appreciated and understood by the majority of our people. That Canada has built up a very large public debt; that the interest alone on that debt calls for an enormous sum of money, greater indeed than the total expenditure of Canada but a few years ago; that we have a large pension list; and that in various ways we have added enormously to our obligations, are facts well understood by all close students of our public affairs. I think they may possibly be understood in a way, a vague and hazy way perhaps, by the broader public whom we sometimes typify as " the man in the street." He has an opinion, no doubt, that things are a little more serious than they used to be; but I do not think he has quite appreciated the full consequences, of the change. Borne things are happening as in the good old days. The board of trade, the chamber of commerce, the city council, the town council, and all the other excellent organizations which exist for the advancement of the community, hold their meetings and pass their resolves. They decide at once that for some particular thing which is dearest to their hearts they must instantly have a large appropriation, and then they send sheaves of resolutions to that effect, sometimes following those up with delegations in carload lots to impress upon the Government the necessity of complying with their request. Have these people no notion whatever of the situation? It would hardly he fair to say that. Yes, they have a notion in a way; they have a formula of their own; and they will say to the ministers : " Gentlemen, of course we understand that the situation is a little more

anxious than it was wont to be; of course, there is need of economy. But the particular thing we want, everyone must admit, is entirely an exception to the rule." We are all in favour of economy for the other fellow, but we are not so ready to recognize the need of economy in the case of the things that are nearest and dearest to us ourselves.
I must to-day present two thoughts which are of paramount importance. The first is as to the need, the deep and earnest need, of economy. That means that we must appeal both to members of Parliament and to the people to pass what I may call self-denying ordinances. They must not expect all the things which in the good old days they got so readily,-it may be a railway, a bridge, a public work of some kind, a public building, a breakwater, a pier, or any one of the numerous things which we should all like to have, all in their way useful in the development of the community, all desirable, some of them even urgent under better conditions. But it is unpleasant to have to tell people, in most cases, that these things must for the present stand aside. The second thought is that, with all the economy that we can practise, there will still be need of severe examination into our taxation system. It is not pleasant to have to increase taxes, but the fact is that under our present taxation system, I am afraid, with all the economy we can practise, there will not be sufficient means to meet the various obligations of the country. And so we will have to ask the consideration of hon. members and of the public in order that there may be a proprer appreciation of these new conditions that have arisen.
The accounts for the fiscal year 1920-21 have been published and distributed, so that one need not dwell upon them to any extent. The budget speech necessarily takes some account of three years-the year which has passed and for which we have the public accounts, the year that is sometimes current-in this case it happens to be just finished;- and we have to have some regard to the year ahead.
Income and Expenditure
For the year 1920-21 the public accounts show what is called a surplus, to the amount of $73,268,391. Old members may recall the discussions that have taken place in this House from time to time with regard to the manner in which a surplus is declared. A Finance Minister who has

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
the good fortune to produce a surplus-I have had that good luck on a number of occasions-may find, and very often will find, that he meets with this criticism: Oh, you have no such surplus; you actually have run into debt during the year. The method in the past of showing a surplus has been to take what is called the ordinary expenditure of the country-the everyday expenditure, if I may so call it-and set against it the revenue of the year, which left you either a surplus or a deficit. If that revenue is more than the ordinary expenditure you will have a surplus; if it is less than the ordinary expenditure you will have a deficit.
But every year there are expenditures which do not appear in that calculation. The objection made in times past was well founded. It was and is a fact that there are always expenditures of a special character, and the criticism that has been made in times past is in that respect correct. The distinction that is drawn between capital expenditure and ordinary expenditure has often been a subject of debate. This much is clear, that where you have important public works, large undertakings- such, for example, as this building-they are a legitimate charge to capital account. There is very often much dispute as to what is a proper charge and what is not, but I have observed that notwithstanding criticism of that character, whenever a change of government occurred the new Minister of Finance coming into office fell into the old ways and claimed a surplus even when the country was running into debt.
It is not an unfair claim to make if the facts be clearly understood. It has always been the method by which our public accounts have been conducted. So when the accounts for 1920-21 claimed that there was a large surplus of $73,000,000, the method of bookkeeping was being followed that had existed in the past, yet as a matter of fact during that year there was actually an increase in the public debt of $92,000,000 and over, the difference, of course, representing the charges to capital and special account and that now ever-growing account, the railway service of the country.
If we turn to the year 1921-22, the year that has just closed, although the accounts are not quite complete we are sufficiently informed to be able to make a substantially correct statement of the outcome.
The income tax and business profits tax for this last year show an increase of $14,276,774 over the receipts of the previous year. That, of course, is very gratifying; but on the other side the Customs Department shows a decrease of $57,000,000. The total revenue from all Sources we place at $381,271,000, against in 1920-21 $434,386,000. There was, therefore, a very large decrease in the revenue of the year.
The expenditure charged to consolidated fund was $348,145,000, a decrease of $12,972,000, as compared with the previous year. With a revenue of $381,271,000, and an expenditure on consolidated fund of $348,145,000, there is therefore an apparent surplus, according to the method which I have spoken of, of $33,125,000 on the year just closed. There were, however, other expenses on capital account of $23,073,000, cost of loan flotations $80,218, demobilization $9,180,000. Then there are other payments which are classified as investments, active or non-active; only the active investments are taken in the reduction of the public debt.
The result of the operations for the year just closed is that while we have according to one calculation a surplus, we have to acknowledge an addition to the public debt of $86,417,000.
For the fiscal year 1922-23, on which we have entered, on the basis of our present taxation I would estimate that the revenue would be $332,629,000. In this we are including customs at $103,000,000, which is $2,500,000 less than the receipts of the past year. If our anticipations of improving business are realized, we should do a little better than this.
With regard to income tax we could not expect to be so fortunate. This tax is levied on the income of the past year, which was not a good business year; indeed, I think it was a year of exceptional depression, and the effect of that depression will be marked in the reduction of our income tax receipts for the present year. We received last year from income tax and from business profits tax $101,500,000. We would not feel justified in estimating for the coming year more than $60,000,000 from that source.
With a loss of revenue last year as compared with the previous year of $53,000,000, and with a prospect of a shortage of $40,000,000 on the income tax for the current year, the House will see that the situation is a very serious one indeed.
From these and other receipts we estimate a total revenue for the present year of $332,629,000, based, of course, upon our present system of taxation.
The estimates of expenditure which we have submitted to Parliament called for a

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
total of $466,983,359. Supplementary estimates yet to come will add something to this total, but I hope not much.
From our present sources of revenue we could provide for all our ordinary expenditure and have a modest surplus-in the way that surpluses are now made up- but there would still be a large expenditure on capital account and for the railways, and this would have to be provided for by additions to the public debt. That would not be a very cheerful prospect. We must soon begin to consider the question of the reduction of our public debt rather than aim to increase it. Great Britain with all her troubles has since the war paid olf £500,000,000 of her public debt. The United States is making efforts to reduce her public debt. We have not only made no reduction, but we have to acknowledge a steady increase in the public debt every year since the war. Last year, three and a half years after the armistice, we increased our debt by $86,500,000. If we cannot reduce our debt, we should at all events make strenuous efforts to guard against increasing it. We should endeavour to balance our budget, that is, to pay all classes of our expenditure. It would be a joy to me if I could tell the House that we have an expectation of that during the present year. I am afraid, however, the situation will not permit us to do so much. Let us ever recognize our obligation to move in that direction and make every possible effort toward the end in view. We cannot do this if we are content to rest on our present methods of taxation. Even if our estimates of revenue, which are conservative, should be exceeded -and I hope they will-we shall find ourselves short by a considerable sum. If we are to avoid that situation we must accept the responsibility of additional taxation.
The Public Debt
I want to call attention now to the increase of our public debt. Against the gross debt are set off what are called the assets of the Dominion. In former years practically all our assets were treated as good. When the amount was not very great in proportion to our business, perhaps there was no need of any discrimination, but when these assets, under the operation of our railways, grew to very large figures, it became desirable or necessary that there should be discrimination. My predecessor in office, very properly I think, made that discrimination by dividing

those assets into active and non-active. It makes no difference with regard to the general expenditure, but if only the good assets are set off against the gross debt we get a fairer statement of the real debt of the country. Now, we are continuing this method of treating the assets: we treat these railway moneys as loans. Perhaps there can be some just objection to that. The Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern are now virtually owned by the Dominion of Canada, and when we adfvance money to them we are, in a sense, lending money to ourselves. When we represent these debts as assets, a keen critic might find some fault. But it may be that it will be necessary to continue that system; we are following out the accounts for 1922 in that way. There may be an advantage and a convenience in separating the railway operations from the rest of our expenditure. However, there is another view of the matter. We have a justification for charging to capital or to a speeial account some particular thing-the building of a railway, for instance. Various classes of public expenditure having permanent results may properly be classified as assets, may properly be classified under capital account. But if from year to year we are to provide for the ordinary expenses of thi railway; if we are to provide for the deficit, the difference between receipts and expenditure; if we are also to provide large sums for interest on the bonds and other securities of these so-called railway companies-if we are to do that unfailingly every year, with a reducing figure we may hope, it will be open to some to say, with much justice, that this is no longer a special account but part of the ordinary expenditure of the country; and if so, that ordinary expenditure should be included before we undertake to declare a surplus. However, as I said a moment ago, there may be some advantage in keeping the accounts of the railways for the present as separate and apart from the others. If we clearly and definitely understand the nature of the transaction, I suppose there may be no serious objection to it.
The net debt on the 31st March, 1914-I am taking that year as one of great events -was $335,996,850. That was the accumulation of half a century of confederation. It included what remained of all the old provincial debts taken over by the Dominion. It included the construction of great public works. It included what we once thought were large expenditures. The

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
result of it was that that debt in 1914 was a shade under $336,000,000. That was considered in its day a large debt, and many a speech was made in this House as to its magnitude, many a cautious member wondered how we were ever going to stand it. But what are we to say of it to-day in comparison with the enormous debt that we now have? As against a little less than $336,000,000 in 1914, our estimated net debt on the 31st March of the present year was $2,427,296,798. Our largest increase was in 1920-$674,000,000; the smallest increase was in the year recently closed- $86,000,000.
Loans
During the year four Canadian government loans have been floated. Three of these have been in the names of the railway companies and one a direct government obligation. We still keep up the theory of corporations in regard to these railways; the railway loans are issued in the names of the railway companies, with guarantees by the government. As a matter of fact, the government to-day are both makers and endorsers of those securities; so that practically they are now government loans. Three of these loans, therefore, have been railway loans guaranteed by the government; the fourth was a direct government loan, of which I shall speak in a moment. In July, 1921, there were sold $26,000,000 of 6i per cent Canadian Northern Railway bonds guaranteed by the government. These were sold at 921; they were afterwards sold to the public at 961. There was thus on that transaction a clear margin of profit to the buyers of 4 per cent-the spread between what the government got and what the investors who got them paid. This, I think, indicates that it was rather a better transaction for the buyers of the bonds than it was for the government. In September, 1921, a $25,000,000; fifteen year 6 per cent loan of the Grand Trunk, guaranteed by the government, was placed. It was sold in New York to realize 92; subsequently it was issued to the public at 951, a spread in this case of 31 per cent-a little less than in the case of the previous loan, but still a pretty large margin for a transaction of that kind. A third loan was one of $11,000,000, floated by the present Government in March of this year, $11,000,000 of three year Canadian Northern Railway five per cent notes guaranteed by the Government. We needed $11,000,000 to retire obligations of the Canadian Northern Railway arising in New York and London.
We thought the arrangements that had been made on former occasions for the sale of these bonds had not worked out to the advantage of the Government, and we adopted a different method; we invited tenders in New York for the loan, receibed the bids, awarded the contract, and sold these notes at 99.03. They were sold again to the public at 991, a spread between what we received and what the investor paid of 59 cents on the $100, as against $4 on the hundred in one case and $3.25 on the hundred in the other.
Then, we come to the $100,000,000 5 per cent loan which we recently placed in New York. That loan was to run thirty years, with our right to redeem it, if we wished to do so, in twenty years. It was sold at 971; it was afterwards placed on the market at par. Some reference has occasionally been made to commissions. I ought to say that the word is not appropriate. In all these transactions to which I have referred there was no question of commissions; the price mentioned in each case was the net price received by the Government. Our $100,000,000 loan sold for 971 net; there were no commissions or charges of any sort to reduce it. We shall probably need for our financial operations some further borrowing at no distant date. I am hoping that when the moment arrives the condition of the money market in Canada will be such that we can have a domestic loan. I think many people regard it as important that we should place our loans at home, because the interest then is payable to our own people. That is an excellent idea, but it may be pushed too far. There are times when it would be manifestly advantageous to Canada to go abroad. But to begin with, times are not so favourable now for placing loans at home. The loans which were so successfully placed a few years ago had for their support the war spirit and the war fever of the .time. Men entered into these transactions largely from patriotic purposes, and they had money to invest in those days, for money was being made. That situation is not exactly repeated to-day. The last year has not been a good business year. Not many men have made money. Not many men have money to invest in government bonds to-day, and there is no longer the patriotic zeal for the war. A loan to-day must be looked upon as a coldblooded proposition. It might be you would have to offer, to induce our Canadian people to invest in a loan, a higher rate of interest than could be obtained

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
elsewhere. On anything like even terms I should prefer the domestic loan, if the money is available.
There is still another thought. Canada is still, I won't say an undeveloped country, but a partially developed country; Canada will still have to be a borrowing country for many years. We shall have to go abroad for capital. If we have too much money locked up in government bonds at home, there will be less money available for mortgages and industrial enterprises in this country. Much will depend on the condition of the money market. If there is an abundance of money, it may be wise for us to have a domestic loan. If there is not an abundance of money, it may be wise to go abroad, because if foreign capital is to be brought in it is easier for the government to bring it in probably than it would be for others. We may still hope, however, that conditions will favour a domestic loan when the moment arrives for us to make another move of that kind.
There is an interesting account that we have with the British government of which it is perhaps worth while passing mention should be made. In the early days of the war, arrangements were made by the government of the day with the British government whereby moneys were advanced by the Mother Country for the payment of our troops in England and France. For a considerable time that continued, and at one time we owed a very considerable amount to the Imperial government. In 1915, on December 31, we owed the British government almost $141,000,000. Then a change took place. The British government desired to buy munitions and supplies of various kinds in Canada, and they arranged with the Canadian government that advances should be made in Canada to the charge of the British government. Since that point was reached, the account has
turned the other way, and we have ever since that been the creditor of the British government to a large amount. At one time, on the 31st of August, 1919, the British government owed us the enormous sum of $333,000,000. On March 31, 1922, the year just closed, subject to some questions of readjustment with regard to exchange, Great Britain owed us on that date, $117,859,630. Arrangements have now been made by which this account is to be paid off in installments of $5,000,000 per month. We have received two payments of that character and no doubt in due course the whole matter will be settled.
Trade
Coming to the question of our trade, the effects of the depression of the past year are clearly seen in the returns of our import and export trade. As compared with 1921 our imports from the United Kingdom fell from $213,000,000 to $117,000,000, and our imports from the United States dropped from $856,000,000 to $516,000,000. Our exports to the United Kingdom held better, the amount for 1922 being $299,000,000, and for 1921 $312,000,000. Our exports to the United States showed the course of the decline, being $293,000,000 against $542,000,000 in the previous year. I do not wish to ask the privilege of the House to put in many statistical documents, but there is one statement prepared by our Bureau of Statistics which I shall ask the House to let me insert. It shows in a condensed form the trade of Canada with each country of the world for a number of years. It will not occupy a great deal of space, and it presents that aspect of the matter in a very quick form. If the House has no objection, I shall see that it is included in my speech.
