speechtext: Twelve Months ended March 1921

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
Trade Agreements and Negotiations
Several things have happened with regard to the tariff lately with other countries. An agreement was made by the late government, as the House will remember, with the British West Indies, which came into operation at an early date, and affected most of those islands. One of the islands, however, which remained outside for a considerable period, was Jamaica, but she has now joined the arrangement, and the agreement of that 'day is in force as between Canada and all the British West Indies.
We have many inquiries with regard to our relations with Australia. There have been communications for some time, under the late government, and under the present government, with the Australian government in relation to that. In the early days of our preferential arrangements, one of the Australian colonies received the benefit of the preference. New South Wales was a low tariff country and she was entitled to the preference. The neighbouring colony of Victoria had higher tariffs, and was not entitled to the preference. Soon after the Australian Commonwealth was formed a new tariff was adapted, which was less favourable than that of New South Wales, and from that time forward Australia has not had the benefit of our preference. Efforts have been made by the late government and by this to bring about a friendly arrangement between the two countries. Recently a member of the Australian government passed through Ottawa and we had an opportunity to discuss the subject with him. He manifested a warm interest in the matter and gave us every reason to expect that the Australian government would take a friendly view of our proposal. Thereupon we proposed to the Australian government that they should give us the preference which the United Kingdom enjoys, and we in return would give them the benefit of our preference. That proposal has not been accepted nor have we received any counter-proposal. However, we fully anticipate that some opportunity will occur for further negotiations, and our hope is that we will be able to make a satisfactory arrangement with the Australian Commonwealth.
Not many months ago this House ratified a treaty that had been made with France. It seemed to have been of a temporary character, contemplating a larger treaty at a later date. I believe the French Consul General approached the late government with a view to further negotia-
tions, but the time was not then deemed opportune and nothing was done. We have recently been asked iby the French Consul General to take up the matter, and have intimated our willingness to do so. That is the way the matter stands at the present. I hope at no distant datte we shall have some further negotiations, and possibly we may be able to revive the old treaty with France, or make some other treaty which will be fair and just to both sides.
Tariff Revision
Now I come to the question of tariff revision. In the Speech from the Throne His Excellency the Governor General said:
You will be invited to consider the expediency of malting some changes in the Customs Tariff. While there are details of revision, the consideration of which will require time and care that are not at present available, there are features of the tariff which it is felt may properly be dealt with during the present session.
The work of tariff revision may be divided into two parts. What I shall call part 1, the part wtoibh most concerns the public, I think, is that which touches the revision in the direction of re-
4 p.m. duction, if there is to be a reduction, in the duties of customs. That is probably the subject most keenly interesting both to those desiring the reduction and to those who do not desire it. The other part relates to what I may call readjustments in a different way. With the progress of time new conditions arise, new interpretations of the Customs tariff are given, new questions come before the Board of Customs, allegations are made that there is inequality between the duty on the raw material and the duty on the finished article. Many questions of that kind arise, not of wide concern to the public generally, but each of concern to some interest which is affected by it. There may be questions of that character to which we shall have to give attention at another time. Some of such there certainly will be, perhaps not so many as some people imagine, but with that portion of the question which relates to the matter of tariff reduction, we propose to deal at once.
The line upon which we ought to be expected to deal, and upon which we intend to deal, is expressed in a resolution that I had the pleasure of moving in this House a year ago:
That, while recognizing that existing financial requirements of the Dominion demand the maintenance of a Customs Tariff, the House is unable to concur in the declarations by the Government that the tariff should be based on the

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
principle of protection; the tariff is a tax, and the aim of legislation should be to make taxation as light as Circumstances will permit;
That the aim of the fiscal policy of Canada should be the encouragement of industries based on the natural resources of the country, the development of which may reasonably be expected to create healthy enterprises, giving promise of enduring success;
That such changes should be made in the Customs duties as may be expected to reduce the cost of living, and to reduce also the cost of implements of production required for the efficient development of the natural resources of the Dominion ;
That, while keeping this aim clearly in mind, the House recognizes that in any readjustment of the tariff that may take place, regard must be had to existing conditions of trade, and changes made in such a manner as will cause the least possible disturbance of business.
This resolution declares for tariff reduction-a tariff reduction that should be made with great care, guarding against any interference of a serious character with the business of the country. The policy so laid down is the policy we are prepared to carry out to-day. With the exception of one item, an increase for strictly revenue purposes, every change I shall propose to-day is a reduction in the Customs tariff; it is a revision downwards at every point.
British Preference
We maintain the British preference which the Liberal government established in 1897 and 1898. When that principle was adopted by the Canadian government it gave offence for a while to some of the people of other nations. Germany, in particular, took offence at it, and for a while undertook to penalize us because of the action we had taken, Other countries, perhaps, did not like it, but still took no very strong part against us. Germany and Belgium were in a particularly favoured position. Other nations had the benefit of what is called " Favoured nation treatment That is, that any nation having what is called a " Favoured nation " treaty shall, at all times, be on even terms with any other nation. That is the general principle of what the favoured nation condition requires. Germany and Belgium had more than that. Germany and Belgium had made treaties-Lord Salisbury called them " those unlucky treaties "-under which they had a right to claim not only the same conditions that were extended to other foreign nations, but the same terms and conditions that were extended to our Mother Country. We had to get rid of
those old treaties before we could establish the British preference, and in the end we did.
In the United States some objection was taken, but not in an official way. There was a good deal of discussion in the American press as to this, as was said, " unfriendly act"; but the American government never took (Objection. When the matter came up they understood that it was entirely a question within our own family circle. And that is the situation to-day. We stand by the British Preference today, and the world recognizes that it is our right to make any arrangement we desire within the Imperial family without any other nation having cause to take offence at it. So we adhere to the British Preference in the arrangement we make, and the effect of the change that we make will be to increase, in some respects, that preference.
Trade with the United States
For many years we regarded the United States as pursuing an unfriendly policy towards Canada in tariff matters. I do not think it was ever deliberately intended to penalize Canada; but we were the nearest neighbour and the tariff policy of the United States unquestionably did seriously affect us, and produced a good deal of hostile feeling in Canada; for years we had reason to complain and we did complain. There came, however, a happier moment when a change occurred. There came a moment when the American government sent representatives to Ottawa to ask us to reopen negotiations, and see whether we could not come to a friendly arrangement. The result of that negotiation- first held in .Ottawa and afterwards in Washington-was the making of a comprehensive agreement. It was not a treaty but a comprehensive agreement which was entered into in 1910-11 as the House will remember. I am wondering whether we did not miss the golden opportunity then.
There is a tide in the affairs of men
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.
The flood tide of goodwill in trade matters from our American neighbours came to us in 1910-11, but unhappily the Canadian people did not accept the agreement. I do not want to dwell upon that further than to have the fact clearly understood that though, in former years, we had reason to complain of unfriendly action, at that moment we had every reason to recognize

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
the fairness of the American government. A happy combination of circumstances arose then which has not arisen since; which perhaps may not come again. A Republican administration, an administration representing the party of high tariff, was in power at Washington; and yet that Republican administration had come to us with a willingness to give us what we thought was a fair deal. The Democratic party was traditionally a low tariff party; and so, with the Republican administration supporting the agreement, the Democratic party naturally gave it their good will. The agreement was confirmed by the American Congress. It was not confirmed by Canada, much, as I think, to the regret of many of the people to-day who at that time did not view it with favour. Now many things have happened since that time. The Democratic party coming into power established trade arrangements which, for some years, gave us some of the benefits which reciprocity would have given us. The Democratic tariff gave us a chance still to do business, and we did a very extensive business. Unfortunately, however,-no I should not say that; we do not want to meddle in the politics of our neighbours-the people of the United States in their wisdom turned out the Democratic party, and the Republican party were restored to power. Since they were restoi-ed to power they have introduced what is called the Fordney Emergency Act, which deals largely with agricultural products. That Act unquestionably worked great harm to the Dominion of Canada, and especially to our western provinces. There is no doubt in the world-we may frankly acknowledge it-that the trade relations that had grown up between the two countries were sadly marred by the Emergency Tariff Act, and our western country in some branches of industry-notably the cattle business-has suffered severely in consequence. Now there is another Tariff Bill at Washington-a bill that has passed the House of Representatives and is now before the Senate-which proposes to enlarge on the Fordney Emergency Act. It includes, I think, all the duties of that Act, and in some instances they are increased. It proposes to establish a schedule of duties which is very high indeed. We have no right to complain of our American friends for doing that; but if they assume that position they cannot expect us in Canada to be as willing as we otherwise would to deal liberally with them. If our American brethren try to persuade 
themselves that you can sell all the time and never buy, we can only regret that they are failing to understand an economic truth; but since they want to pursue that policy we regret it because it must affect our own attitude towards them. I have had the privilege of being at Washington to discuss this question. I have had the opportunity to say to the President of the United States, and to the leading Congressmen of the Union, that Canada, notwithstanding the events of 1911, was prepared to open negotiations. We were glad that we had a friendly offer before. We were sorry on account of the difference with respect to it amongst our own Canadian people. However, we thought that was past and gone. We thought that the Canadian people to-day were prepared- at all events we the Government of Canada were now prepared-to undertake negotiations with the desire to obtain something like the agreement of 1911. Anyhow we took that course feeling that if would bring about better relations, believing that good relations will be 'better for both countries. We do not say that we are dependent on the United States, and still less that the United States would admit that they are dependent on us; each country can live and prosper and flourish without the other, but both will live and prosper and flourish more if they have friendly relations and intercourse as good neighbours should. A distinguished American, who himself was closely identified with the reciprocity movement in 1911, said some months ago that if the reciprocity movement was ever to be revived it must come from Canada. The United States, having made a friendly offer which was rejected, could not be expected to come to Canada again. That was a fair criticism. It was our move; we have made the move, and we have intimated to the American government in the way that I have described, that we are quite ready to re-open negotiations, with every desire to make a friendly arrangement. Whether anything will come of that or not remains to be seen. For the present, while our American friends are not prepared to meet us in the generous spirit they did in 1910 and 1911, while, in their judgment, it is necessaxry to adopt the higfh tariff policy which is now before Congress and which, in all probability, will become law, they will surely admit that, at such a moment, they cannot reasonably expect us to make concessions towards them. Therefore, we propose to hold our hands in that respect

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
and to await the turn of events at Washington. We shall be open at all times to friendly negotiations; but for the present, we are about to make tariff reductions which we are not prepared to extend to them. Whether we shall later be able to extend any of them to the United States or not depends entirely upon the attitude which they assume. I think myself there is a hope for better things. The bill at Washington is not universally popular; there is very strong opposition to it, and there is a possibility that it may not pass. But at all events, I think

and I am sure the House will agree with me-that until we have a clear understanding of what our American friends are going to do, we should hold our hands as regards the United States.
The reductions which we are going to make are almost entirely in the British preference. We are not going, except in a few cases, to reduce duties on American goods, which come to us under the operation of the general tariff. There are a few things which we desire in Canada which can be obtained most conveniently from the United States. As regards agricultural implements, for example, to offer a reduction of the British preferential tariff on agricultural implements would only provoke a smile, because such things are not brought from Great Britain; they are made in the United States. In that case, and in a few similar cases, we reduce the tariff on American goods, that is the general tariff, because that is the tariff that applies; but speaking broadly and generally, our reductions are being made in the British preferential tariff and not in the general tariff which would apply to the United States.
Marking and Valuation
I shall come shortly to the details of what we propose in that direction. Meantime, let me say that there are some other features to which I wish to call attention. The budget of last year introduced a number of features which, though I am sure they were well intended by the minister who introduced them, did not work out well. They have proved to be unsatisfactory, and I think there is no question about that now. One of these provisions was an amendment to the Customs Tariff Act providing that all goods that were imported should, where possible be marked, stamped, branded and so forth, and penalties were imposed for failure to do this. The government which passed that regulation evidently had occasion to reconsider their judgment on the matter; at all events they Were reluctant to enforce it. The law required that the act should take effect on the 31st of October, 1921, I think it was; but when that date arrived, the then government decided that they would not enforce the act, and they gave notice by Order in Council that its enforcement was postponed until the 31st of December. When the 31st of December came, another Government was in power by one day-it got in on the 30th1- and the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue of the present Government shortly after advised that the thing was unworkable and that it be postponed until the present Parliament should be consulted. We are now in a position to determine what to do. Our opinion is that, as a general law, this provision should be repealed. We propose, in any particular case of an exceptional character, when there are reasons why articles imported from abroad should be marked, that we should have the right by Order in Council to deal with the matter; but we propose that, as a general law, this provision shall be repealed.
Another provision of that kind was with regard to the valuation of goods. The time-honoured system of Canada was that the value of goods for customs purposes was the fair market value in the country of production. That has been our custom for ages. A proposal was made last year to enact that the customs officer must determine the value; that the value for duty must be not less than the cost of production in the country which produces the goods, plus a fair profit. How an unfortunate customs officer, any one of the hundreds scattered throughout Canada, was going to be able to determine the cost of production of these things in a far-away country, I cannot readily understand, and still more would be his difficulty to determine what, under all the circumstances, was a fair profit. However that may be, we are of opinion that that also is an unnecessary interference with trade, and we propose to wipe it out.
Another regulation of a somewhat similar character dealt with the question of depreciated currency. The German mark, for example, is normally worth nearly twenty-four cents; it is actually worth today one-third of a cent. The act of last year provided that in no case should depreciation of currency be recognized below 50 per cent. That is to say, in the case of German trade, whatever might be the value of goods for customs purposes, the mark was to be declared worth 50 per cent of its original value; that is, roughly

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
speaking, it should be worth about 12 cents. The normal value of the mark is 24 cents; it is declared to-day to be worth 12 cents, whereas, the actual value to-day is one-third of a cent. What you do by this is really to multiply the duty by a fictitious value, to multiply it by 36 times to-day. That is to say, the thing which is worth only one-third of a cent, you say shall be worth 12 cents. That multiplies its value, as I said, 36 times. So, while you keep up the pretence of a duty of 35 per cent, you are actually taxing those goods 1,000 per cent. If you want to say that German goods shall be prohibited, say so; if you shrink from saying that in such a direct way, then put on the 1,000 per cent duty; but do not humbug the world at large by pretending that we have a duty of 35 per cent when the real duty is about 1,000 per cent.
Another feature of the matter to which I should like to draw attention is this: The design, no doubt, was to give an enhanced protection to some industries which desired it; but what was the effect? The late government have not succeeded in shutting out German goods. What they have succeeded in doing is in shutting out the Canadian merchant from an opportunity of doing direct trade and in obliging him to pay tribute to somebody else. For example, if a merchant in Holland buys goods in Germany, takes them to Holland and then sells them to a merchant in Canada, the invoice is expressed, not in German marks, but in the currency of Holland which is not depreciated. The Hollander is allowed to purchase the goods at their real value, and the Canadian merchant can go to Rotterdam and buy the goods; but he has to pay the real German price plus the cost of transportation to Holland, plus the Holland merchant's profit-that is, the invoice price of the goods. The Canadian merchant can bring the German goods into Canada in that way; but he cannot bring them in direct. He can do better than that: he can go to England, where there is no duty. The English merchant can buy the German goods at the real value of the mark; he takes them to England, and he sells them to the merchants in Canada at an English price. The merchant in Canada still gets the goods; he is getting them to-day; but he has to pay tribute to the merchant in Holland or in London, and the real effect of this is to prevent the Canadian merchant from doing * a direct trade and to oblige him to pay 
tribute to somebody else. We propose to abolish the whole thing.
Another regulation at that time-it was a busy time in the Budget last year-contemplated the establishment of commercial agencies abroad and the requirement that a commercial agent of Canada should have his certificate attached to every invoice of $100 or more. It could |be seen at once that if that was to be effected, we would have to have a large army of commercial agents, scattered throughout the wide world. After adopting that, the government seem to have had some hesitation in applying it. They did not bring it into force at once. They provided that it should be brought into operation by order of the Governor in Council. They have never brought it into operation. To-day it is a dead issue and we propose to make it doubly dead by wiping it out.
We are making a numerous list of reductions. I shall not detain the House by giving every one. My recollection is that there are forty-nine or fifty items in the tariff that are affected. The resolutions to be placed on the Table immediately will give them all in detail. In the meantime I can state some of the particular items. Last year an arrangement was made whereby the duty on alcohol was increased to a very high figure. It is now $9 per proof gallon. Provision was made that in the case of men engaged in the making of pharmaceutical preparations, where they are largely engaged in the business, and are put to the expense of keeping a bonded warehouse, they are allowed to get alcohol at $2.40 per proof gallon as against the rate of $9 charged others. Now, the druggists of Canada, a very large and respectable body, require alcohol in the making of various preparations, and they are obliged to pay a duty of $9 per proof gallon for it, while the man who has a big warehouse and does business on a large scale pays only $2.40. We think that is inequitable. It was a great mistake on the part of the late government to adopt that scale, and we propose now that the druggists of the country shall be allowed-and we think we can devise a scheme whereby this can be done-to obtain alcohol for their own legitimate purposes, for the manufacture of the preparations they make, at the same rate enjoyed by the large manufacturing concerns. Of course, it is a matter that might easily lend itself to abuse. I realized that, and my

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
first thought was that there might 'be a danger of that kind. The druggists of Canada, however, are a most respectable body. They are, as a rule, among our foremost citizens, being organized under provincial laws, and I do believe that they will be only too anxious to see that this privilege is not abused. We believe, at any rate, that we can surround it with devices that shall make it absolutely sure that the druggists will use the alcohol only for their legitimate purposes and in no other way. We are doing this in order to meet what we feel to be a reasonable demand on the part of a large section of the Canadian people.
Now I shall give an intimation of some of the reductions in duty that have been made. We are making some changes in the law respecting tobacco, and these I may as well mention. It is proposed to change the duties on cigarettes and cigars and on Canadian raw leaf tobacco when taken into a licensed tobacco or cigar manufactory. The excise duty on all weights of cigarettes is increased $3 per thousand. The present rate is $6 per thousand for cigarettes weighing not more than 3 pounds per thousand, and $11 on cigarettes weighing more than 3 pounds. It is proposed to increase the rate in the customs tariff on imported cigarettes from $4.10 per pound, and 25 per cent, to $5.25 per pound and 25 per cent. It is estimated that the increase in both excise and customs tariff will give an additional revenue of over $5,000,000 per annum, after allowing for a reduction of 10 per cent in the consumption owing to the increased rate. The consumption of cigarettes has grown to immense proportions in Canada, the number consumed last year being equal to 267 for each man, woman and child in the country. It is proposed to readjust the duties on cigars. This will have the effect of reducing the duties on the low priced, and increasing it on the higher priced, cigars. The intention is to impose a graduated rate according to the value of the cigars. At present there is a tax of $6 per thousand irrespective of the value or character of the cigar. We want to introduce something like the principle of ad valorem, so that a cigar of medium character will still pay about the same rate, while the more expensive cigar will pay a higher rate. We think it is only reasonable that the cheaper cigars should be allowed to come in and be sold at a lower rate than the expensive cigars, and one effect will be to 135
increase largely the consumption of Canadian native leaf.
Then with regard to the duty on raw leaf tobacco. There is a duty of 5 cents per pound on raw leaf tobacco. At present raw leaf tobacco is of very low value. I was told the other day

possibly the case was an extreme one-that the value in some cases is little more than the tax, and therefore the tax seems to be a heavy burden. We propose now not to abolish the duty altogether, but to abolish it when the tobacco is taken into a licensed tobacco or cigar factory. We think that in that way it will lead to ah increased quantity of native tobacco being used in the cigar factories, and when the tobacco is used in the factor ies we shall get the duty of 20 cents pei pound. This, therefore, is a move that is intended to help the native tobacco industry, which we all desire to see flourish, while it will not involve us in any considerable loss of revenue.

Financial Situation
I am not going to detain the House by referring to all the items dealt with. I shall lay the resolutions on the Table, and they of course will be scanned carefully by hon. members as opportunity occurs.
I have deemed it proper in this address to present very clearly what I regard as the gravity of the financial situation. I would not, however, have any one draw the impression that I have a gloomy view of the future. There is, happily, a brighter side. I have unbounded faith in the resources of our country and in the intelligence and patriotism of the Canadian people. The worst of the commercial and industrial depression is, I believe, over. Already the sun of better times is beginning to shine. I do not look for any rapid restoration to prosperity, but I believe that from this time forward there will be a quiet and steady improvement. Everywhere there seems to be hope and confidence that such improvement is coming. That hope and that confidence will ' have much influence in bringing about a better day. If Providence sends us a blessing of good crops this year, we may look for the beginning of the prosperity of former times. While we have diversified industries, all of them entitled to careful consideration, we shall do well to remember that agriculture is and will continue to be the occupation of the largest class of our people and the industry that has the widest influence on general prosperity.
No nation in these days liveth to itself. Whether we like it or not, every country is in some degree dependent upon events in other countries. It has been a topsyturvy world that we have been living in, and we cannot look for satisfactory conditions until the world generally recovers in some degree its balance. In our own country, if one thing more than another is necessary, it is the establishing of better relations between labour and capital.
Admirers of the British constitution claim as a virtue for it that wherever a grievance exists a way of relief can be found. Why should it not be so with labour and capital to-day? In nearly every relation of life we are obliged to submit to the judgment of authority. Why cannot labour and capital agree upon tribunals to which disputes can be referred? The lockout and the strike of to-day are evidences that our so-called civilization is

Budget Speech-Mr. Fielding
still far from perfect. Why should either labour or capital deem it necessary to resort to force? The general public, whose interests are so often affected by the conflict, have a right to expect that both capital and labour will endeavour to find a better way of settling their disputes. If labour at times seems to be unreasonable, let us not forget that in the days that have gone, too often the workingman, so-called, did not receive a fair share of the wealth which his labour created; too often he saw his employer grow rich and prosperous while the workingman had little more than an existence. There has been a happy change in this respect. We cannot return to pre-war conditions. The workingman's position has advanced. His standard of living has improved. He is unwilling to go back to pre-war conditions, and nobody should expect him to be content to do so. He has a right to expect better conditions for himself and his family than in former days. But he has duties to perform on his part. Labour has come to a sense of its power. Has it come to a sense of the responsibility and duty which should always accompany power? We cannot doubt but the mass of the working men, as we call them, wish to be good citizens of Canada. They hold interests in common with other classes of the community. They have wives and mothers and children and homes to protect, and protection for these can only come when law is upheld and order observed. There are so-called labour leaders who, unfortunately, preach the doctrine that the employer is the enemy of the workman. They preach the doctrine that the workingman should play an entirely selfish part, that his duty is to get all that he can in the way of wages and give as little as he can in the way of labour. Such men are a menace to the true interests of labour as well as to the interests of society generally. There are in Canada many labour leaders who refuse to preach these dangerous doctrines and who, while zealous in defending the interests of labour, are no less zealous in maintaining the interests of society. Let us pray that on this vital question capital and labour may alike recognize their responsibilities, that they may put aside every temptation to play a selfish part, and co-operate in efforts which will mark Canada in the eyes of the world as a land of peace, and progress, and prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to avail myself of the usual custom and to move the adjournment of the debate before attempting to answer my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) at length. Not having knowledge of the resolutions-indeed, not having heard theim -I could not be in a position to discuss the matter in detail. Perhaps, however, there are one or two things to which I ought to allude before moving the adjournment.
My hon. friend has referred to the question of loans, and he has given us particulars as to loans made, either railway loans or government loans. Of course, the question of the rate at which you should put out your securities, depends entirely on the state of the market at the time the issues have to be made. Let me say to my hon. friend at once that he chose a rather favourable time for his large issue in New York when he chose the date he did. But I was sorry, and I am still sorry, that my friend went to New York for the purpose of getting that money instead of getting it at home. He points out that to-day we have not the urge of war and the whip of necessity on our people, and that there might be difficulty in getting the money in the domestic market. Sir, I do not anticipate any such difficulty. The urge of war was over in 1919, when we raised a very large sum of money and had a very successful taxable issue. My hon. friend has referred to costs. Well, I think I should also refer to the question of costs in connection with these loan issues.
I would like to contrast the cost of doing business in our own country with the cost of doing business in New York, and to point to the advisability of raising money in our own country, thus saving the additional cost, except, of course, where the money has to be spent in the foreign market. To-day we have no maturities ip

New York; our next maturity there, if I remember rightly, is in 1926. The money, therefore, was not required for New York purposes. Well, we raised $100,000,000 in 1915 at a total cost to the country of .425 per cent, considerably less than one cent on the dollar-less, indeed, than one half cent on the dollar. In 1916 we raised another $100,000,000 at a cost to the country of .797 per cent, again less than one per cent. The third war loan of 1917 cost .888 per cent. The Victory loan of 1917, when there was a most intensive organization and a tremendous amount of work was done, and when the amount of $397,591,200 was raised, cost us 1.185 per cent. The Victory loan of 1918, when we raised $638,176,250, again cost less than one per cent- .903 per cent. The taxable issues of 1919, involving an amount of $607,691,300, cost us 1.061 per cent.. I point out also to my hon. friend that over and above all the considerations that he has mentioned in favour of a domestic loan as against a foreign loan, there is the further circumstance that when the loan is domestic we get a return in income taxes on the interest which we have to pay, and that is a very substantial amount.
The minister has referred to commissions paid on other issues. Well, Mr. Speaker, commissions that are paid, as well as rates that have to govern, depend on the state of the market. Where the risk is small, where the olferings of money for investment are great, money can be raised more cheaply from the point of view of interest as well as from the point of view of commissions to be paid. In the present year, as everybody knows, we have had a culmination of the collection of gold in New York; we have had an accumulation of idle money which cannot to-day be used in American commerce, and is awaiting investment.
I am not going to make a comparison of the values of our own issues at different times, but let us take the issues of Great Britain sold in the New York market. In 1917 Great Britain issued twenty-year bonds at 51 per cent, payable in 1937. The obligations were issued at par, with a commission cost to the British Government of 4.4 per cent. In 1919 sales were made of this issue as low as 93; in 1920 the issue sold down to 811, and in 1921 to 831. On April 25 of this year, when our $100,000,000 loan was marketed, that issue sold at a premium of 103, 191 points higher than the low of 1921-that is, there was a difference between the time our loans
{Sir Henry Drayton.]
were brought out and the time the $100,000,000 loan was made of 191 points-and 211 points higher than the low of 1920, a rise of ten points as against the low of 1919.
In 1919 an issue was made through the Morgan house by the British Government of 5i per cent ten-year bonds. The issue sold on a basis of 961, yielding over 6 per cent. In 1920 these bonds sold as low as 83i; in 1921, as low as 881. On the 25th cf April of this year, when the large issue was made, this issue sold at a premium, the price being 1071, an increase of 191 points over the low of 1921 and of 231 over the low of 1920. A further issue of three-year notes was also made by the British Government in 1919 and marketed at 98, yielding 61 per cent. This sold down in 1920 to 90J, and in 1921 to 941. On the 25th of April of this year that was up to 1071, an increase of 121 points over the low of 1921 and an increase of 16i over the low of 1920.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is as I say, in making loans questions both of commission and of cost are matters which have to be governed by the rates obtaining and the scarcity or plenty of money available at the time. I think it will usually be found that the smaller the issue, the less difficulty there is in placing it, and my hon. friend is entitled, of course, to consideration upon that point. I would point out that he has had two loans in this very good period. As to his first loan, of $11,000,000, he disposed of that on a cost basis of .59 per cent, a little over half of one per cent. There he is approaching something like the cost of domestic loans, a little lower than some of them, perhaps lower than most of them. A very short time afterwards, however, when there was still a bull market, he pays two and a half per cent on a loan of $100,000,000. That was the only matter that I ever questioned at all one way or the other. There is no doubt, as I said, that it was a good time in which to get the money. Other people also found it was a good time. This issue is costing us to-day, with all the costs incurred, something like 5.20. If I am wrong, my hon. friend will correct me. At that same time, the Greater Winnipeg Water District sold on the New (York market, according to the New York press, bonds to yield 5.1. The City of DesMoines, Iowa, sold their bonds at a price to yield, 4.2. The New York issue of $45,000,000, which came about the same time, was sold to the syndicate that took it over to pay on the basis of 4.12 and it was offered to the

They spent many years on the force in the early days when the pay was so small that, as a consequence, the pension which they are today receiving is totally inadequate to keep, I might almost say, body and soul together. Many of them are receiving pensions which would not provide more than one meal a day, and I personally know some of them who are not able to earn a day's pay. I am sure it was not the intention of the government or of the country that these men should be left in that state. I know it would be objectionable to open up the pensions question, but
these men could be provided for in some other way. I would ask the minister to look into the matter and if possible make some provision for them, so that they may not suffer. They deserve everything that can be done for them, for they have done their best for the country.

This is what I am anxious about. I am told that a great many settlers will eventually lose all the money they put into their homesteads, due not to the failure of the scheme in the first place, but because the farms, stock
and equipment were bought at a time of inflated prices. Now that prices have gone down I fear that these soldiers will lose all their original investment. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed there are very few such cases. I judge from the report here of the five hundred and twenty-three odd cases I mentioned as being held for final adjustment, that that is with a view of distributing any balance among these men. The case mentioned by my hon. friend in which the homestead or other property was pledged, is quite a different case from one in which no property was pledged, or from the purchase of both land and equipment without any other property being pledged. In that case I am free to say I doubt if the settler would get any return; the government, owing to the inflated values at whfch this property was purchased, would, I think, lose on it. I am also informed that no action has been taken by the board w'here there is any possibility of the settler making good. I am hopeful that the recommendation of the committee will be such as to give those men a chance to make good if there is any possibility of their doing so.

I feel that the soldiers should not bear the whole burden of the deflation of prices. The committee will admit that it is a pretty serious situation for the soldier who comes back from overseas, goes into a venture that looks good to him at the time

that possibly looked good to us all-pays ten per cent down on his property and later makes further payments, and then, because he fails to meet subsequent payments, is sold out and loses not only the money he has put into it- amounting in some cases to quite a considerable sum-but one, two or three years of his time, as the case may be. He is turned out on the road, possibly with a family of small children to support-absolutely destitute. The situation is a serious one, and I think the Government has responsibility in the matter. Just how far the Government realize that responsibility is what I would like to know. In reading the report of the chairman of the board, I find, although it is a very full statement- no reference to this aspect of the question. The report is a very rosy one; it shows that

Supply-Soldier Settlement
the Government has realized more money out of these properties than it invested in them, but there is no mention of the soldier or how he is going to come out financially on the venture. That is the feature which,
I think, we must consider.
There is one other thing I would like to mention to the minister. I have had a number of letters from assessors and tax collectors all over the province of New Brunswick inquiring what they are going to do about collecting the taxes on farms which were formerly occupied by soldier settlers. I believe that invariably the Government has refused to pay the taxes on these farms. It is well known that Dominion lands are not taxable, and it is open to question whether or not that principle is a correct one to follow. But in the case of these farms, there should be no question whatever. The soldier settler who has been operating the farm has been paying the taxes on it; he must furnish his tax receipt to the board every year. But when he leaves that farm-and I know one or two cases of this kind-and the farm is leased, producing a larger return annually than would have been obtained from the soldier settler by way of rent, the Government refuse to pay the taxes. In some cases the result is to cripple the school district. There is one such case of a small district adjoining mine, a district which is having a hard struggle to keep the school running. There is only one farm in that district, fortunately; had there been three, it would have meant the closing of the school. I imagine that other districts are affected in the same way. I think, therefore, that this is a situation that Parliament must deal with. Certainly the Government should pay the taxes on these farms. They are very different from wilderness lands which have never paid taxes.

Mr. Chairman, I had intended to direct this matter to the attention of the minister. I do not think it is necessary to say very much to the minister on this subject, because he knows as much about it as we do. Last year I was secretary and treasurer of the Union of Manitoba Municipalities. I sent a resolution on this subject to the minister, to the leader of the Opposition, and to all the western members. I do not think I got the courtesy of a reply from many of them, though I did get one or two. The difficulty is more apparent in the Western provinces, I think, than it is in the East.

We have several school districts where as many as four different quarter-sections, on which taxes have been paid for thirty years, have been thrown up. Debentures have been issued and money borrowed on that security; those debentures have to be met and the school taxes have to be paid. The government has refused to pay those taxes. In many cases these soldier settlers-and my sympathies go out to them -have not paid taxes during all the time they have been on the land. I believe the arrears of taxes have been paid by the government, but they refuse to be responsible for them after the soldier leaves the land. I think something ought to be done to remedy that condition.

This whole subject will be discussed in the special committee that is dealing with the matter, and when their report is brought in we can deal with it fully. But I assume that part of this amount of $12,000,000 will go to the further extension of the scheme that has been followed. How many applications are in hand from those who wish to take advantage-for it was supposed to be an advantage-of the scheme?

speechtext:
Perhaps I can answer that question best by giving the hon. member the following statement:
Certificates of qualification, entitling the holder to participate in the benefits of the act, have been granted to ,23,786 returned soldiers who have not thus far received any loan privileges. There is no way of estimating exactly how many of these men may be applicants for loans, but a considerable number will undoubtedly desire to be established on the land. Loan applications have been received from 576 men during the month of April, and inspection of the land is under way. Advices from district offices indicate another 700 as pending. In addition, there are 416 men in training, who must be provided for. Provision must also be made for additional loans for settlers only partially established in previous years. Loans authorized during the past year have in some cases been unexpended as yet, and provision must be made for meeting the requirements of the settlers concerned. The estimate of $10,260,000 for loans must cover all these requirements, and with the utmost care in administration and in the granting of loans, the appropriation will barely cover the applications already in hand and pending, and the settlers in training.
As to the question of taxation of these lands when they fall into the hands of the board, and therefore become Crown lands, I may say that this matter will be further discussed in the committee. I have a great deal of sympathy for the school boards and municipalities concerned; for I have some knowledge of the effect of

Supply-Soldier Settlement
such conditions in our school districts in western Canada, having had to deal with the exemption of the railway lands in our own province. It would be hoped that the period during which these lands are in that position would be short. But as I say, the matter will come before the committee and I should like to attend its meetings when that discussion takes place. We may then be able to learn what is the general concensus with (respect to this matter. Therefore, I am not to-day taking any definite stand in connection with this . particular matter.

I have some interest in the Soldier Settlement Board and its work still, and I am anxious if it is within my power to make any suggestion that may be of value. I am glad for my part that if this important trust is to be committed to hon. gentlemen opposite, it is in the hands of the Minister of the Interior. He understands as well as any other member of this House general farming conditions in Canada, and particularly in those provinces where the great body of soldier settlement is. I am glad that he has found the general policy, the general features of the enterprise, and the general organization efficient, and that he is proceeding along the lines we pursued. I would not be disposed at all to suggest a reduction in the appropriation that he asks for, in the face of the statement he has just read to the committee. I am surprised rather that there should be so many applicants yet seeking to come in under the plan. I thought by this time the number would have been much more reduced. That information is to me encouraging, and I am sure is to the minister as well.
As to the matter of taxation, there is something to be said for the relief asked for. I know there is danger there, just as there is in meeting the request of the hon. member for Brandon, but because there is danger, it does not mean that a distinction cannot be drawn in such a way as to place the department safe. I do not purpose, however, to make now any specific suggestion in that direction. As to the complaint raised on behalf of the settler himself, there are of course some who have failed in the work. Their number is small in proportion and is mainly due, no doubt, to the reversal in prices of lands and products that has been general throughout the whole farming community of our country, and indeed has had its repercussion in every other calling in life. We ought rather to be surprised that the
number of failures is as low as it is, and that the consequences of failures to the government at least have been so slight. The difficulty is to meet such a situation in a manner that will not involve further insurmountable obligations all down the whole line of the returned soldier list. I know that difficulty because I have faced it myself. If the soldier who fails is to be regarded as still in a sense a government cestui qui trust, a man to whom the government owes special obligation because of his failure, that doctrine has very far reaching implications and would carry the liabilities of our country to a prodigious extent.
This suggestion I offer as a commence, ment. In the case where the soldier, being a homesteader either prior to the war or after the war, enters into obligations and as a consequence loses his homestead, say, in the case where he buys another piece of land and mortgages his home, and then because of that obligation finds himself submerged, there might, it seems to me, be a rule that the board should hold that his homestead right was not exhausted and that he could come in under the class of cases that homesteaded before 1894 and have the right to homestead again. It seems to me that would only be an extension of the principle of aiding in the development of cultivation, by giving special assistance for the purpose of securing more cultivation, more farming in this country.
If you give the right to the soldier to take up another homestead, how would you finance him until he got a start?

I had not made any suggestion in that direction. The government, of course, ordinarily does not finance a homesteader, and I did not suggest financing him if he is given the right to homestead again. I am afraid to do so would carry our obligations very far. But put him in the same position as though he never had entered at all. It would not, of course, be a restoration of the man to the position he hoped to be in; I know that; I do not pretend it is doing a great deal for him, because good homestead land now is very hard to secure. If the government found it in their power to do more, no one would be more pleased than I, but it seems to me it could safely do that much. If there are difficulties in the way they do not occur to my mind at present.
Of course, hon. gentlemen to my left must bear in mind that a new day has just

Supply-Soldier Settlement
dawned for the farmers of our country. A new light, a "larger liberty", a "new freedom" has dawned to-day for Canadian agriculture. No doubt the returned soldiers, when they know that the duty on their implements is to be reduced by two and a half per cent, will take new heart and courage. They will hereafter see in their balance sheets at the end of the year, no doubt, a vastly improved return. Even those who have abandoned their farms, will at this encouraging news surely make haste to return and take up the pursuit of agriculture once more.

I would suggest that this item stand over until the sub-committee that is considering land settlement have reported, because I know a number of hon. members who do not wish to discuss this item until that report has been made.

Mr. Chairman, representing as I do a constituency which, I think, has the second largest number of returned soldiers settled under the Land Settlement scheme in the Dominion, and having observed to some extent the conditions surrounding these settlements, and the effect the present scheme is having not only upon the soldiers themselves but upon the country as a whole, I must say that I am absolutely opposed to another dollar being spent for the encouragement of new settlements under that scheme. I do not, however, wish to be misunderstood in making such a statement. I do not for a minute accuse the Soldiers Settlement Board, or the late government, of insincerity. I believe they both started out in all sincerity, believing they were going to do something really effective for the returned soldiers. Unfortunately the moral status of the human race has not developed to a stage where selfishness does not enter into these 
matters. Consequently the moment the board came into being, it became surrounded with a group of land speculators, grafters and job seekers, whose operations defeated the very purpose for which the board was created.
The conditions surrounding these soldiers are such that unless immediate steps are taken to relieve the prevailing economic conditions under which they are labouring, a very large percentage of those in my constituency will be forced to leave their farms. It is humanly impossible for them to continue operations if they are to pay the inflated prices at which these farms and equipment were bought. As we all know, in the years 1919, 1920, and 1921 the prices of materials of all kinds were at the peak. In some cases those prices were inflated to a figure many times beyond their real value; inflation was witnessed to an extent we had never before seen in western Canada. Unfortunately too, we have had, as yet, no definite statement from the minister, nor from the committee that they are considering this question, as to what is proposed to be done with these returned soldiers that are now settled on the land.
I have visited a great many of these homes and made a personal inspection of their conditions and I am convinced that if a practical man were sent in to re-value this land the valuation would be reduced by at least 200 per cent in many cases. It has been suggested that the interest paid by these men might be withdrawn for three or four years. Even if that were done it would only be deluding the settlers with false hopes, because where the land has been bought for 200 per cent above its fair value it is not humanly possible for the returned soldiers ever to make good. In many cases they bought binders at $330, waggons at $150, horses at $450 a team, and cows at $100 a piece. Burdened with such overhead charges as these even the most experienced farmer could not achieve success. In the area known as the lake Manitoba district, which is possibly the largest district settled by returned soldiers in Western Canada, the land is only of third class quality; and yet many of these quarter sections were bought for sums approximating $2,500,$3,000, and $3,500. There is not a man in this House would value those farms at a price exceeding eight or nine hundred dollars if he knew anything at all about farming.
I think, therefore, we should have some

Supply-Soldier Settlement
definite announcement from the minister as to what he intends to do with the settlements that have been made in the West under such conditions. If he will give an assurance that full recognition will be given to the claims of these soldiers before entering upon any fresh scheme of settlement I am perfectly willing to support the voting of any amount of money deemed to be necessary for the maintenance of our returned men, who are now settled on the land. But I certainly am opposed to another dollar being spent under the old scheme, because I think it is physically impossible for that scheme to be a success. If the minister can give us a suggestion along those lines, I would be perfectly willing to allow this item to pass; but if he cannot, I certainly am opposed to any further settlement being made under such a scheme that ties the soldier up financially, morally, and every other way.
I may say that I never was in favour of the soldier land settlement scheme, not because of any prejudice against the government or the board or anyone else, but simply because I believe that it was humanly impossible for such a scheme to be worked out satisfactorily, and I think my fears have been quite borne out. I have in mind at the present time several cases. For example, I know of a young man who had clerked in a store all his life. He and a farmer's son enlisted together from my district in the fall of 1914; they went over to France, and after serving about three and a half years in France, they were fortunate enough to come back. The government said to the boy who had been reared as a farmer and who was inclined to go on to the land: "We will lend you four or five thousand dollars to go on the farm." On the other hand, they said to the other boy who had clerked in a store and who was inclined to go back to his old job: "We will not give you anything."
I am inclined to ask why discrimination was shown, and I am convinced that the majority of the people of Canada will bear me out in this, that had the late government made some sort of a cash settlement, if it had been only $500 apiece to the returned soldiers, it would have cost the taxpayers much less and been more satisfactory than the settlement that was made. I have seen people throw up their hands in horror and say: "Where would you have got this money to make a settlement with the soldiers?" I ask: "What would have happened had the war gone on for another
year?" Would the soldiers in France have thrown down their arms, or the people of Canada withdrawn their sympathy and their money? Of course, they would not. The war would have gone on just the same; it would have been won just the same, and it would have cost the people of Canada probably another billion dollars.
In all fairness to the returned soldiers, it is up to the government to take off the farms at the government expense those men who are facing impossible conditions of which there are many, and to repudiate their debts and at least set them free. A large percentage of them are facing an impossible proposition; and while in some cases probably the soldiers may make good, every case should be considered on its merits, and a revaluation made of the land and equipment, and the returned soldiers given a fair show to make good. I have had it said to me: "If we had made a cash settlement with the returned soldiers, they would all have gone broke in a short time." Well! If they had gone broke, that was their own business, and they would have been dealing with their own money. But I have too much faith in the men who went over to France, who endured what they did there and who saved this country and helped to save the British Empire, to believe that a large percentage of them would have squandered their money in any such manner. If they had been given a cash gratuity, a much larger percentage of them would have made good than is making good as under the present scheme, and would have done just as well as any other class. All we have to do to-day is to give the returned soldier a fair show, and that is something which he has not had in Canada up to the present time.
I do not wish to open up a new question; but I cite this merely to point out that, when many of these boys came back from France, they were single men on their own resources, and if they had squandered their money, they had nobody dependent upon them and nobody to blame but themselves. In what situation do we find them to-day? We find them away out on homesteads today absolutely stranded; their hope is gone; their morale is wrecked; and when these principles are lost you have lost about all there is in the human life. Many of them have now a wife and a family of small children. Nothing is left for them to do but to drift back to our towns and cities and fill up the bread line. Is that what the people of Canada want t ohand out to the

Supply-Soldier Settlement
returned soldiers? I think not. That is exactly what is being done in my constituency, although it may be the only constituency in Canada in which that treatment is being meted out.
I therefore could not allow this estimate to pass without registering my protest against conditions that now surround the returned soldier settler. I should be glad if the minister would give us a statement of what he intends to do in the future and how rigidly he intends to examine every settlement that is made. It may be said that the soldiers have the privilege of going out and examining these farms before purchasing. That is very true; but in my district there are very few farmers' sons who, after they examined the soldier settlement scheme, would take land under it. It was only the men and boys who did not understand farming or conditions surrounding the primitive stages of agriculture, who took land under that scheme. That proved that had the scheme been a good one, the farm boys would have taken land under it; but they simply would not take the risk. If I to-day were given a choice between stepping into the shoes of some returned soldiers in my district and spendig the rest of my days one one of their farms, and undergoing a term in a penitentiary, I would prefer to take a term in the penitentiary. I would then know when it ends. I trust the minister will make some definite statement in regard to this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Many
members who are present to-night were not present when I made my explanation before the committee rose at six o'cloc.k I said then that I had to accept the Soldier Settlement Board as I found it. I say now that I cannot very well give any explanation of what is past. My hon. friend is dealing very largely with past history in regard to the Soldier Settlement Board, and I thoroughly agree with him in his statement that the purchases were upon inflated values; but they undoubtedly were the prices prevailing at the time the purchases were made for livestock, implements and land. I am not going to argue with my hon. friend as regards his statement that land purchased in his locality was purchased at too high a figure, even under inflated values, because I do not know anything about that. But, for the future, there will not be so much difficulty in that regard, because if we admit that livestock was inflated in value at the period when 
most of these men were re-established, that is not the case to-day, and one would not have that difficulty to encounter in reestablishing men on the land at the present time. Something might be said still about the price of implements, and to come to the main question, that of the purchase of land, I think a great deal of care should be exercised with respect to the settlement of the man upon the land and the price that is paid for the land. I do not wish to be dragged into a general discussion of this matter; but so far as I am able to influence the board and its officials, my elforts shall be to the end that every purchase of land that is made for the re-establishment of a soldier may be made at a rock-bottom price. There are two reasons. First, it will be necessary that the security of the Government in that land be maintained; and, secondly it is desirable to give to the man himself the most favourable opportunity possible to make good.
Now, as to the general question raised by my hon. friend as to what we are to do in the present circumstances, that is a matter which I trust will be thoroughly threshed out by the committee who are dealing with this whole subject, and who will recommend to the Government what, in their opinion, is the best method to be pursued in order to meet a very difficult situation. I do not think there can be any difference of opinion on the fact that the deflation in values has left not only these men, but every man who is engaged in agriculture, in a very difficult position; but more particularly has it affected these men who are just only entering into agriculture on their land.
I hope the committee will give this matter their very serious consideration. I am anxious to co-operate with them when the question is being discussed, because I fully appreciate its importance, and the difficulties it presents. I do not want to go minutely into the matter to-night. There are a great many phases of it that will have to be carefully considered by the committee before any conclusion can be arrived at as to what will be the best course to take. As to the future I can assure my hon. friends that the greatest care will be exercised. When I say that I fully realize that the difficulties that existed in the years just passed will not be so great henceforward. The situation will not be as difficult as it was at the time when so many of the men were being settled on the land.

Supply-Soldier Settlement

Many of the returned soldiers who settled in the locality between lake Dauphin and lake Manitoba did so in the expectation that the Rorketon line of the Canadian Northern would be built. In fact it is only reasonable to suppose that the board made this promise. The grade is already completed from St. Rose to Rorketon. Many of the soldiers are between 15 and 25 miles distant from the railway and it is not reasonable to expect that they will remain on the land unless they are afforded transportation facilities. I am sorry that the Railway Department cannot see its way clear to relieve the soldiers of the handicaps to which they are subjected, at least to the extent of laying the steel on the line between these two points. To delay this- work is simply breaking faith with these men, and the Government may rest assured that they will not remain in that district much longer unless this line is built in the very near future.

I do not feel like blaming the late government, as some do, for the course they took. It was a sincere effort to meet a difficult s'tuation. I cannot, see that the officers of the government could foresee the deflation in prices that would follow the establishment; of the board and the attempt to place soldiers on the land. I know that there are few business men who could have foreseen it, at least to the extent to which it occurred. But I should like to say a word or two in regard to the men who were chosen to appraise the land. Now, I will not repeat the rumours I have heard, but I will give two instances to show the importance of the greatest care being exercised in the choice of the men who carry out the scheme, if it is the intention to purchase more land. There is quite an impression throughout the country that those who have been sent to appraise land have, in some cases, got a little rakeoff themselves. I am not prepared to prove the assertion in any case and therefore I will not repeat the rumours that have come to me. I will, however, mention two cases as matters of fact.
The land belonging to a certain man was to go to a returned soldier who had been working for him and in whom he was keenly interested. After the appraiser had looked it over he got the seller by himself and asked him: " How much is there in it?" The seller of the land is quite convinced that the question that was really implied, although the actual words were not uttered, was: "How much is there in it
for me?" He replied that there were 320 acres. In another case a certain man told me he had driven one of the appraisers signed a receipt for $12 but got only $6. Of course, if there are only one or two isolated cases of that sort they are hardly worth mentioning; and I cannot say whether or not there are more. But it just goes to show the importance of being exceedingly careful in choosing men who will do the honest thing.
I have no doubt that care was taken in the choice of these men. I do not suppose that the late government picked up anybody and everybody; but there is an impression in some cases that farms that were suitable were turned down by the appraisers in favour of poorer farms. That would be a great injustice to the soldiers who were to occupy the land. As I say, I cannot give any actual proof.
I had thought that when money was expended to place soldiers on the land and assist them, the scheme might have gone a little further and given assistance to men who wanted to engage in mercantile business or in any other occupation for which they were fitted by previous training. While it is a difficult matter to deal with, some re-adjustment of values ought to be made, and land, implements and horses bought at inflated prices should be re-valued in order to give the returned men some chance of escaping from the burdens they are carrying at present. According to what has been said, some of them cannot possibly, under the most favourable circumstances, throw off the burden. That, I believe, is quite true. Many of these men, if compelled to pay a hundred cents on the dollar would, I doubt not, go to the wall, and the most careful consideration should be given them. I realize that the minister has been in office only a short time,-in fact, too short a time for him to be able to map out any policy that can settle the matter immediately. I feel willing, therefore, to allow the item to pass in the hope that he may find a way out of the difficulty.

The member for
Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) ought to give by letter, to the minister the facts upon which he bases the statement he has just made as regards the two officers of the board. I personally would ask, no matter who appointed them, that the member give the facts to the minister and that the minister investigate each case and deal

Supply-Soldier Settlement
mercilessly with the individuals if they are found guilty.
In this connection I may say that in the three sessions that passed during which I came before the House with estimates for the Soldiers' Settlement Board, I heard only three hon. members criticise the honesty and fidelity of officers of the board, either in relation to valuations or to services of any other kind. In each of those three cases I had the chairman of the board communicate directly with the member, earnestly asking him to give the name of the officer, the description of the lands, and such other facts as would enable identification, and promising definite and immediate investigation. In each case the member declined. In each case we pursued the matter, pressing to the utmost to get the facts, but never were we able to secure any. One of the hon. members I refer to is to-day a member of the Government. Now I hope the minister will press that the facts be given in this case, and if they are-and I do not wish to intimate that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle will decline to furnish the required information- I ask that a searching investigation be made and the result reported to the House, and that if any party is guilty he shall be punished. As respects remedying these matters, I do not know anything to hinder the minister doing so. He has been in his office four months, this is not an arduous task, all the pioneering work has been done, the trail is blazed, and it is merely a matter of pursuing a definite policy, which I have confidence the minister is quite able to do. If there is anything waiting to be done I for one ask him to get busy and have it done.
I am not at all unwilling to give the names of my informants, provided I can secure their consent. I shall try to do so.

I might as well say here and now that so far as I am personally concerned, whether a member of Parliament or any one else raises any question with regard to the honesty of officials in any department over which I have charge, if he will give us any evidence upon which we can work, a thorough investigation will be held at once. I have heard very frequently statements made that too high a price has been paid for the land upon which these men have been settled. Members of Parliament can help the board very considerably by at once 
bringing to our attention any such cases and I shall welcome their co-operation.

I do not know what method was in force in other constituencies, but in my constituency it was generally the returned soldier that endeavoured to make the bargain in the first place. He looked over what he considered would be a suitable farm, then he inquired the price, and later on he made application to the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and the board as far as possible acquiesced in his wishes. 1 do not know of any case where the board authorized a higher price than the soldier wished to give. I think the same is true m regard to implements and other things. But at the same time it must be remembered that these farms and implements were bought at inflated prices, although they were generally recognized as being fair at that particular period. I do not know whether the minister has under favourable consideration a revaluation or not, but in view of the serious conditions, and of the charge made by my hon. friend on my left, I would ask the minister if he could tell us what percentage of money has been repaid to the department by the returned soldiers, as that would give us some conception of their success or failure on the land.

Perhaps it would be in order for me to say a few words on this matter, because I am, perhaps, as deeply interested in it and possibly as conversant with the facts of the case as most of the hon. members here. I had not proposed to speak on the subject to-night; as chairman of the special committee which has this matter under consideration with a view to bringing forward recommendations, I felt it would be out of place that I should speak now, preferring to reserve anything I had to say until our report was laid on the Table and opportunity for a full discussion could be afforded. But in view of the line of debate that has been followed and in view of some of the statements which have been made, it might be of interest to the committee if I should give them an idea of the activities of the special committee which is dealing with this matter. I shall not go into detail, nor shall I anticipate the report. I simply wish to say, in all justice to the minister, that he has placed the matter entirely in the hands of that special committee; and he is 'deferring any action until its recommendations are forthcoming. The matter was turned over to that committee in its entirety; there were no strings on it. We were told to go ahead; we were given free access to all books and the right to call any witnesses we wished to examine and to question the officials of the department; then to make up our own minds and submit our recommendations to the House. I am fully cognizant of the condition of the returned men on the land at the present time; I think I can say so, because I believe I was the first man in the House to advocate this measure of revaluation. We are fully cognizant, I say, of the condition of the returned man, and we are giving it full consideration. At present all I can say is this: When our report is brought down we shall have done what we could to alleviate his condition and, I believe, will be able to have considerably improved his prospects for the future. I am expressing only my own opinion, but it seems to me that further discussion on the policy to be pursued might more profitably be carried on when our report is brought down and hon. members know just what our recommendations are.

If the minister has the
information for which I asked him, I should be glad to have it.
