With regard to the statements made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I am not at all surprised that in an organization of this kind there may be an occasional crook, or a man who will fake his expense account. However, I have had a very close connection with the work of this board in New Brunswick since the work first started, and I just want to say this: I wish I had the same faith in all departments of government that I have in the Soldiers' Land Settlement Board,
r.Mr Charles Stewart.!
both as to its honesty, its selection of suitable officials, and so forth. There is no doubt they will get a crook once in a while, but so far as New Brunswick is concerned, I think the men who valued the farms there were the best men that could have been got in the province. I think-no, I will say I know-that we bought these farms cheaper in New Brunswick than private individuals were able to buy the same farm for in many cases. Sometimes we refused to buy farms that we did not think were value for the money asked, and within two weeks the owner would sell to a private individual at the same price we refused to pay. I say "we" because I was on the loan committee that bought the farms the first summer, and was also chairman of the qualifications committee that judged of the men's qualifications for holding, so I was in a fair position to judge of the ability of the men who valued these farms, and I think that the work was well done. The men who went out and bought the stock, say, a team of horses, did not handle the money, but they made the deal and bought the team for the man, the bill was sent to the superintendent of the Soldier Settlement Board, and the cheque was sent direct from the board to the man from whom the stock was bought. The procedure was the same in buying farms. The committee, of which I was a member, which bought the farms did not handle any money, but they put the deal through, and the money was paid by the officials of the board direct to the owners of the farm. I think the scheme was well conceived and well carried out. I have no doubt there were some cases of faking of accounts, but from my experience of the board, in any case of this kind that was brought to their attention the culprits would get short shrift.

I had not intended to say anything about this matter, as I think it is only a waste of time to discuss it until the committee's report has been brought down. However, I will say this. During the campaign I heard a great number of insinuations against the officers of the Soldier Settlement Board, and after the election campaign was over I 'spent the greater part of my spare time until I came down to Ottawa sifting these matters out. There was not one insinuation that I heard of before the election that I did not try to follow up after the election in order to get the facts. In some cases I asked for an

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When
the civil government immigration estimates were up, I promised that when the general estimates were under consideration I would have something to say about the policy to be pursued in connection with immigration for this year at least. One cannot say very much about immigration without taking into consideration the condition in which Canada finds herself at the moment. During the past winter this committee has had evidence with regard to conditions in this country in the amounts they are being asked to vote, and will be asked to vote in the future, for unemployment relief, from one end of Canada to the other. Furthermore, in what we fondly call these reconstruction days, we find a great many people apparently dissatisfied with conditions as they find them, a great many who'are loath to engage in enterprises that will provide employment, and on the part of labour we find no desire to accept a reduction in wages and thereby help us to get back to normal times. These conditions have been fairly general from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Then when we look abroad to the countries from which we hope to secure immigration, we find that by far the larger proportion of the people who would be willing to emigrate are men desirous of obtaining employment. They constitute by far the greater proportion of those who are willing to settle in Canada. Of course, there is a fairly large number of people who are anxious to change their home and would be willing to come to Canada, who are in a better position and have the necessary funds to establish themselves here. I hope I am not too pessimistic when I make the assertion that probably not for some time to
come shall we be able to receive all those who would be willing to come to Canada and who would make desirable citizens, and by that I mean those who are mentally and physically fit and are desirous of finding employment here and becoming Canadian citizens.
I think at the moment it would not be wise to encourage, or to invite, any large numbers of people who have to maintain themselves particularly by manual labour, but I do hope that that period will pass very rapidly. That is the condition of affairs we must face. With respect to our policy for immigration, and the amendments made to the Order in Council dealing with-the subject to which I will allude later, some criticism has been offered inasmuch as we apparently have been closing the doors to all but people with means to purchase or to become agriculturalists, agricultural labourers, and household workers. But taking into consideration the situation that I have outlined, these apparently are the only classes of individuals that we can absorb in Canada at the moment, and therefore any amendments to the Orders in Council in existence have been made with that object in view.
I do not think it is necessary to touch upon the question of oriental immigration at this moment. Let me say to my hon. friends from British Columbia that I am endeavouring to find a solution that will meet, in a large way, the desires expressed by those gentlemen the other evening. Let me also say, in passing, that I sympathize very much with them in their desire to have a larger percentage of the population in British Columbia of the white race.
It being a fact that we can only absorb the three classes I have mentioned at the moment, I have endeavoured to organize the forces we have, for the purpose of securing for Canada its fair share of those classes both in the Old Land, in the United States in Scandinavia and to some extent upon the continent of Europe. One matter that I would like to speak about, an allegation that frequently appears in the press of Great Britain, is that we in Canada are setting up too rigid an inspection of the immigration that would come to us. It has been frequently stated that has been, and still is, the attitude of the department. Well, Mr. Chairman, clearly there is no use in augmenting the ranks of the unemployed. As I said to you a moment ago, we could undoubtedly get a great number of people who would come to Canada and would go to swell the ranks of those who
Supply-Immigra tion

are ,out of employment at the moment; but we are making the endeavour to get every agriculturalist from Great Britain that we can induce to come to Canada. That work is being carried on there by our agents, and through the medium of lectures and advertising, we are endeavouring to reach all of that class of people that it is possible for us to reach. The same may be said of agricultural labourers and household workers.
Before I leave the subject of immigration from Great Britain, I want to mention one other class of immigration that has been found very desirable in the past, and that I think we can very well encourage to the fullest extent-that is the child immigration coming to this country. I was astounded the other day, when discussing this matter with Mr. Smart, who is in charge of this work, to hear from him that last year 1,500 children were brought to Canada, and that there were applications for 15,000 more. In other words, the department could have placed 15,000 children in the homes of Canadian citizens. There seems to be a wide field there; and the policy of the Government will be to secure a larger proportion of the "teen-age" boys and girls who would come to Canada and fill this demand that appears to be prevalent for those children. Mr. Smart is about to leave for England on this mission, to see if we cannot, in a larger way, secure those boys and girls.
Australia has become a very strong competitor with Canada, and South Africa as well, for the immigration of adults as well as of children. Ever increasing inducements are being offered for British immigration to go to those two countries; and, in some measure, we will have to meet that competition. It is possible, therefore, that I will ask for increased grants for the purpose of encouraging the assistance of the people who are engaged in this class of work in the Old Land. Before leaving this question I would like to say, Mr. Chairman, that this is a class of immigration I think it is very desirable we should get to Canada. It is the class that appeals to me very much, because these children will go to our Canadian homes, grow up in our schools and become thorough Canadians if we can express the sentiment in that manner. Of course they are British stock but, I think, will turn out to be settlers much more desirable than persons more advanced in years. And I say that I am rather keen on the question of securing for 
Canada all of the child immigration that it is possible for us to obtain.
In the countries of Scandinavia and Iceland-indeed in Holland and in Belgium as well-although I am told that a year ago immigration and immigration propaganda were not looked upon with favour we to-day find that condition changing. I am hopeful we will get from Iceland this year a fair amount of the Icelandic people who, it is needless to say, make splendid settlers upon our western lands. We also entertain the same hope with respect to Scandinavia which has also furnished many fine settlers to western Canada. In these countries there is an ever increasing interest in immigration and I believe the authorities there will be willing to consider allowing their citizens to leave their homeland for Canada. In Holland we have a complete change with respect to immigration to Canada. Whereas a year, or a year and a half ago, the Dutch government were unwilling that their people should leave that country and come to Canada, to-day they are anxious to assist, and are assisting us in a very large way in bringing a splendid class of people to this country, and we are working that field for all it is worth.
Will the minister permit me a question? Can he say why it is that the Dutch government are so anxious to have their people leave Holland in order to settle in Canada? What is the reason of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One of the reasons, perhaps, is that they have more people than they can absorb at home; I am speaking now purely and simply of the agricultural class; I am not referring to any other class of citizens.
They are all right; let them come.

But Holland has its own colonies to which it can send its people, and in that way they would not be lost to the home land. Why have the Dutch shown such a strong desire to settle in the West at the present time? Is it because they have heard, from the remarks of the farmer members in this Chamber, of the splendid conditions there?

I should like to draw the minister's attention to a letter which I have just received from one of my constituents and which bears upon this very matter. He encloses a clipping from a Re-

gina paper showing a despatch dated May 4, to this effect:
The provincial Government, in co-operation with the federal Department of Immigration, has made arrangements to bring contingents of farm labourers from Holland, it was announced officially to-day.
My correspondent says in part:
I might say that the people of your constituency are not in favour of voting money for agricultural purposes, nor are we in favour of spending money to bring in immigration, as it is almost impossible for the people who are here to make a living.
In December last, there were 246 quarter sections of land sold for arrears of taxes in this municipality, a total in this and the two adjoining municipalities, of 846 quarters, 137,160 acres in all.
I very much question the wisdom of bringing in immigrants at the present time, when it is, as this correspondent says, and it is undoubtedly correct, impossible for the people in that district to -make a living.
In that connection also, I might say that when we are inducing immigrants to come to Canada, we should at least -endeavour to give them a square deal. I have a matter that I have been dealing with and corresponding with the department over for some time, the case of a Highland Scotch family, who sold their home and their few chattels in May, 1921, preparatory to coming to Canada. They purchased their tickets, and they were all ready to sail, when the doctor passed on a little girl of the family as feeble-minded. The family were left in a very awkward position. Their baggage had already come forward to Canada, and it had to be returned. They were left in that way for nearly a year, and they spent almost the last cent they had. In fact, when they came to Canada just recently, it was only through their relatives sending them money that they were enabled to continue the voyage. They were held up for a whole year on account of something that, I think, is radically wrong in the Department of Immigration. I will read just a statement from the report dealing with the explanation given recently why these people were held up for a whole year. The report reads:
This decision was conveyed to the Superintendent of Emigration, in London, by letter of November 16, and on January 25, he replied, by cable, to the effect that the medical officer of the Health Department recommended the admission of the girl and, moreover, was of the opinion that the Assistant Deputy Minister of Health would understand that the girl was a characteristic Highland country girl and not feeble-minded.
I would ask hon. gentlemen and particularly the minister if he can see any connection between a normal Highlander and something that is feeble-minded. I appealed to the department to give justice to this family, at least to do something for them to help them to come to Canada, in view of the fact that it was carelessness on the part of the officials that was responsible for their being held up for a whole year and being compelled to spend their last dollar. But nothing was accomplished, and it was only through the charity of some of their friends that they were enabled to come to this country. If we induce people to come to Canada, we should at least give them a square deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) interrupted me about immigration from Holland and the hon. member (Mr. Campbell) ihterrupted me in connection with the matter in which the medical examiner appeared to have been in doubt or to have made a mistake, I was endeavouring to cover the field in a statement of what we hoped to do in connection with immigration into Canada. Before I have finished, my remarks, I will deal with some of the matters raised by my hon. friend.
I wish to make my statement as brief as possible, and yet I want in a fairly comprehensive way to cover the field. From Poland we hope to get and I think we undoubtedly will, a large number of people who will go upon the land. That fairly well covers the field in Great Britain and on the Continent. In the Scandinavian countries outside of Iceland we are not permitted, as I said before, to canvass or to advertise for settlers, and we have newspaper advertisements appearing in Iceland at this moment. As regards the Continent, We have taken three of our best trained men, one from Vancouver, one from the central office and one from Niagara Falls and sent them over to Mr. H. M. Mitton, who is the agent at Antwerp. Our idea in doing that is to endeavour to avoid some of the difficulties that have resulted from having to send back a considerable number of people who arrive at our shores. I can scarcely concei /e of any people with Scotch blood in them not being mentally sound, but there might be an odd case. If there is, however, it is important; and if my hon. friend knows anything about conditions in the Western provinces where a large percentage of immigration that has come to Canada has settled, he must know that too large a percentage of people who are mentally unfitted to come to this countrr

Were the majority of
those people who were mentally unfit drawn from country or from city life?

My hon.

Oh, oh.

I do not exactly see the
reason for the laughter. Perhaps, I am a little Scotch, but that does not mean that I am feeble-minded. From a woman's standpoint, lack of social life is important. What would some hon. members do if for six months they did not see a man to speak to? Some hon. members might be all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know a great deal of criticism is levelled at the officials. I am not making any defence of them; I am speaking simply of conditions as we are facing them to-day, and, indeed, in my short tenure of office, I have had the most strenuous representations made to me, after medical inspection, that individuals should be allowed to enter Canada, it being represented that otherwise families would be separated and also that these individuals

would be able to maintain the members of their families who were living under very severe conditions; and I frankly admit these things do appeal to one. But after all, one must do his duty. One must keep in mind the fact that every time one of these individuals gets into the country he too frequently becomes a public charge on the community. Undoubtedly mistakes will be made, and I anticipate that perhaps at the next session of Parliament, if I am here occupying the same position, there will be innumerable cases in which hon. members will be able to criticise me severely. But while I am prepared to deal with these cases from the most sympathetic standpoint, we must remember that we are trying to build up a strong and virile race in Canada, and it is necessary that we should keep that ideal constantly before us.
I do not expect that we shall get a large number of people of the character and class 1 have mentioned to come to Canada; I mean agriculturists from Great Britain. I think, however, that it is our duty to get as many of these people as we can possibly secure from the Motherland. I am not unmindful of the fact that some of the people whom we call alien enemies to-day, who have come from countries that were our enemies in the Great War and are now settled in western Canada and elsewhere, have made splendid settlers and have been successful on the land. There is no doubt about that; I do not think that any one who has lived among them will deny the fact. It is said that they are not accustomed to the comforts which we find indispensable, and that they will put up with more hardships than we do. That is true. Some of the people whom we are endeavouring to get from the Highlands of Scotland are coming in at present. Some are settled in Ontario and they will undoubtedly make splendid settlers. They are hard workers and will do well on the land, probably they will be satisfied with very much less in the way of returns than the people coming from the United States or those people of the Old Country who were in much better circumstances before moving here. I am not suggesting that we should get that class of people, because I realize that it is difficult to make a livelihood on the land. Before concluding I shall deal with the question which has been raised with regard to the difficulty of living on the land. I think I know something about the question.
I want to deal for a moment or two, however, with -the possibility of getting im-

Supply-Immigration
migration from the United States. We are trying to get as many as we can of the Canadians who left Eastern Canada, particularly Quebec and the Maritime provinces, who are now settled in the New England states, and are showing a desire to return to this country, to come back and once more take up farming in the Dominion. In the central states, also, our agents are busily at work. Many of them are on the way at the moment owing to the conditions that have arisen there. During the war land and the products of the land became so inflated, and such high prices were paid for real estate, that the people in the United States, in common with the farmers of Canada, now find themselves in a difficult situation. Many of them are forced to surrender their lands and are looking for some place in which to make a fresh start. Our propaganda has evoked a counteracting campaign on the part of the central states which are making a great effort to hold people. Montana and the more northerly states are making a great effort to hold their population. I feel confident, however, from the reports I have just received from the superintendent, that a very large number of desirable farmers who know the conditions in western Canada will cross the line and take up land there this year.
Let me deal with the question as it affects us in western Canada. I quite agree that farming was never more unprofitable than it was in the past year, and probably we never suffered to such a serious extent as we did during last year and the year before. One farmer will blame one set of conditions, while another will attribute the trouble to other causes. We have had adverse weather conditions on top of a falling market, and all our difficulties seem to come at one time. We had taken on very large obligations in the hope that the inflated prices of live stock and farm produce would continue as they were; and as every one knows, those prices dropped over night and left us in a precarious financial situation. But to say that because of the inability of the people to pay their taxes, and because of the difficulty that our farmers find themselves in to-day, it is unwise to place more agriculturists on the land in Western Canada and in other parts of the Dominion is, I think, a mistake.
While admitting all these difficulties, Parliament is asked to vote large sums of money to carry on the National Railways, part of which money is for deficit in operation, to say nothing about interest charges
that are accruing from year to year and that undoubtedly must be taken into account and paid from revenue, seeing that it is doubtful whether they will ever be paid by the operations of the railways. Within twenty miles of practically all these lines of railway that are now in operation to-day, with school houses built, with towns established, and with all the facilities for carrying on business, it will be admitted that there is indeed a very sparse population. We do hope that conditions will change and that agriculture will be made at least reasonably profitable, because, if that hope is not fulfilled, there will be very little done in any other line of business in Canada. If we cannot place the people on the land and assist in production so as to create business generally in the Dominion, if we cannot fill up these vacant spaces, all within twenty miles of railways, then we have a very dreary outlook indeed in Canada. I am not suggesting for a moment that these spaces are immediately to be filled up; we cannot fill them up in a hurry. But I should like to see policies adopted that would make possible a genuine success on the land throughout the country. While perhaps we have not been as prosperous on the land as we should like to have been, and while we may not have made all that we had hoped to make by reason of the inflated values of farm land, it must be remembered that other businesses in Canada, although they may have had prosperous days, are probably themselves in a rather difficult situation to-day.
In bringing immigrants in I think it is a mistake to tell them that the moment they get upon the land they are going to be prosperous. Speaking of my own experience in western Canada, I know it was a few years before I began to get prosperous at the homesteading game; but I am not going to say that I did not make a considerable amount of money out of farming in Alberta. I am not afraid of the future of western Canada so far as agriculture is concerned. I know that the difficult situation depicted by many of my hon. friends opposite is absolutely true, but I may refer the committee to a period in our history, 1892 and 1893, when I was farming in the old province of Ontario. In those days prices for produce dropped very much lower than they have dropped at the present time. You will retort by saying: But living conditions were very different then. I reply that they were not so very different from the conditions under which we are living to-day, bearing in

Supply-Immigration

mind the prices we were receiving then compared with those we are receiving now. We survived that trying period, and the farmers of Ontario are perhaps richer today than they were in those days, having made more money perhaps because they were established more firmly than we were. But I do say, through the mouths of our immigration agents both in the United States and Great Britain, where we are seeking to get settlers upon our vacant lands, that while this is not a country in which immigrants can pick up gold on the streets, yet it is a country where they can do as well as, indeed better than, in any other country that may invite them. I hope I shall not ba misunderstood as holding out glowing hopes for settlers coming here under present conditions, but I do say that if we are to be successful we must get more people on our vacant land. I am not going to deal with the question of how greater success can be attained; that will be dealt with at another time.
What other time has the minister in mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There
will be a discusion on the Budget, mentioned by my right hon. friend to-night, and perhaps we will then have an opportunity to discuss that matter. Let me deal for a moment or two with the question of regulations. There was a regulation in force providing that each immigrant must be in possession of at least $250. We have not altered that provision in so far as it affects oriental immigrants, but we have removed what is claimed to be to a certain extent a disability in another connection. We are anxious to let all people-except of course orientals-into Canada who can maintain themselves. There is a class that I have mentioned, the labour class, and similar people without means who are desirous of obtaining employment, but we cannot permit them to enter at the present time. We do hope by the establishment of agents on the Continent and a more rigid inspection of intending immigrants before they leave home, to avoid some of the unfortunate incidents that have happened. Such incidents will perhaps happen again, but by viseing of passports by our own agents we hope that when people sell up their homes on the other side and embark for Canada there will be the least possible difficulty in their passing the test at our port of entry. In the changing of these regulations that is the principal feature I had in mind, so that many of the hardships complained of may be eliminated.

I think I have covered the ground sufficiently, Mr. Chairman. Possibly hon. members will be desirous of asking a number of questions.
Where do the homes exist for the 15,000 child immigrants?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In Ontario and the eastern provinces.
In what sort of homes?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Largely farm homes.
Will the children be adopted or merely engaged as helpers?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In some cases they will be adopted, in other cases they will be taken for a certain term.

I was rather pleased, Mr. Chairman, with the remark the hon. Minister of the Interior made that, "they were all right when you caught them young." Unfortunately I was not caught very young, but I have done the very best I could since I came here to make good.
Now, I do not know if I am going to talk in a strain that will be very pleasant to some of my friends on this side of the House; I am going to speak very much along the same lines as the minister in regard to the necessity for further immigration. I think we all recognize to-day that the greatest difficulties we have to meet in business, on our farms, or in any other calling are our large overhead expenses, the rate of taxation, and our railway deficits. I believe I mentioned once before that if we could double our population we would halve our difficulties in that respect. I know agricultural conditions are unsatisfactory at the present time, but I believe that point of view has been stressed quite enough. I will, however, read a very short extract from a communication received from a private association which has been looking toward Canada as a field for immigration. This is the extract:
It is our considered judgment that while the serious condition of the agricultural industry may have been exaggerated in some quarters, its position is nevertheless sufficiently grave to justify reasonable measures to improve the lot of the settler now on the land. The prosperity and happiness of the people already in the country is basic to the success of any great immigration movement.
As I have already said, I think perhaps we have stressed that point enough. I do

Supply-Immigration
not know what its effect may be outside, but I am sometimes just a little afraid of the psychological effect it is haying upon ourselves. We are looking upon the black side so much that probably we are beginning to lose heart at the very time when we ought to take courage and move forward resolved to do better in the future.
Of course, it may be asked: Why invite more people to come to this country when conditions are not satisfactory for those who are already here? I should like to point out some of the remedies that I think might help to mitigate the evils under which we suffer. It has been mentioned frequently that we have gone through a series of bad seasons. But we believe things are mending. Already the weather is making a decided improvement in that respect, and we hear nothing but glowing reports from the western prairies these days about the conditions under which the seed is being put in the land, and that dried out districts are getting a good wetting. Consequently I am looking towards the future with renewed hope. However, I believe that we can have better marketing conditions in the future than we have had in the past.
There is another matter I would like to speak of, and that is the question of the distribution of our labour and our goods. I believe that we can obtain greater benefit from satisfactory distribution than can be obtained in almost any other line of business. The question of distribution has not been sufficiently considered in our economic life. We have specialized and specialized until we find that in every line of business there is over-specialization. I want to mention a circumstance in this connection; it is of a personal character, but I think the committee will pardon my referring to it. During the campaign this fall I had the pleasure of staying at a very humble home-and I think it was a happy home. The head of the household had a few sheep, and I found that the good wife was carding the wool, spinning the yarn, knitting the stockings to supply all the members of the household, and selling her surplus stock at $1 a pair. At the same time, I, who had a large flock of sheep, had them shorn and shipped the wool, did not get enough money to pay for the cost of the sheep-shearing and the transportation of the wool to its final destination. Now, there is a case of difference of method. I am not advocating that we go back, to the old system where the blacksmith and the millwright did all the
work in the village, but I do believe we have over-specialized in a great many ways; it takes too many men to do a single job. I was told the other day that when the headlight on an engine goes out of repair-and I want my labour friends to pay attention to thi-s-it takes six men to repair it, whereas a few years ago one handy man could have done the job. That is the result of specialization. We have distributed our labour into too many quarters, and it is costing too much to run the machine. I believe that farm life and the distribution of our goods can be improved very largely in this respect.
Then, we are going to have cheaper transportation; we see signs of it coming. In regard to our markets, I think we are waking up to the fact that we must seek for markets in all directions. Of course, we realize the difficulties that we have to meet so far as our neighbours to the south are concerned, but there are markets and plenty for the produce of our farms over in Europe, when they are in condition to buy them. I think I mentioned this once before-and I am speaking only of the Prairie provinces, because it is with the conditions there that I am most familiar and of which I am, perhaps, best able to speak. But I believe that the day of large farms has passed and that we have come back to smaller holdings and more intensive cultivation. I think that the practice of holding large tracts of land is one of the great mistakes we have made during the last few years. When we first went to those prairies we went not so much to establish a home as to grow thousands and thousands of bushels of wheat, to make a fortune and to retire, wealthy men, in a very short time. That idea has passed away; what we are looking for to-day more than anything else is to establish comfortable and happy homes out on these prairie lands.
We hear a great deal to-day about the trekking to the cites. I think I know something about city conditions. I had the honour and the privilege of serving on the Public Welfare Commission for three years in the city of Winnipeg. Evidence was placed before that commission from all classes in the city, including philanthropic and benevolent societies, and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I came to know something about the seamy side of city life. I know that all is not gold that glitters and that the city has its troubles as well as the country. Now, I am not
Supply-Immigration

one of those who believe that every boy and every girl should be kept on the farm. If boys or girls show an aptitude for certain lines or display ability in matters pertaining to business vocations and other lines of life, by all means let them go. But I would like to see the conditions made such that all our bright boys and bright girls should not leave the farms for the cities.
One of our troubles to-day is not so much over-production as it is under-consumption. We find our warehouses full of goods; we find people without clothes. There is something wrong, something has to be made right. I wonder who is going to solve the riddle? What is the trouble? What is the matter?
Now, I believe we can better our conditions by having more people on the land.
I realize the importance of industrial Canada. Some of our friends seem to think that we farmers do not realize the importance of industrial life. I think we do;
I for one am proud of any implement, well made, when I find it has been manufactured in Canada. And I want to make the statement here, Mr. Chairman, that I have farmed for forty years and I do not know that I ever bought an implement that was not made in Canada-and I am a bit of a free trader, all the same. Now, coming to immigration:	Where are we
going to seek for immigration, and how are we going to get it? The minister has dwelt on this matter to some considerable extent. We can look towards the United States, and I believe that in that country can be found the very best class of people we are likely to get, because they understand the conditions and can adapt themselves readily to our social and political conditions. Not only that, but I believe we should do everything possible to bind ourselves to those people on the other side of the line; the more we encourage a friendly feeling towards them, the better it will be for Canada as well as for the United States. Then, we may look to the British islands for immigration. Unfortunately, Britain is an industrial country. Her agricultural population is not very numerous, and most of them can find employment at home if they wish it. At the same time, I know exactly what it means: to the agricultural labourer or to the small farmer who is paying a large rent for land over in the Old Country, the idea of owning a farm of his own makes a very strong appeal. I think quite a large per-
centage of immigration can be got from the British islands if we go the right way about it.
The minister spoke to-night about the efforts Australia was making to get British immigration. I do not know whether sentiment is a thing that goes very far in this House, but it is a fact that you cannot lose sight of sentiment; it has a great deal to do with human life, with human affairs, with everything with which humanity is concerned. And when you come to deal with British immigration you are dealing with something upon which sentiment has an important bearing. When a man decides to leave England, do you not think it means something to him that the old flag flies over the public building's of the Dominion of Canada? I think that gives Canada an advantage to begin with. It may be said that Australia makes the same appeal to his patriotic feelings. But I would like to point out the difference so far as distance is concerned. Those who leave the British islands to go to another country always have the feeling that they will go back either for a. visit or, perhaps, to remain there altogether. We know that as a matter of fact they do not go back. If they do return for a visit, they realize, much as they love their native land, that it is not their country; that Canada, after all, is their home and their country. Nevertheless, as I say, when they leave home first they imagine that some day they will go back. Canada is only seven days from Great Britain, but to go to Australia means a long sea voyage-and that militates to a large extent against Australia and in favour of Canada. Canada appeals to British people in many ways. The part we played in the war, the close contact which took place on that occasion between Canadians and the British people-for a great many reasons, there is nothing but the most friendly feeling towards Canada over in those British Islands. I believe if we go about it in the right way we can get a jgood many people from the British Islands, especially from Scotland and the north of England. From those places and from the north of Ireland you will get the very best class of settlers for Canada. Not that I have anything to say against the south of England or the other parts of the British Islands, but the climatic conditions of those sections to which I have just referred are more like those which prevail in Canada, and the people who come from that part of the Old Country can, perhaps, adapt

Supply-Immigration
themselves more readily to the circumstances than those who come from other districts. Very many splendid people have come here from all parts of the British islands and have been successful.
The minister spoke of the countries of Europe, of France and the Scandinavian countries, of Iceland, and Holland. There are no better people than these, and we should try to get them. I think we can get them if we try. They would be only too glad to come here and make a success. Some other parts of Europe have been mentioned and the inhabitants of those parts severely criticised, sometimes rigntly and sometimes not. I do not know if they deserve all the criticism that has been levelled against them. I met a Canadian Pacific Railway land inspector the other day, who had been inspecting land away up northeast of Edmonton and he said he had found in that rough country, settled on quarter sections of land, Ruthenian people who were hewing down the wood and cleaning up the land and making a success of farming. They were happy and contented, and raising families who are going to be farmers for the next three and four generations. That is worth remembering. Perhaps their idea of comfort is not the same as ours, but they are bringing into cultivation land that our people would not touch under any circumstances, and I would think twice before I condemn these people. They are creatures of circumstances, to a very large extent. I wish to quote a short extract from the literature of an association for the encouragement of immigration. In speaking of the Ukrainian people in the cities, it says:
There are, for instance, in the city of Winnipeg many hundreds of hardy Ukrainians, who came to Canada direct from the soil of eastern Europe, and who have saved a few hundred dollars, and who with a little direction and assistance would "make good" on the land. The fact is, that the majority of continental Europeans, now resident in Canadian cities, migrated to the Dominion with a view to tilling the soil. By force of circumstances they have drifted to the urban centers, and many of them would gladly return to the occupation from whence they sprung if they only knew how.
I believe it was the force of circumstances that brought these people into our cities and that has been responsible for a great many of the troubles they have caused, owing to the conditions under which they lived. I would not advise bringing in too many of these people. We should be very careful as to the numbers admitted, because their circumstances and way of living are so different from ours. All the same, I do
not like to hear them condemned offhand. Let me point out that 18 per cent of the students in the University of Manitoba today are of foreign extraction, and they are taking the highest places in the university. They are going to make good Canadians.
Coming down to Ottawa for the first time, for the opening of the session, as we passed at dusk through that rough country north of lake Superior it was snowing heavily, and the country looked very wild.
I went on the rear platform and
10 p.m. saw the men who were patrolling the track; they were the men with the skeepskin coat that Sir Clifford Sifton speaks about. Mr. Chairman, we can go into the pullman and tuck ourselves into our berth and feel quite safe and contented, and yet the very men who are patrolling the right of way and ensuring our safety are those despised people whom we are told it is not safe for us to trust. While we do not want too many of these people in our country, at the same time we should not despair of those we have here, if they are treated properly.
I am going to say a few words now on the immigrant and his welcome to this country. A great deal depends on first impressions. Perhaps there are a few in this House who can understand the feeling of an emigrant as he stands on the deck of the westbound steamer and takes a last look at the receding shores of his native land. I do not blame him if emotion surges over his soul and he feels a little bit downhearted. But "Hope springs eternal in the human breast, man never is but always to be blest." He turns his face westward, looking with hope towards this new land. I had an opportunity along with other members from the West to visit the city of Quebec some little time ago, and we all enjoyed the beautiful scenery and the splendid harbour, and looked with interest on the historic places that are so numerous in and around that city. We enjoyed the hospitality of that fine people. I had the opportunity on the same occasion of visiting the immigration buildings at Quebec. I have no word of criticism to offer, no fault to find, but at the same time I could not help thinking of the immigrant's feelings as he disembarked from the ship and came up that gangway and into those buildings. I am not criticising at all, but I want the minister to realize just what an effect it has upon the people who are coming into this country. I think we should adopt a sympathetic attitude towards these newcomers, the glad hand should be extended
Supply-Immigration

and a welcome given. It will go a long way towards helping these newcomers to get a right start. I am not criticising the immigration buildings at Quebec; I think they are splendid, but they are in an unavoidable condition. I have no doubt the attendants there are courteous and kind, and we know that the officers of the railway company as a rule are very good in looking after the immigrants and seeing them to their destination. Nevertheless, it needs courage, and courage of the best kind, to face a new life in a new country, and the Government has not done its full duty, it has not gone to the end of the story or fulfilled its duty to these immigrants until it has followed them up.
I am ready here to-night to pay a tribute to the Canadian people. They are a kindly people. Perhaps this comes with tetter grace from me than from many other members of this House because as you know, Mr. Speaker, I had attained the age of manhood before I came among the Canadian people. My heart warms to them to-day. I am one of them. Never for one moment has my birth on the other side of the water militated in the least degree against my advancement in any waik of life in this Dominion. I point to that with pride, because I think it is one of the advantages we have to offer to the immigrants who come to our shores, but unfortunately, in this very imperfect state of human affairs, there are exceptions everywhere, and all Canadians are not of the type of the great majority in this country. I think it is the duty of the government to see that incoming immigrants shall not be taken advantage of through their ignorance of conditions here. They should rather be assisted and looked after. The new settler should1 be helped and guided towards the vacant land adjacent to the railways that can be had for a moderate price. I for one believe that land that can be got at a moderate price within a few miles of the railroad is a very much cheaper proposition than a free homestead away out in the wilderness. I do not think I would be at all inclined to advise any one, except perhaps these settlers who come with the sheepskin coat, to settle any distance from the railroad, if they are going to make a success of farming under present conditions. I have been told that the Canadian Pacific have some five million acres of land, the Hudson Bay railroad something like three million acres, and the Canadian National railways eight hundred

thousand acres. I do not know if these figures are correct, but I believe they are approximately so. I have no doubt the railway companies themselves, including the National Railways, will do something towards colonizing these lands, but we have still twenty million acres of land held by speculators along the line of our railroads in western Canada.
Now I want to say a few words about the speculator. There was a time, Mr. Chairman, when the word " speculator " had very much the same effect on a western farmer as the holding up of a red flag to a bull. But conditions have somewhat changed. I am going to speak more particularly for the province of Manitoba, because I know the conditions that exist there to-day. All land in Manitoba today is assessed by unprejudiced valuators at its actual valuation, and there is also a wild land tax such as they have in the other Western provinces. Now no speculator is going to hold land very long and pay the taxes that he has to pay at the present time; he will be willing to sell if he can at a fair valuation. But there is a point worth considering-and I want the minister to pay attention to this: I believe that a lot of land held by speculators and offered for sale ought to be fixed at a special price for a certain number of years so that if we had an influx of settlers it would not immediately raise the price of that land, as we know often occurs when the demand increases.
Now I do not know that I have very much more to say. I am not going to elaborate any plan of settling those lands. There is an association at the present time that is willing to undertake some of the work. I cannot say much as to the capabilities of the promoters; perhaps the minister will look into that matter and see whether or not the scheme is worth putting through; but I do know there is such a corporation or association making an attempt to settle vacant lands at the present time. I hope the government will devise some well considered scheme whereby the settler who is seeking land will obtain land that is suitable for him, and get every chance to make good under proper conditions. I believe in the future of this great land. I know that the people on our side of the House have stressed, and naturally perhaps, the hardships and the vicissitudes, to a very large extent, of farm life. I know the conditions which have existed and I can appreciate the suffering,

Supply-Immigration
and perhaps hardship, which has prevailed during the last few years; but I can look back and recall that we have had good times in the three Prairie provinces. As I have already said, I am speaking for the Prairie provinces because that is the only part of Canada I am well acquainted with. Let me say that I believe there is a great future for this country of ours. We have a virile and energetic population, we have great natural resources; and the climatic conditions, with all its faults, are just as good as are to be found in the great majority of other lands. Then why should we lose hope? I for one intend more and more to look with hope to the future, believing that there are better days in store, and that some of us who are now living will yet see good and prosperous times in this Dominion of Canada.

I really think that immigration to Canada has now reached the point where it is no longer a question of getting people on the land but a question of keeping them there. I, for one, do not favour the sort of immigrant who wears a sheepskin coat unless he has a better one some place else. Of course, we have to have sheepskin coats and we all wear them at home sometimes; but by that reference I mean the class of people who go upon the land, but whose standard of living is lower than that of others who are already located there, and that is low enough. Such a policy would be a good thing for Canada rather than one of an opposite nature that would work to her final detriment. Because my own opinion is that the difficulty with the Canadian farmers has been that their standard of life has not been high enough. They have been willing to work long hours and to receive from their investment far less return than any other class of people; and if those immigrants who come to Canada are willing to work longer hours and receive less pay than the existing farmers are, then the condition of affairs instead of being improved will rapidly be rendered worse.
The minister has spoken in favour of bringing a large number of children to Canada; he has pronounced himself in favour of further developing child immigration. If those children were very carefully selected and came from the rural parts of the Old Land there might be something to be said in favour of such a policy, but in the past a great many children that have been brought from Britain have come not from the country but from the city,
and they were not always carefully selected either. They were brought out here and placed in homes where sometimes they did not have a very nice time but where, on the other hand, they did not return very much value for their keep. The result in most cases has been that between the ages of seventeen and twenty they have drifted into the cities and, not being experts or skilled in any certain line, and not having a very excellent education-possibly not as much as, or at all events not any more than, any other class-they have helped to form bread lines when such were needed; and then the country that helped to bring them out here has had to keep them. It would seem that we have come to a time in the history of our country when we must be very careful about further immigration. Agriculture is no longer an occupation that poor people can afford to engage in. Many people would like to farm but cannot afford it; it is too much of a luxury.
Do you know that old Ontario, with which I am quite familiar-it is the only part of Canada with which I am familiar- is losing its rural population at a truly alarming rate. The condition is one that we should all try to understand if we love Canada. Many a time in the past I have wondered, when we were spending thousands and hundreds of thousands-yes, millions-of dollars to bring immigrants from the Old Land and settle them in the West, why that same encouragement was not held out to the young men and women of old Ontario, to say nothing of the young men and women of Quebec and the maritime provinces. Why were they not given the same opportunity as that accorded to those who came from other countries? Do you know that in my own riding of Southeast Grey and the ridings that touch upon it- South Bruce, Wellington, Dufferin and North Simcoe-we have lost from the farms over 18,000 people since 1911, and so it would seem to me-

Is it not possible those people went to the Northwest, because, as I understand it many of the people have come from the various districts to which the hon. member has alluded?

It is quite likely that before 1911 a number of them did; but

western conditions have not been so splendid for farming: that there has been a very-great trend from the East to the West. Rather is it a fact that those who were lucky enough to leave the West have come back to the East. And so I think my hon. friend's explanation is scarcely applicable this time; I think they have not to any con-sirable extent gone upon the land elsewhere. This I know to be true. I went to some little trouble to find out how many women and children used to live on a tract of 2,000 acres of which my father's farm of 150 acres forms a part, and fifteen years ago there were sixty-five women and girls on that much land. To-day there are about twenty-three and of the number mentioned only about four or five live on land elsewhere. Taking that as a guide I would say that not a very great number are living on the land in other places. Rather than spend any lavish sum of money to bring other people to Canada it would be well for this Parliament to bend every energy it has towards making farming conditions liveable for its own citizens.

I am afraid the minister who has charge of the immigration policy of this country has laid down for us only half a policy. He has outlined the course the Government is going to pursue with regard to the encouragement of further immigration to Canada; but I failed to gather from his remarks that he had any very definite plans with regard to the discouragement of undesirable immigrants. I have, perhaps, more particularly in mind a movement on foot by our transportation companies to bring large immigration into this country. Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific, on May 3 urged that greater immigration should start forthwith. As he is a transportation man, to my mind, his only motive for urging this would be, of course, to get transportation, and, perhaps, it would not worry the Canadian Pacific very much what class of immigration came to this country, provided that the Canadian Pacific got the fares.
As hon. members are well aware, we have in our large centres many people who come from central European countries, and at the present time a large number of people in central European countries want * to come to our shores. I disagree with the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) in his view that these people want to come to Canada to settle on the land. My experience has been that they drift very

quickly into the large centres, and the result is that they take hold of the rougher class of work in those centres and deprive our English, Irish and Scotch Canadians of the opportunity of doing that work. They are able to do this largely because their mode of living is so much cheaper than is the mode of living of the average Canadian, and to my mind, it is going to be a question with the average Canadian labourer whether or not he is going to get down to their standard of living if he is going to compete with them on the labour market of Canada.
What do you find in the city of Toronto -"Toronto the good", as it is very often called? You find that 50 per cent of the cases that are in the municipal wards of our hospitals are those of people of foreign extraction who have no intention of staying in this country. We also find in our jails and penitentiaries not quite that percentage of people of foreign extraction. I would like very much to have heard from the minister some concrete suggestion or policy on the part of the Government towards the discouragement of this class of immigration.
A month or so ago when we were discussing the Speech from the Throne, I made some suggestions in this House in this connection, and with your permission, Sir, I will repeat them now. We recognise that the average English, Irish or Scotch Canadian labourer is, as a rule, a man who wants to have a stake in the country, who intends to stay here and to raise a family. In my riding, which, perhaps, contains the largest number of the class of people I have in mind, these people out in the suburbs of our great city are working nights, holidays, Saturday afternoons and sometimes Sundays in order to build a little two or three-roomed shack to cover themselves, paying for the lot; and when they go back to their day's work, what do they find? They find that they have to compete with these aliens, and at the end of the year they have to face a tax in this country for the little bit of land and the house that they have. They find also, if they are moderately prosperous, that they are subject to a provincial and, perhaps, even a federal tax. The same condition does not obtain with the foreigners right in the centre of our large cities, for this reason. They, as hon. members know, herd together in houses. I have known houses to contain upwards of twenty of these people, and their conditions of living are such that they are not under the
