same expense as are our Canadian labourers.
During the discussion on the Speech from the Throne, I suggested that it might be tvell, if it were at all possible, for this Government to bring down legislation which would tend to tax transient aliens who want to come to our shores and stay here for a little while until they make a little money on which they can return to the countrv which gave them birth and, perhaps, spend the rest of their days there. If they intend to stay here, I would gladly welcome them; but if they intend to stay here, they must become Canadians. On the night that it was reported that Lord Kitchener was drowned, I remember seeing twenty or thirty of these people-and this will give the committee an idea of the British spirit imbibed by these Serbians, Bulgarians, Albanians and Greeks -who immediately they heard the news, rushed out and procured three kegs of beer, and they had a celebration because Lord Kitchener was drowned.

All of these people were supposed to be in Kapuskasing camp and other places. Were they not interned? How could they possibly be in Toronto at that time when the law declared that they had to be interned?
They were interned in Toronto.

The hon. gentleman, (Mr. Jacobs), I think knows a little more about conditions in Canada at that time than to suggest that. Large numbers of them were not interned. Our alien enemies, I will admit, were interned; but does my hon. friend contend for a moment that Serbians were alien enemies at that time?
The hon. gentleman, I think, referred to Bulgarians.
Yes, I referred to Bulgarians but many Bulgarians were not interned. It was only the dangerous ones who were interned at that time.
They were interned in Toronto.

The subject of immigration is a very large one, and not only is it exceedingly interesting, but it is natural that there should be, in this House as well as out of it, a variety of views as to the best methods and, indeed, as to the desirability, of promoting it, as well as concerning the sources from which immigrants to Canada should be drawn. I have frequently stated that in my judgment immigration to Canada is needed, and badly needed, and I cordially support the minister (Mr. Stewart) and the Government in the efforts they may make to bring to our shores immigrants of a desirable type who will go on the land and in time become adapted to our Canadian institutions, get our Canadian spirit, and be assimilated into this Dominion as good citizens of it. I do not think that we can have too many immigrants of that type. In the discussion this evening a good deal has been said regarding the need of adding to our agricultural population, and, in order to do that successfully, of improving the conditions surrounding agriculture. To my mind that is a very essential thing in connection with the whole subject of immigration. Without doubt at all, the best immigration officer, the best immigration agent you can have in the Dominion is the contented settler whom you bring to these shores. Experience, I believe, has shown that. If we bring to Canada the Scotsman, the Englishman, the Irishman, the Scandinavian, or the man from the United States, when he comes here and gets located and finds conditions onerous, when he finds he is not accorded the welcome which perhaps he thought he should have, what is the effect upon him? He writes home to his friends and gives them the impressions he has formed of the country to which he has come. He recounts to them the experience he has had in Canada, and they are influenced accordingly. Consequently I say that the best immigration agent you can have in Canada is the contented, happy and prosperous settler. For that reason, the conditions that make agriculture prosperous and that enable those who are engaged in it to succeed are of 
the very highest importance. The minister and the Government will be taking altogether too narrow a view of the question of their energies and efforts are confined alone to the expenditure of so many hundreds of thousands of dollars in this or that country for the purpose of inducing people to come to Canada. That is altogether too narrow a view to take up this important question. I believe that efforts directed within the Dominion along the lines I have indicated, as well as along the lines suggested by a good many of my friends from this side of the House, are just as important and essential to a successful and practical policy of immigration, as is the securing of good agents and sending them abroad. There has been a good deal said in the House by some of my hon. friends around me as to the dreadful condition that agriculture is in to-day in this country. It may be that some hon. members think the picture is overdrawn, and perhaps at times we are inclined to stress that aspect too much. But the facts that were pointed out by the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) to-night should not be lost on the Government or on the House. It is a fact that in the finest agricultural counties of the province of Ontario there has been an actual and very serious decline in the rural population in the last ten years. Indeed, not only in the last ten years, but in previous decades, has that occurred. My hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) suggested that possibly those farmers descended of sturdy Scottish stock, in the old counties of Ontario, the Bruces, the Middlesexes, the Hurons and the Greys, had gone to Western Canada. Some of them have gone; but that does not account by any means at all for the decline in the population there. And I will make this prediction to my hon. friends from the province of Quebec, that as time goes on they will find the same condition obtaining in that province. We have had a tremendous growth in our city population in the last decade. There are certain causes that conduce to that. I am not at present going to discuss the fiscal question, but I do hold most firmly that the fiscal policy of Canada, the policy of protection that we have practised in this country, has been the greatest single agency in retarding the development of agriculture in Canada. If you are going to make agriculture prosperous you cannot igiore these facts. We have proceeded in Canada on the assumption that we should be largely an industrial

Supply-Immigration
people, and our policy for the last forty years has been directed to that end. What are the fruits of that policy? What are the fruits of it in Ontario, where it has been in full bloom and effect? Its fruits have been a tremendous increase in your city population and a decline in rural population; and that will foil''- inevitably in a cauntry such as Canada is, at this stage of its development. I know that the conditions in the West are in many cases onerous and difficult. We may a's well frankly recognize the fact that there are difficulties and handicaps to the success of agriculture in Western Canada, although it has progressed with tremendous development in the last thirty years. But let me point out to hon. members that the greatest single factor in promoting the development of agriculture in Western Canada in the last thirty or forty years, and in attracting people to that part of the country, were the cheap fertile lands available there. The people were looking for cheap lands. Our immigration agents could go to Europe, to the United States, and advertise the fact, as they did: You can get 160 acres of the finest land you wish to fix your eyes upon in Western Canada for $10. That was the lodestone that drew people to Western Canada. What are the conditions to-day? Our homestead lands are practically a thing of the past, and the immigrant to-day to that portion of the Dominion must pay from $10 to ,$25 an acre for land. Consequently that has narrowed the area from which our immigrants can be drawn.
The questions of freight rates and tariff as far as the West is concerned, Mr. Chairman, are pressed upon the House and the country by my hon. friends around me not because of purely selfish local reasons, but because the proper solution of those questions is essential to the development of our agricultural industry; and I would point out to my hon. friends from Ontario, and particularly to the hon. gentleman who preceded me in this debate, that if your factories there are to be kept running you must have a market for their output. When did our manufacturing industry develop at its greatest speed, when did it find its greatest prosperity? When people were flowing into western Canada by the hundreds of thousands and that country was opening up at a rate never known before. If our manufacturing industry is to continue to develop, you must lay the foundation and create the conditions that will keep the country prosperous.
What is the position of western Canada so far as its products are concerned? We are fortunate at the present time in that Russia, that great competitor of ours in supplying wheat to Europe, is out of the market. Bad for Russia, but good for us. In 1914 Russia exported 175,000,000 bushels of wheat to the western countries of Europe. And Russia will again be a factor in that market. Therefore I say to the House and to the Minister of Immigration that to have a permanently successful policy of immigration one of the vital factors is to reduce our cost of production in agriculture so that we may successfully compete with other countries in the markets of the world. Consequently in this whole question these issues to my mind are involved, and they are vital issues.
A good deal has been said to-night about our immigrants from central Europe. I wish to say a word for the people whom we brought from that part of the world fifteen, twenty or twenty-five years ago. My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) informed the House that 18 per cent of the undergraduates in the University of Manitoba were of foreign birth. Without doubt in twenty-five years' time the de-cendants of those people who came from Europe in their sheepskin coats twenty-five years ago will be among the leaders in our professional life. Is that an undesirable type of settler to bring to this country? I submit not. The Slav is one of the most adaptable of our immigrants. He can be assimilated as quickly at any rate as the immigrant of any other nationality, for his temperament is such that he quickly responds to his environment. While I agree with the observations made by some hon. members that it is unwise to open our gates full width to these people, I do submit that we can take a considerable number of wisely selected settlers of that type and they will prove a useful asset to the Dominion. I hope my hon. friend, the minister, will not overlook that in his plans for promoting immigration. Without doubt we can also secure settlers of a very desirable type from the Scandinavian countries, from the Old Land and from the United States.
But when we bring those people to this country, let us do a little bit more for them than we have done in the past in holding out the hand of welcome to them. That is a suggestion I would offer to the minister. I do not know what plans he may have to carry out that idea, but I do
Supp ly-Immigra tion

know it has often happened in the past that we have brought immigrants from the United States and from Europe who naturally were entirely unacquainted with conditions here, and far too frequently they have been the prey of the exploiter who has traded upon their ignorance in order that he might enrich himself.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that what we need is more population. It is the only way by which our taxation and our railroad problems will be ultimately solved. The Minister of Immigration has a position of the greatest responsibility in that respect. I am glad to say, Mr. Chairman, that knowing the minister as I have for a great many years, I have full confidence in his ability, his desire and his intention to make a success of this very important work.
There is one other suggestion I have to make to the minister. Our immigration statistics give a very full record of the number of people who come to Canada but we have no record, so far as I am aware, of the people who leave Canada and where they go to. I am informed that for the expenditure of a few thousand dollars a year this information could be secured, and in view of the importance of the question I would impress upon the minister the desirability of his department taking the necessary steps to secure such records. If we study the census statistics for the last decade we find that something like a million and a quarter people have gone somewhere who should be in this Dominion. Where have they gone, and why have they gone? Are not these questions of the greatest importance if we are going to handle this problem in an intelligent manner?
Like my hon. friend from Brandon, I have great faith in the future of Canada. We have a great country, but in order to assure its complete development there must be the fullest co-operation among all sections of our people, and if we work with determination for that goal there is little doubt that success will be ours.
This vote is probably as important as any in the whole department that the minister presides over. I trust that when he comes back to the House another session he will have a year of progress to report, and that in the meantime his department and the Government will make every honest legitimate effort possible to bring to our shores the class of people that we stand so badly in need of to-day.

We have heard a great many facts during the debate this evening,
[Mr. Crerar.J
but there are a few that have not been touched upon. This question goes back a great many years. We have been trying to build this Canada of ours for some twenty years, but during that period we have increased our population only by a little over 3,000,000. During the last ten years, as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has just told us, we have lost 1,500,000 people. Now, from what part of the country have those people gone? They have gone from the land. The whole policy for years past has been to people the land; the whole cry has been "Back to the land." And what do we find at the present day? In Ontario, the province of mixed farming, the province nearest the home market, there are no less than 5,000 vacant farms. I would be the last to try to stop immigration into this country when we are ready for it; when we can welcome it; when we can find a place for it. But what is our position? Never before in the history of our country has our financial position been so difficult; never before has there been so much unemployment. I want to point out that there is a very close relationship between unemployment and the condition of the farms. If the conditions on the farms were economically sound there would not be enough men in the ranks of the unemployed to go round. The whole trend of our immigration policy has been to bring people into the country to go on the land, but what is the good of bringing them in and having them go on the farms if they do not stay there? One would think, from some things that are said, that the people on the farms and those in the city belong to a different class. If the conditions are better in one place than they are in the other, the people will naturally drift from one to the other. I would like to make mention, for a moment of those people from Central Europe who were mentioned by an hon. member here a moment ago. It has often occurred to me that when these people are brought into Canada to go on the land they are good Canadian citizens, but when they drift into the cities they are usually termed enemy aliens. Yet they are one and the same people; and I assure you that no one knows the value of the dollar more than they do; when wages are good they will ask for the higher wage just as quickly as anyone else.
Just before this debate started we were given some figures in regard to the cost of soldiers' settlement. Now it has always appeared to me that instead of being known as a soldier settlement

Supply-Immigration
scheme it should have been called a land settlement scheme, because there was no attempt to settle the soldier who did not go on the land. It has cost this country, I understand, a little over $7,500,000 to administer the land settlement-money that will never come back. We also find that some 2,352 of these soldiers who went on the land, with government assistance, have failed, and abandoned their farms. We have to-day over 200,000 unemployed in Canada. I say again that there is a close connection between our unemployed and the state of agriculture. We also have marching on Ottawa at the present time some 3,000 unemployed soldiers. If conditions on the land are such that we need to have all our newcomers make their homes there, why should we to-day have 3,000 unemployed returned soldiers marching on Ottawa? We are told that the immigration from the old land is some 60 per cent less than it was last year; the reason is because the people who have come from the old land are so discontented with the present conditions that they are writing to the people they know and warning them about coming here. The only sane way of bringing people to this country is, in my opinion, to make the actual conditions in this country such that they will be the source of attraction, not the advertising medium on the other side.
We find that no less than 28,000,000 acres of arable land within 15 miles of railway in western Canada are held by speculators. We also find that there are just about as many farmers living in districts from 15 to 100 miles from the railway as there are farmers who live on lands close to the railway. Demands are continually being made for extensions of railway lines-extensions that have been promised for the last ten, twelve, or fourteen years. The people have asked for these railways; their construction has been promised, but has not been carried out. This year the Government, in their wisdom, say they are not going to spend any money cn construction. Can we, in the face of that-knowing full well that the people in the West are dependent upon railway facilities; knowing that hundreds of men are ready to pick up their belonging and leave, because of their being cut off from transportation-can we honestly ask others to come to share their fate?
I was just looking up some figures in regard to the amount of grain produced in this country per head of population, and I find that in the year 1871 we produced
some eight bushels per head; to-day with our improved machinery, we are producing no less than 42 bushels per head; yet we find the conditions of agriculture so bad that we have a continual drift from the country to the city. If that is the state of agriculture, one at once asks: who is getting the extra profit arising from that increased production?
The census that was taken last year was in many respects very complete. I noticed that the questions asked went into detail as to what was in the country in the way of stock, land, fruit, grain, poultry, and everything else, and the result was to show that the country has enormous wealth. But although they showed the enormous assets of the country, they did not show a single liability. I would like to have seen these questions asked: How much is owing to the banks? How much is owing to the mortgage company? How much is owing to back payments to the Canadian Pacific Railway? How much is owing in back payments on the school lands? If we had these figures, the people of this eastern country would be surprised to learn how little of the great wealth of western Canada is owned by the people on the land. I do not want the Minister of the Interior to think that I am criticising his position. I have a great deal of sympathy with him; I think he has one of the hardest positions to fill of any minister. But if conditions are not altered on the land so that people when they come to this country will be induced to stay on the land, then whatever plan the minister brings forward, however many people he brings to this country, his scheme is doomed to failure. There is no one who does not see the great possibilities and the enormous potential wealth of this country, but we must pay more attention to the building up of homes in this country so that the people will stay, and until we do that, it is not much good trying to bring more people here.

I see in the Edmonton
Journal of Friday, May 19, this headline: "Four Hundred Thousand Settlers for the Prairies, Shandro's Plan." I want first to show the minister that he has my sympathy, and next to assure the House that I do not intend to inflict on them any speech. Any thunder which I had has been stolen already. I rise simply because of the old saying that silence gives consent, and because one thing has been said here tonight to which I take objection. It is said that we are going to spend money to bring children from Great Britain to this country. I think it is a shame to bring out these young people, because I do not think they realize what they are going to be up against when they get here. I have seen some very sad cases of children who have been brought here from other countries and put out with people who had no children of their own, or if they had, had driven them away from home, and did not know how to use them. I want to register my protest against any such policy.
There has been a good deal said here to-night about the class of people we should encourage to come to this country. I must confess that this immigration problem and the advice offered upon it is certainly inexplicable to me. A couple of weeks ago we discussed in this House for a whole day the question of excluding two races of people from this country. I gathered from the debate that the chief objection to these people was that they were too good workers, and that Canadians could not compete with
them. That advice came chiefly from our friends from British Columbia. Now, I think there is no class of Canadians who have advocated the exclusion of that class of immigration to a greater extent than the people in Vancouver. I have here a clipping from the Vancouver Sun, and I anl totally unable to understand why that newspaper should have given utterance to such expressions as it has. It says:
What Canada needs is a tremendous influx of broad-backed, short-legged people who can get close to the work of digging a living out of the ground; and who will be satisfied with just whatever kind of a living they can dig, until, as the result of their own industry and economy they climlb up to better things.
Beavers.

If there are any hon.
members in this House who know exactly what class of people is referred to in this excerpt I will be glad to be enlightened. We have on the prairies an animal that is very short-legged, and is a good digger, but he is not popular with the people there; we call him a badger. I wonder if the editor of this paper expects the class of people he is going to bring in to dig holes for themselves to live in like badgers; it almost sounds that way. The last part of the editorial is the worst part; it is the cruelest cut of all, as we say. It reads thus:
Our present stock of Bachelors of Arts and Students of Botany can keep the Chautauqua tents well filled all summer without any assisted additions.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of the Interior told us to-night, and he spoke from his own experience, that a great many people on the prairies had been driven to the state where they had to be put into homes for the feeble-minded because of the lonesome conditions on the prairies. When the prairie people try to mitigate that condition and hold Chautau-quas for the entertainment of the people that is the kind of drivel we have from the Vancouver Sun. Now for the enlightenment of the committee let me state that the Premier of Alberta had a statement prepared last year showing the amount collected in amusement taxes in the cities, towns, villages and rural districts of the province, and this will show just how much amusement the people in the rural districts get. In the cities the per capita tax collected was 92 cents; in the rural districts it was 6 cents. Is not that a sufficient answer to the Vancouver Sun?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon; he is right.

I have been up and down so often that I am a little bit like the young Scotchman who came from the Old Country. His first experience was not very good, and he worked about fifteen hours a day. On one occasion, he said he was going upstairs, and he was so sleepy that he fell against the stairs and relapsed into slumber. On awaking he did not know whether he was going to bed or getting up. At this late hour I am not going to make any extended remarks on this important question, save as to foreigners and the kind of settlers they make. I would like to speak briefly on that subject. Those who have had experience of the settlers coming from European countries, as well as those coming from the United States, must have been struck with the fact that they are splendid settlers. Allusion has been made to some foreigners who, it was said, appeared to be disloyal at the time Lord Kitchener was drowned. I can refer to a case where a number of young children of foreign birth, having a new teacher come to their district, after a few days went to him and said they had been accustomed to sing "God Save the King" when the school was opened. That was the kind of new settlers they were. Just one more reference to that. Some two or three years ago, I believe it was, a very important educational conference was held in the city of Winnipeg, and there were brought from the United States two of the greatest educational experts in the land. One of these was an Italian who had come to the United States some twenty years before with his father and mother as an Italian immigrant. That shows the progress that some of these people will make.
In the budget speech this afternoon, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) made a
remark that struck me. During this session I have been watching to see whether this House fully realises the seriousness of the condition of agriculture, and I was struck by his remark to the effect that he was afraid that the country did not fully realise the seriousness of our financial situation. In answering a question, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) stated that those whom he thought of bringing out would be settled in eastern Canada. I just wondered, and I feel like asking now what kind of settlers the minister proposes settling in western Canada. I differ with some of my colleagues in their attitude towards bringing immigration to western Canada. Conditions in the West are as bad as has been stated, and while I am not going to harry the House by reiterating them, I will say this. While some have prophesied that some farms are going to go back to grass; that they will cease to be cultivated, in the main that is not so. Those farms must be cultivated. Many of those who are on the farms at the present time must give up farming. Some gave up last year; some will give up this year; nothing that this Government can do will save them; but those farms are to the speculator, to the incoming settler, to those who have money, a very desirable purchase. Think what it means to see a farm that could have been sold for $60 an acre two years ago, offered for $30 an acre to-day. That is the case however, and a man who has the money will buy such a farm, and it will be worked. Even though it may not be profitable this year, it will be cultivated and kept up. That is one reason why I would urge upon the minister the necessity of bringing in, as far as he possibly can, settlers who have money. That is one class of settlers that the West needs. Another class is the class to which he has referred. Many farmers in the West are short of help, and yet they cannot afford to pay the wages of the men who are available and of the girls who are available for housework. Help in the house is undoubtedly very hard to get and very high in price when obtained. If girls, as well as boys, of, say fifteen years of age, were brought to Canada they would be well and gladly received, and they would be a great help in developing the West. Reference has been made to the bad treatment that some of these have received in the past. I have no doubt that occasionally such may have occurred; in fact, I know of some cases where it did occur; but in the main, they would be well treated; the boys would be given an opportunity of learning farming, and in u



Supply-I mmigra tion
few years when conditions became better, they would become farmers themselves and would be very desirable farmers.
In these times of economic stress, I think I might strike a hopeful note in this. The financial and industrial greatness of Great Britain was laid in a time of low prices, a time which we are now approaching, just after what were called the Napoleonic wars. The United States had the same experience, their greatness was laid after the Civil War. We are coming to that time; the price of farm products has gone down very materially and other prices must come down. Therefore, while conditions are very bad, we cannot afford to lie down on the job. Agriculture must proceed.
While I had a few other points on which I wished to speak, as the hour is getting very late, I will not speak further to-night.

speechtext: Four or five members came to me and asked me to notify them when these estimates would be brought up, and I certainly was quite convinced that I had covered the whole list. 1 am sure my hon. friend understands that I would not have in any way endeavoured to deceive him.
I do not doubt the minister.

There is one phase of this subject in reference to which I should like to say a few words. I cannot profess to give this committee any real information upon the subject of either agriculture or immigration, and I do not intend to do that; but there is one matter in reference to immigration to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister and also of the members of the committee. I do not start with the least bit of faultfinding in regard to the devotion of the energies of this country towards filling up

Supply-I mmig ration
the great West. The policy has been a good one, a necessary one, and I am in entire accord with the remarks made recently in the House by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), when he spoke of immigration placed along the lines of our western railways, affording, at least a partial solution of the very grave question which confronts the country at the present day.
At the same time, I think the House will be broad enough in its view to realize that some consideration ought to be devoted to the provinces down by the sea. I do not feel that members of the House will consider that we are obtruding our views on the country, but will rather receive any remarks made on the subject in the light of a presentation of the hopes of those provinces that they may yet be admitted to share in the prosperity which we hope will ultimately come to this country, as a result of wisely selected immigration. Will hon. members consider for a moment that immi-' gration to the maritime provinces is almost nil. In my own province there is immigration of a valuable character. In the northern part of the province, where the forest has been invaded and replaced by settlers, we are adding to our population. That applies to several counties. That immigration has given settlers of a fine type who are splendid agriculturists. But they are simply coming over the line from the province of Quebec. We are glad to have them, of course; they are adding to our population. But as hon. members will see, that represents no addition to the population of the Dominion. It is only, so to speak, a shifting of ballast. Whether they are in the province of New Brunswick or in the province of Quebec, they are doing equally valuable work; but they do not add to the productive power of the country. There is only a change in location.
We have running through the province of New Brunswick, almost diagonally, the Transcontinental Railway. That railway, from Edmundston down to Moncton, runs through what is practically nonproductive territory. I will not say that none of the land in that territory is occupied, but a very large part of it is not. Rails have been laid there at great cost and are not affording any local development. There are certainly in the province districts much more fertile, I believe, than that territory to be. But you must realize that every question of immigration in New Brunswick is practically met by conditions that
138i
differ from those in the West, and are more difficult perhaps to deal with. In the West, as I understand it, there is no clearing of the land to be done. The land has to be broken, but not cleared. In the maritime provinces, on the other hand, you have to clear the land; and when you ask a settler to go there, though he travels a shorter distance to reach that part of the country, he is faced with a greater immediate task in turning the portion of land he settles upon to profitable use. It is not all settlers that can come with money enough to buy farm land that has already been worked. Many of them, a quite desirable class, will face difficulties and hardships; but having broken up the land, in time they can make use of its latent fertility.
I want to suggest two things to the minister. One of them is that it might be found worth while to give to the proper class of settlers some sort of bonus for settling in Eastern Canada. Some compensation might be given them for bringing-land into such a condition as will make it equivalent to the state of the land in Western Canada. I do not think that this is unfair, because, unless we are to have our population greatly increased in the maritime provinces, I fear we shall gradually dry up. I do not think that we shall altogether blow away, but at all events there will be no growth there. It is desirable to promote and stimulate growth in the maritime provinces, because they are useful, in the things they possess, in the rounding out of the whole Dominion. In the second place, that policy might be considered from the standpoint of the railways, in which the Government has so largely invested in that part of the country. It is worth while to settle people along these lines of railway and thereby add to their earning power in that quarter.
What I have to say is not affected in any degree by considerations of political partisanship. I can, I think, quite fairly include every preceding government in about the same condemnation. Every government in its immigration policy has seen only the western part of Canada and no other portion. As I say, I do not altogether complain, nor do I wish to rob the West of anything. The East does not wish to do that; but we do say that the immigration policy ought to be for the whole of the Dominion, and that Eastern Canada should not be neglected or overlooked. I would ask the minister to pay some special attention, through his agen-
Supply-Immigration

cies overseas, to the end of securing for the Eastern provinces, not the whole of the immigration that is coming, of course, but a reasonable percentage of it. Let us help all the Dominion and in doing so realize that population is just as valuable in the East as it is in the West. And considering the history of Canada, considering the growth of the Western provinces, and the fact that, judged by the scale of representation in this House, the West is going ahead magnificently while the East is not able to hold its own, I think the question is well worth the careful attention of the Government if bringing to Eastern Canada some relief from the unfortunate condition into which it is falling for lack of population. The class of people required for the East would, of course, be different from the class that can be assimilated and probably be made happy in some portions of the West. For the East we must have people who are either accustomed to farming or else are of such an age that they can be broken into farming. And we must have them either of the English or of the French type. It is no use asking the East, with its slender population, to assimilate a large population from Central Europe. I would suggest immigrants from France, Great Britain, or the Scandinavian countries.
Do you object to German immigration into New Brunswick?
My hon. friend can have the German immigration and the German measles together. We want none of them in New Brunswick.
Surely the grand old United Empire Loyalists stock would stand up against German immigration.

I am glad my hon. friend has such confidence in that stock, but perhaps he would be surprised to discover how few of the original settlers of New Brunswick are now represented in the public and the commercial life of that province. The stock has gone to the United States and to the West of Canada and has done very good work. But it is not a question of old or young Loyalist stock. We do not want Germans. We shall do very well without them. It has cost the life-blood of 60,000 Canadians to prevent them from dominating the world, and we shall extend no invitation to them to settle in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island.

Would the minister assure us that even if this item does carry a general discussion may be permitted, at a later date? I am not particularly interested, but my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Maybee) and hon. members from the Pacific coast who are interested are not in the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) :
speechtext: Yes, there will be some supplementary estimates which will afford an opportunity for general discussion.

Has the hon. minister
given any consideration to the advisability of putting the fisheries under a deputy who will have sole charge? It is a subject of very great importance with us in the maritime provinces and with our friends on the Pacific coast, and it seems to me that the country cannot give too much intensive consideration to the development of our fisheries and to the marketing of our fish. A predecessor of my hon. friend, now the Chief Justice of New Brunswick; did much during the war period to have people, as far west as Toronto at least, taught to consume more of the products of our fisheries. Fish is a good, palatable, wholesome food, and it seems to me much may be done by providing the means of transportation to bring the fish to our people inland while it is still fresh, and so teach them to rely on it as a substitute for other forms of food which are more expensive and cannot really replace fish as a diet for mental and bodily efficiency. To do that it seems to me you need to appoint an official who can devote his whole time to the fisheries alone as a separate department.

Since I took
charge of the department I have received many resolutions from associations and individuals making the same suggestion. Of course, I have not had sufficient time to make up my mind as to the desirability of the suggested change, and, furthermore, as strict economy has to be practised, the formation of another department might involve expenditure which would not be altogether welcome. But the matter is engaging my attention.

I am very glad indeed to hear that the hon. minister is interested in this subject. The fisheries on both our coasts are of great importance. As has

Supply-Fisheries
already been pointed out, the fishermen on the Pacific coast have long felt that the fisheries there would be much more rapidly developed if a separate department were created and placed under a deputy minister. I am sure the minister will find on further investigation that the little extra expenditure required will be well spent and give excellent returns.

I must admit that
this suggestion seems to have the support of all those who are interested in our fisheries.

Item agreed to.
Building fishways and clearing rivers, $40,000.

I come from an inland district where probably we do not have a chance to buy the excellent fish that is obtainable along the coast. However, we have fish commonly called suckers that come up our streams in the spring. While the water is cold they are somewhat of a delicacy to people who have never had an opportunity of tasting other fish. I live on a little stream called White Mud river, and on it there are two dams, one in the neighborhood of Gladstone and the other in the neighbourhood of Westbourne, built by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in order to hold back the water for their railway tanks. For the last eight or ten years at least we have been trying to get fishways in those dams so the suckers may get upstream to the shallow water and spawn as nature intended. While the war was on I myself sent two or three telegrams to the food controller and the fisheries department, but by the time any move was made it was too late. The fish come up to those dams and in a short time most of them die, the survivors returning to the lake. We were assured that before the next fishing season the necessary slides would be put in. That has been the promise year after year, and I am informed that this season the fish have died in large quantities and the stench along the river is almost unbearable. There is no reason why those fish should not be allowed to get up into shallow water, and there is no reason why the settlers along the streams should not get the benefit of this fish diet. While the water is cold the settlers eat large numbers of these suckers. I would impress upon the minister that we want those fish to come up our streams. We do not see any reason why the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should have the privilege of erecting dams to the detriment
of the fish and of the settlers who are thus deprived of what is a very valuable article of diet.

I may inform my hon. friend that under the law it is possible to compel the owners of such dams to provide fishways, and if they fail to do so we can perform the necessary work at their expense. I can asure my hon. friend that the matter will be considered by the department, and if possible something will be done.

In this connection
there is a matter I have already called to the attention of the minister, and I cannot help but think that his information in regard to it is not correct. It is with respect to a dam on the Salmon river, so-called, in my riding in Victoria county, New Brunswick. This river derived its name from the fact that so many salmon used to go up it. I am advised there is a dam on that river at the present time with no fishway. The former dams that went out with the spring freshet were provided with proper fishways. I received a reply from the minister that this river dries up in the summer. If it had not been such a serious thing I would have been amused, for I know the river well. It is navigable for lumber drives for at least fifty miles, and I could not imagine there was ever a time when the water would be so shallow that the largest salmon could not come up stream. There might be times in a very dry summer when the water would get low, but at such times the water is very low in all our rivers. However, I cannot believe that the information is serious; I cannot believe that the water gets so low in the Salmon River that the salmon cannot go up. Of course, the mill owner, the man who builds the dam to hold the water, does not like to put in a fish-way. In order to do that, he must waste a certain amount of water. I think, however, the regulations might be such that when the water is very low this fish-way might be closed. It is when the water is high in the spring that the fish go up. I would strongly urge on the minister the necessity of putting a fish-way in this dam on the Salmon river. As I say, the mill owner will put up all kinds of objections; but the statement that the river goes practically dry is too absurd to be entertained.

I am informed that
there have been fish-ways in that dam for many years, but that no salmon have been going up.

I can hardly credit
that, either. I have no doubt the minister has that information, but I cannot help thinking it has been given to him by some interested person. This river was called the Salmon river because of the fact that at one time it was well stocked with salmon. It is a tributary of the St. John river. There is a hatchery near the mouth of this river which we are maintaining at large expense for the hatching of salmon fry to supply these streams with fish. I believe that a quantity of these fry have been put into the Salmon river. I would urge upon the minister the necessity of making a thorough investigation and getting information upon this subject from a reliable source.

I shall be glad to do
anything in that respect.

I would call attention to
the fact that these fish chutes do not fill the bill, if I may use a colloquial expression. I have received complaints from the reeve of a municipality out west; it is evident that the conditions are such as have been described by the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Milne). Thousands of fish are unable to get up and die at the bottom of the chute. I remember writing to the game guardian about the matter, and the reply I got was that the Canadian Pacific had fulfilled all the conditions of the law. I think something more might be done if the minister could point the way toward making these fish chutes more easily ascended by the fish. These prairie fish do not jump like the salmon, as you can readily realize; and that is one of the difficulties they have to contend with. Th"-are good food; they are relished by the people of the prairies, and it is a pity that so many of them die every spring, being unable to get up over these chutes.

We have the same complaint to make against the Canadian National at Dauphin. There is a dam across the river there which the fish are unable to get over. Several requests in regard to the matter have been made at the Department at Ottawa, but nothing has ever come of it. When the minister is looking into this matter, I hope he will not forget Dauphin.
We will at least make the Canadian National railways observe the law.

There is one other matter to which I wish to refer. I know that the provisions of the Canadian law with regard to the pollution of streams by mill owners with sawdust and other refuse material are very well enforced. That is the case in Carleton county, and the minister assures us that steps are being taken to have the law observed by the mill owners in Victoria county. What jurisdiction have we over the mills situated on the American side of the St. John river where the St. John is the boundary between the United States and Canada?
We have no authority there.
What are the regulations in the United States.
The authorities in the United States take action only upon petition signed by a certain number of citizens in the locality asking for it. I understand that the regulations there are very inadequate.
The petition must be signed by residents of the United States?
Yes.
Then we have no recourse?
No.
Is there not an international fisheries commission which could take up a matter of this kind?
There is no such body at the present time.
There is an international joint commission.
Yes, but that does not apply to fisheries.

I would like to see something done in this connection. While our fishery guardians are enforcing the law on the Canadian side, the mill owners on the United States side are dumping sawdust in the river, and there is little to induce our own mill owners to observe the law. In fact, the sawdust floats down and destroys the salmon fishing in that river. If there is any possible way of taking the matter up with the United States with a view to concerted action, I would urge that that be done.

Supply-Fisheries

The department is in communication at the present time with the American authorities on the subject. Item agreed to.
Fisheries-to assist in the conservation and development of deep-sea fisheries, and of the demand for fish, $25,000.
May we have a brief explanation of that item?

A publicity and marketing division of the department has been established. A press bulletin is prepared monthly and distributed to the newspapers throughout Canada. Specially illustrated articles have also been supplied to household periodicals. As a result, the press has never been so much alive to the great asset Canada has in her fisheries. There are competitions in writing articles on the fisheries, engaged in by the school children of the country. Photographers are engaged to picture the Atlantic fishing industry. The vote is to cover work along these lines.

Item agreed to.
Fish culture, $370,000.

Would the minister
give some explanation of this vote?

The increase is due to the necessity for extending the ponds for rearing young salmon in British Columbia and the Maritime provinces, and for the establishment of a retaining pond for parent salmon on the St. John river.
What value is there in this work? If I remember aright, some criticism was made by some hon. members during this session to the effect that this work was of no value whatever.

I understand that this is the only way to improve our fisheries. The result of the work of the department does not indicate that my hon. friend is right in the view which he expresses. It has been a great source of developing the fisheries. As a matter of (fact, those who are interested in the industry are asking for new hatcheries in almost all the provinces.

I live within twenty miles of one of these fish hatcheries and I never heard any complaint of its being useless. I know the lakes nearby are pretty well provided with fish, and that the hatchery is appreciated by the people.

There is a fish hatchery in the county I represent, and we believe that if it were not for that, the salmon would be depleted very rapidly. I am glad to find the increase in the vote is for the development of fish hatcheries. I do not know whether the minister has any information on the subject, but I understood there tvas a still being run in connection with one of the hatcheries in the province.
1 did not know but that the $5,000 was to provide for the still.
I am surprised there would be such a thing in my hon. friend's riding.
I did not say it was in my riding, but in the province. I did not say it was not, either.

The hon. member for Lunenburg made the statement some time ago that he would be in favour of abolishing the hatcheries entirely. I agree with that myself. I would like to see the Fisheries Department protect our fisheries a little more than they have in the past. I think the sum of $370,000 is a lot of money to spend on the development of hatcheries.

Item agreed to.

Are any fees collected for this service? Is the service self-supporting?
